00-01.title: Why We Are Starting This Series
00-01.description: Why Shincheonji doctrine needs to be examined, and the attitude and standards this series follows.
00-01.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Is it wrong to look into Shincheonji's doctrine for yourself and test it? Doesn't the Bible tell us to discern the truth?

## The Purpose of the "False Doctrine Refuted" Series

This series sets out to test the doctrine of Shincheonji Church of Jesus, the Temple of the Tabernacle of the Testimony (hereafter "Shincheonji"), against the text of the Bible and against official sources. Its aim is not to condemn Shincheonji or to attack its members.

Shincheonji says it **"teaches the Bible exactly as it is, adding nothing and taking nothing away."** It also stresses that its teaching is **"the word of revelation that cannot be heard anywhere else."** If that claim were true, there would be no reason to fear scrutiny. On the contrary, the more closely it was examined, the clearer that truth should become.

Yet when Shincheonji's doctrine is actually compared with the context of the biblical text, with the internal consistency of its own interpretations, with historical fact, and with Shincheonji's own earlier materials, contradictions surface that are hard to explain.

**This series examines those contradictions one by one, in concrete terms.**

## What This Series Will Not Do

- It will not mock or belittle Shincheonji members.
- It will not claim that established churches are perfect.
- It will not pressure anyone to leave or try to stir up fear.
- It will not draw conclusions from unverified rumors or personal anecdotes alone.
- It will not distort Shincheonji's claims into a weaker version in order to knock them down.

## What This Series Will Do

- Summarize Shincheonji's claims as accurately as possible.
- Read the Bible verses Shincheonji relies on within their context.
- Check whether the same principle of interpretation is applied consistently to other passages.
- Compare Shincheonji's past materials with its present explanations.
- Examine whether Shincheonji's account matches the historical record.
- Offer questions that help readers judge for themselves.

## The Standards of Examination

This series examines Shincheonji's doctrine by four standards.

1. **Textual test** — Does the interpretation arise directly from the biblical text and its surrounding context?
2. **Consistency test** — Is the same principle of interpretation applied equally to other passages?
3. **Historical test** — Do the people, organizations, and events Shincheonji points to match the actual record?
4. **Change test** — Do its past textbooks, sermons, and official explanations agree with what it says now?

We will not call something false simply because it "differs from the interpretation of established churches." Instead, we will point to specific logical and documentary contradictions.

## What the Bible Says About Discernment

>! Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
>! — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)

>! These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:11 (KJV)

The Bible does not tell us to accept teaching without question. The Bereans checked even Paul's words against the Scriptures every day, and the Bible calls this **"more noble."** John warns, **"believe not every spirit, but try the spirits."**

If Shincheonji's teaching is the real truth, it will only shine brighter after this kind of examination. But if examination itself is blocked by calling it "the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil" or "betrayal," it is worth asking yourself why.

---

## Summary

This series looks at Shincheonji's official claims and doctrine through sources that can be verified. It does not force a conclusion on the reader. We encourage you to compare Shincheonji's materials, the biblical text, and the historical record for yourself and reach your own judgment.

**The truth does not fear examination.**
selfCheckQuestions: Have I ever compared the doctrine I was taught with the surrounding context of the biblical text?
Is the same principle of interpretation applied consistently to other passages?
Can I find out what Shincheonji taught in the past?
Why would examining doctrine count as "the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil" or as "betrayal"?
Why should searching the Scriptures daily, as the Bereans did, be forbidden?

00-02.title: Five Standards for Testing Shincheonji Doctrine
00-02.description: We test Shincheonji's doctrine and its claims of actual fulfillment by five standards: the biblical text, consistency of interpretation, the historical record, doctrinal change, and the possibility of outside verification.
00-02.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Shincheonji and established churches both say they follow "what the Bible says." How, then, can we tell whose "what the Bible says" is right?

## Why We Need Standards for Testing

Shincheonji claims that its teaching is **"the true meaning of the Bible"** and that it is [the only denomination that has mastered even the actual fulfillment of Revelation](https://jeju.shincheonji.org/post/%EC%8B%A0%EC%B2%9C%EC%A7%80%EB%8A%94-%EC%98%A8-%EC%84%B8%EA%B3%84-%EC%A4%91-%EA%B3%84%EC%8B%9C%EB%A1%9D%EC%9D%98-%EC%8B%A4%EC%83%81%EA%B9%8C%EC%A7%80%EB%8F%84-%ED%86%B5%EB%8B%AC%ED%95%98%EB%8A%94-%EC%9C%A0%EC%9D%BC%ED%95%9C-%EA%B5%90%EB%8B%A8-%EC%8B%A0%EC%B2%9C%EC%A7%80%EC%98%88%EC%88%98%EA%B5%90-%EC%A6%9D%EA%B1%B0%EC%9E%A5%EB%A7%89%EC%84%B1%EC%A0%84-%EC%9D%B4%EB%A9%B0-%EC%B0%B8-%EC%A0%95%ED%86%B5%EC%9D%B4%EB%8B%A4-2026-05-14). Its [official website](https://www.shincheonji.org/ko/introduce/organization) also presents Chairman Lee Man-hee as the angel of Revelation 22:16.

> "God and the Bible are the ones who judge what is truly orthodox and what is truly heretical."

If these claims are true, there is no reason to fear scrutiny. This series tests them by five standards that can be applied equally to anyone.

## Related Bible Passages

>! And the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto Berea: who coming thither went into the synagogue of the Jews. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:10-11 (KJV)

>! Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
>! — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV)

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

The Bible speaks approvingly of people who check the content of a teaching rather than resting on the authority of the teacher.

## The Five Standards

### 1. Textual Test — Does the interpretation come directly from the text?

We check whether an interpretation arises directly from **the surrounding context of the biblical text**. We need to distinguish between what the text itself says and an interpretation built by stitching other verses together.

For example, saying that "mine angel" in Revelation 22:16 exists is one claim; concluding that this angel is a specific individual is another. The second requires its own proof.

### 2. Consistency Test — Is the same principle applied to other passages?

We check whether formulas such as "seed = word" or "bird = spirit" are applied consistently **everywhere** in the Bible. Applying a rule to certain verses while making exceptions for others is not a consistent principle; it is **selective application**.

### 3. Historical Test — Does it match the actual record?

Shincheonji claims that the events of Revelation took place at specific times and in specific places. That can be checked against records, news reports, court rulings, and other documents from the time. We examine whether the number of people, their positions, the sequence of events, and their dates match the explanation.

We also need to distinguish whether an event happened first and was linked to the Bible afterward, or whether it was specifically announced before it happened.

### 4. Change Test — Are past and present explanations the same?

We compare past textbooks and sermons with current explanations. Polishing the wording is one thing; changing the key figures, events, or conditions of salvation is another. If core doctrine has changed, we need to determine whether this is "food in due season" or an admission that the earlier explanation was wrong.

### 5. Outside Verification — Can it be confirmed without Shincheonji?

This is the most fundamental question. If no one could arrive at the interpretation without Shincheonji's explanation, is it "what the Bible says" or "what Shincheonji says"?

> "Shincheonji's explanation is true because the promised pastor testified to it. That man is the promised pastor because Revelation, as Shincheonji interprets it, says so."

In this structure the two claims rest on each other, so there is no independent starting point from which to verify either one.

## A Possible Objection from Shincheonji

> "You can only know the true meaning and the actual fulfillment by learning from the promised pastor, who personally saw and heard the fulfillment of Revelation."

The claim to be an eyewitness and the claim that all of that person's interpretations are accurate must be kept apart. The reasoning "you have to learn from the promised pastor to know he is the promised pastor" uses the conclusion as its premise. Like the Bereans, we should be able to check even a leader's words against the Bible and the evidence.

---

## Summary

These five standards should apply not only to Shincheonji but equally to the claims of any church or leader. When we are willing to test even the explanations we ourselves believe by the same standards, examination stops being an attack and becomes a search for the truth.

**When the standards are clear, the conclusion becomes plain on its own.**
selfCheckQuestions: Could I reach the same conclusion by reading the biblical text alone, without Shincheonji's commentary?
Do I apply the interpretive standard used for one verse equally to other, similar verses?
Can the people and events identified as the actual fulfillment be confirmed by independent sources written at the time?
If past textbooks differ from current explanations, have the changes and the reasons for them been made public?
What evidence, if discovered, would lead me to admit that the claim is wrong?

00-03.title: Is It Wrong to Check Sources About Shincheonji?
00-03.description: We examine whether it is biblically justified to treat looking at outside sources, which Shincheonji labels "the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil" and "betrayal," as forbidden.
00-03.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Shincheonji's classes forbid looking at outside sources, comparing it to eating "the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil." But does the Bible really teach us not to check our sources?

## What Shincheonji Claims

During its courses, Shincheonji strongly warns against looking at outside sources, especially material critical of Shincheonji. It usually reasons along these lines:

- Outside sources are "the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil," and eating (reading) them brings spiritual death
- Looking at critical material is itself the beginning of "betrayal"
- It is Satan's tactic for making you doubt the truth, so you must not look
- You have not learned enough yet and might get confused, so wait until after you graduate

The story of the forbidden fruit in Genesis 2–3 is often cited as the basis for this teaching.

## Related Bible Passages

>! And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
>! — Genesis 2:16-17 (KJV)

>! Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
>! — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV)

>! Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God
>! — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Tested

### 1. Does "forbidden fruit = outside sources" come from the text?

In Genesis 2–3, the forbidden fruit is the fruit of a particular tree in the Garden of Eden. In the context of the passage, it is tied to **disobedience to God's command**. The idea of "looking at outside sources" appears nowhere in the text.

Within Shincheonji's system of parable interpretation, the forbidden fruit is read as "false doctrine" or "a different teaching." But applying this reading creates a contradiction, because from the standpoint of established churches, Shincheonji is itself "a different teaching." If established churches used the same logic, "Shincheonji's teaching is the forbidden fruit."

### 2. Does the truth forbid examination?

The Bible's attitude toward truth is not "believe without question" but **"examine and discern."**

Paul urges the church in Thessalonica to "prove all things; hold fast that which is good." John says, "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits." The Bereans compared even Paul's teaching with the Scriptures, and the Bible records this with approval.

If something is the real truth, it should grow clearer the more it is examined. A teaching that can survive only by forbidding examination gives us, by that very fact, a reason to question it.

### 3. Is "look after you graduate" a reasonable request?

Shincheonji's classes say, "You haven't learned everything yet, so outside sources will only confuse you." At first glance this sounds reasonable, but the logic has problems.

- After graduation, is there really a culture of freely checking outside sources?
- If you raise questions after graduation, aren't you judged as "lacking faith"?
- In the end, doesn't "check after you've learned everything" have the same effect as "don't check"?

## A Possible Objection from Shincheonji

> "If you encounter false information before your foundation is laid, you can get confused. Of course a teacher teaches things in order."

It is reasonable for education to follow an order. But **setting an order** is different from **forbidding the sources themselves**. A university professor says, "We'll cover that topic next semester," not, "If you read another professor's book, you will die spiritually."

Genuine education should also equip students to respond logically when they meet opposing views. Cutting off opposing material at the source is not education; it is information control.

---

## Summary

The Bible does not tell us to accept teaching without question. Instead it says again and again, "prove all things," "try the spirits," "search the scriptures." Checking outside sources is not eating the forbidden fruit; it is searching the Scriptures as the Bereans did.

**Ask yourself why checking the sources feels frightening.**
selfCheckQuestions: Does the interpretation "forbidden fruit = outside sources" come directly from the text of Genesis?
What kind of response do I get when I raise questions about Shincheonji's teaching?
Have I ever freely checked outside sources after graduating?
Why should comparing teaching with the Bible, as the Bereans did, be forbidden?

00-04.title: Is a Faith That Asks Questions Wrong?
00-04.description: We look at the difference between doubt and discernment, and at what a questioning faith means biblically.
00-04.content:
## A Question to Ask First

You have probably heard the words, "Don't doubt, just believe." But is the "faith" the Bible speaks of really a matter of accepting things without asking questions?

## What Shincheonji Claims

In Shincheonji's classes, questions or doubts about doctrine are sometimes treated as something negative. Common expressions include:

- "If you doubt, you have been deceived by Satan"
- "Don't judge God's will by human thinking"
- "If your faith is weak, you won't be able to understand"
- "Believe and follow first, and you'll understand later"

When a student or member has a question, teaching like this turns the question itself into a problem of faith. Before anyone examines whether the question has merit, the attitude of asking is what gets put on trial.

## Related Bible Passages

>! Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
>! — John 20:29 (KJV)

>! If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.
>! — John 15:7 (KJV)

>! and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:11 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Tested

### 1. Are doubt and discernment the same thing?

Shincheonji tends to classify questions about doctrine as "doubt." But the "doubt" the Bible warns against and the "discernment" it encourages are different things.

- **Doubt**: unbelief that rejects God's existence or His love itself
- **Discernment**: checking whether a particular person's teaching agrees with the word of God

Thomas would not believe until he had seen the risen Jesus with his own eyes (John 20:25). Jesus rebuked Thomas, but He also **showed Himself to him directly**. He did not shut down the chance to confirm.

### 2. Is "believe and follow first" a biblical teaching?

"Believe first and you'll understand later" can sound devout. The problem is that this logic can be applied to **any teaching at all**.

Other religious groups also say, "Believe and follow first." This logic alone cannot tell us which teaching is true and which is false. Biblical faith is not blind obedience but **trust grounded in the word of God**.

>! Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
>! — Hebrews 11:1 (KJV)

The object of faith in Hebrews is God and His promises. That is different from accepting a particular person's interpretation without examining it.

### 3. What does a structure that blocks questions protect?

Healthy communities allow questions. Questions deepen understanding and give a chance to correct what is wrong. A structure that shuts down questions, by contrast, does less to protect the teaching than to **block the teaching from being examined**.

Consider these for yourself:

- When I asked a question in class, did I get an answer about the content, or was my attitude criticized?
- Was I told over and over that "you'll understand later"?
- Is it acceptable to ask the same question several times?

## A Possible Objection from Shincheonji

> "Faith means believing without seeing. Jesus Himself told Thomas, 'Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.'"

John 20:29 does say that. But in context, Jesus said these words **after showing Thomas His hands and His side**. He did not refuse to let Thomas confirm; He let him confirm, and then spoke of a higher kind of faith.

The object of this statement is also **the risen Jesus Christ**. Using it to mean that we should believe a particular person's doctrinal interpretation without examining it takes the verse out of context.

---

## Summary

The Bible does not reject a faith that asks questions. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily, Paul urged believers to prove all things, and John told them to try the spirits. Jesus did not refuse Thomas's request to confirm, either.

If the attitude of asking is put on trial before the content of the question, that may not be protecting the truth but avoiding examination.

**In the presence of real truth, a question is not a threat but an opportunity.**
selfCheckQuestions: When I asked a question about doctrine, did I get an answer about the content, or was my attitude criticized?
Doesn't the logic of "believe first" apply just as well to other religious groups?
Did Jesus refuse to let Thomas confirm, or did He show Himself to him directly?
How can I discern the truth in an environment where questions are not allowed?
sources: The Bible (KJV): John 20:25-29; John 15:7; Acts 17:11; Hebrews 11:1

01-01.title: Was the Whole Bible Written in Parables?
01-01.description: Shincheonji claims the entire Bible was written in parables. We check against the biblical text whether that claim holds up.
01-01.content:
## A Question to Ask First

If everything in the Bible is a parable, what did Jesus mean when He told His disciples He would speak to them "plainly"?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the entire Bible was written in parables and symbols. This premise is the starting point of its whole doctrinal system. Because the Bible is all parables, the reasoning goes, there must be someone who can interpret those parables.

The passage most often cited in support is Matthew 13:34-35.

>! All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.
>! — Matthew 13:34-35 (KJV)

## Reading the Passage in Context

Looking at the context of Matthew 13, this verse describes how Jesus spoke **to the multitude**. In the same chapter, Jesus explains the meaning of the parables directly to His disciples.

>! and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field. He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man;
>! — Matthew 13:36-37 (KJV)

After speaking in parables, Jesus **explained their meaning directly** to His disciples. Direct explanation, not parable, is already found within the Bible.

The Gospel of John contains an even clearer passage.

>! These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall shew you plainly of the Father.
>! — John 16:25 (KJV)

>! His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.
>! — John 16:29 (KJV)

Jesus Himself said He would speak "plainly," and the disciples confirmed that He was now speaking plainly, "and speakest no proverb."

## The Bible Clearly Contains Material That Is Not Parable

Much of the Bible is direct record, not parable.

- **Historical narrative**: Israel's history in Exodus, the dynastic records in Kings, the events of the early church in Acts
- **Law and commandments**: the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17), the laws of sacrifice (Leviticus)
- **Epistles**: Paul's letters to the churches are direct instruction dealing with concrete problems
- **Direct teaching**: in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), "Thou shalt not kill" and "Thou shalt not commit adultery" are not parables

>! But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment
>! — Matthew 5:22 (KJV)

If we read this as "the brother is a parable, and being angry is a parable too," the Bible's teaching itself falls apart.

## Summary

Matthew 13:34-35 describes how Jesus spoke in parables **to the multitude**; it is not a declaration that the whole Bible is parable. The Bible plainly contains material that is not parable: historical records, law, letters, and direct teaching. Once the premise that "the Bible is all parables" collapses, the argument that we need one unique person to interpret those parables must be reexamined as well.

**The Bible itself distinguishes between parables and plain speech.**
selfCheckQuestions: Have I read Matthew 13:34-35 for myself to see whether it is a statement about the whole Bible or a description of a specific situation?
How can the passages where Jesus spoke plainly to His disciples without parables (John 16:25, 29) be explained?
How would the meaning of Paul's epistles change if they were read as parables?
If the Ten Commandments are interpreted as parables, what do they actually end up meaning?
If the premise that "the Bible is all parables" is removed, how does that affect the doctrines built on it?

01-02.title: Are Parable Formulas the Bible's Own Method?
01-02.description: Shincheonji interprets the Bible with fixed formulas such as "seed = word" and "bird = spirit." We check whether this method comes from the Bible itself.
01-02.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Does the Bible teach us to interpret parables with fixed formulas? Or does it explain the meaning of each parable within its own context?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that there are fixed formulas for interpreting the Bible's parables. For example:

- Seed = word (the word of God, or Satan's doctrine)
- Bird = spirit (the Holy Spirit, or an evil spirit)
- Sea = the world
- Tree = a person (a leader)
- Beast = a pastor (a false pastor)

The core claim is that applying these formulas unlocks every parable in the Bible.

## How Did Jesus Explain His Parables?

In Matthew 13, after telling a parable, Jesus explained its meaning to His disciples directly, **within its context**.

>! Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower. When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.
>! — Matthew 13:18-19 (KJV)

Here Jesus did not apply an outside formula. He explained **what the parable meant within its own context**, spelling out what kind of person each place where the seed fell represents.

## When the Same Symbol Carries Different Meanings

The biggest problem with fixed formulas is that the Bible uses the same symbol with **different meanings**.

**The lion:**

>! behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed
>! — Revelation 5:5 (KJV)

>! your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
>! — 1 Peter 5:8 (KJV)

In one place the lion points to **Christ**, in another to **the devil**. That is why a fixed formula of "lion = X" is impossible.

**Water:**

>! Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst;
>! — John 4:13-14 (KJV)

>! For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
>! — Habakkuk 2:14 (KJV)

In one place water means eternal life; in another it pictures the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.

## Context, Not a Formula, Determines Meaning

Jesus explained His parables the same way every time: He revealed their meaning **within the context in which the parable was given**. He never plugged in a formula brought in from outside.

A fixed formula ignores context and lays a predetermined conclusion over the Bible. Because this method can steer any verse toward whatever conclusion one wants, interpretation loses its objectivity.

## Summary

Interpreting parables by following the context of the passage is the method the Bible itself demonstrates. When Jesus explained parables, He did not use fixed formulas but revealed their meaning within each parable's setting. The fact that the same symbol carries entirely different meanings elsewhere in the Bible clearly shows the limits of fixed formulas.

**The standard of interpretation is context, not a formula.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any case in which Jesus applied an outside formula when explaining a parable?
If "lion" refers to both Christ and the devil, can a formula of "lion = X" hold?
Where in the Bible are Shincheonji's parable-interpretation formulas written down?
When the same formula is applied to every verse in the Bible, doesn't it produce contradictions?
Can I tell whether the formula came first and the Bible was fitted to it, or whether the formula was drawn from the Bible?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Matthew 13:18-19; Revelation 5:5; 1 Peter 5:8; John 4:13-14; Habakkuk 2:14

01-03.title: Does "Seed" Always Mean the Word?
01-03.description: Shincheonji teaches that "seed" in the Bible always means the word (doctrine). We check against the biblical text whether this claim is consistent.
01-03.content:
## A Question to Ask First

If the formula "seed = word" is applied to every passage in the Bible that mentions a "seed," do all of them still read naturally?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Whenever "seed" appears in the Bible, Shincheonji interprets it as **the word (doctrine)**. God's seed is God's word, and the devil's seed is the devil's doctrine. This formula is one of the core elements of Shincheonji's system of parable interpretation.

The verse most often cited in support is Luke 8:11.

>! Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
>! — Luke 8:11 (KJV)

## The Context of This Verse

Luke 8:11 is Jesus' explanation of **the parable of the sower**. In this verse the seed clearly means the word of God. But that is **the meaning it has within this parable**, not a declaration that "seed" always means the word throughout the Bible. Jesus said, "Now the parable is this," not "Throughout Scripture, the seed is always this."

## Passages Where "Seed" Means Something Else

### 1. Seed = offspring (people)

>! And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head,
>! — Genesis 3:15 (KJV)

The Hebrew word here is zera, "seed." This seed is not a word but **offspring**, and ultimately points to **the Messiah who was to come**.

### 2. Seed = Christ

>! Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ.
>! — Galatians 3:16 (KJV)

Paul states outright that the "seed" promised to Abraham is Christ. Here the seed refers not to the word but to **Christ, a person**.

### 3. Seed = a literal seed

>! But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.
>! — 1 Corinthians 15:38 (KJV)

In explaining the resurrection, Paul uses the illustration of **an actual seed**. The seed in this verse is a seed from the natural world and has nothing to do with the word.

### 4. Seed = the descendants of the righteous

>! His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
>! — Psalm 112:2 (KJV)

Here the seed means actual children and descendants.

## The Problems the Formula Creates

Applying "seed = word" to every passage creates problems like these:

- Genesis 3:15: "between thy word and her word; it shall bruise thy head" — the sentence no longer makes sense
- Galatians 3:16: we would have to ignore Paul's own statement that "the seed = Christ"
- 1 Corinthians 15:38: a literal seed would have to be turned into a figurative word

## Summary

"Seed = word" is correct in the parable of the sower (Luke 8:11), but expanding it into a fixed formula for the whole Bible collides with the Bible itself. The same word is used with various meanings depending on context: offspring, Christ, a literal seed, and more.

**The explanation of one parable does not become a formula for every verse.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is the phrase "Now the parable is this" in Luke 8:11 a formal declaration about the whole Bible?
How do I account for Paul saying "the seed = Christ" in Galatians 3:16?
Does Genesis 3:15 make sense if "her seed" is changed to "her word"?
What is the criterion for when the "seed = word" formula applies and when it does not?
If the formula is applied only to certain verses while others are treated as exceptions, is that a consistent principle?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Luke 8:11; Genesis 3:15; Galatians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 15:38; Psalm 112:2

01-04.title: Do "Birds" Always Mean Spirits?
01-04.description: Shincheonji teaches that "birds" in the Bible always mean spirits. We check this claim for consistency against the biblical text.
01-04.content:
## A Question to Ask First

When the formula "bird = spirit" is applied, can every passage in the Bible that mentions birds still be read naturally?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Whenever birds appear in the Bible, Shincheonji interprets them as **spirits**. The birds of the air symbolize evil spirits, and this formula is used to interpret passages such as the parable of the mustard seed in Matthew 13.

The verses most often cited in support are Matthew 13:4 and 19.

>! And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up:
>! — Matthew 13:4 (KJV)

>! When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart.
>! — Matthew 13:19 (KJV)

Because the birds that eat the seed in this parable correspond to "the wicked one," Shincheonji derives the formula bird = spirit (evil spirit).

## The Context of These Verses

It is true that in Matthew 13 the birds play the role of the wicked one. But that is **the role they play within this particular parable**, not a declaration that birds always mean spirits throughout the Bible.

## Passages Where "Birds" Mean Something Else

### 1. Literal birds

>! Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
>! — Matthew 6:26 (KJV)

Jesus used **real birds** as an example when explaining God's care. Read as "Behold the evil spirits of the air," the meaning of these words changes completely. A God who feeds evil spirits flatly contradicts the lesson of the passage.

### 2. Noah's raven and dove

>! And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth. Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;
>! — Genesis 8:7-8 (KJV)

The raven and the dove that Noah sent out from the ark are **real birds**. Interpreting this as "he sent out an evil spirit and the Holy Spirit" distorts the entire historical account.

### 3. Birds that picture God's protection

>! As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings: So the LORD alone did lead him
>! — Deuteronomy 32:11 (KJV)

Here the eagle is a figure for **God's protection**. Yet the image does not point to a "spirit"; it describes the way God cares for His people.

### 4. Birds used in sacrifice

>! And if the burnt sacrifice for his offering to the LORD be of fowls, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves, or of young pigeons.
>! — Leviticus 1:14 (KJV)

The birds offered as sacrifices under the law are literal birds. This cannot be interpreted as "offering a spirit as a sacrifice."

## The Contradictions of Applying the Formula

Applying "bird = spirit" across the board produces contradictions like these:

- Matthew 6:26: it would mean that God feeds evil spirits
- Genesis 8: it would mean that Noah sent out spirits to check the state of the waters
- Leviticus 1:14: it would mean catching a spirit and offering it as a burnt offering

## Summary

In Matthew 13 the birds figuratively represent the wicked one, and that is correct **within the context of that parable**. But expanding it into a fixed formula for the whole Bible makes countless passages either meaningless or contradictory. The principle that context determines meaning applies to "birds" just as much as anything else.

**A meaning drawn from one parable cannot be used as a formula for every verse.**
selfCheckQuestions: If "the fowls of the air" in Matthew 6:26 were changed to "evil spirits," how would Jesus' teaching change?
Does the passage read naturally if the dove Noah sent out from the ark (Genesis 8:8) is interpreted as "the Holy Spirit"?
What problems arise if the birds in the sacrificial laws of Leviticus are changed to "spirits"?
What is the criterion that separates the verses where the "bird = spirit" formula applies from those where it does not?
Does that criterion come from the Bible, or from Shincheonji's system of interpretation?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Matthew 13:4, 19; Matthew 6:26; Genesis 8:7-8; Deuteronomy 32:11; Leviticus 1:14

01-05.title: Do Trees, Mountains, Seas, and Beasts Always Mean the Same Thing?
01-05.description: Shincheonji assigns fixed figurative meanings to trees, mountains, seas, beasts, and similar images. We check how these symbols are actually used in the biblical text.
01-05.content:
## A Question to Ask First

If the formulas "tree = person," "mountain = nation," "sea = world," and "beast = false pastor" are applied to every relevant passage in the Bible, do they produce consistent results?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji assigns the following fixed meanings to biblical symbols:

- Tree = a person (especially a leader)
- Mountain = a nation or a denomination
- Sea = the world (the world of people)
- Beast = a pastor (usually a false pastor)

It teaches that applying these formulas makes it possible to interpret symbolic texts such as Revelation.

## How the Bible Uses These Symbols in Different Ways

### Trees

**Used for people:**
>! The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
>! — Psalm 92:12 (KJV)

**Literal trees:**
>! And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food;
>! — Genesis 2:9 (KJV)

**The cross (a tree):**
>! The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.
>! — Acts 5:30 (KJV)

The same word "tree" is used with entirely different meanings: a person, an actual plant, the cross.

### Mountains

**Used for a nation (kingdom):**
>! and the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
>! — Daniel 2:35 (KJV)

**Literal mountains:**
>! If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove;
>! — Matthew 17:20 (KJV)

**An obstacle:**
>! Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain:
>! — Zechariah 4:7 (KJV)

**A place of God's presence:**
>! as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.
>! — Genesis 22:14 (KJV)

Mountains are used with many meanings: a nation, an actual mountain, an obstacle, a place of God's presence.

### The Sea

**Used for the world (the nations):**
>! But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest,
>! — Isaiah 57:20 (KJV)

**The literal sea:**
>! And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas:
>! — Genesis 1:9-10 (KJV)

**Something that will no longer exist:**
>! and there was no more sea.
>! — Revelation 21:1 (KJV)

### Beasts

**Used for a false power:**
>! and saw a beast rise up out of the sea,
>! — Revelation 13:1 (KJV)

**Literal animals:**
>! The beast of the field shall honour me, the dragons and the owls:
>! — Isaiah 43:20 (KJV)

**Various figurative meanings:**
>! And four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another.
>! — Daniel 7:3 (KJV)

The four beasts in Daniel point to four empires (Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome). These beasts stand not for "false pastors" but for **worldly empires**.

## Why Fixed Formulas Are a Problem

Applying a fixed formula causes us to miss what the text actually means. If the beasts of Daniel are interpreted as "false pastors," we cannot understand the course of world history that Daniel describes. If the sea in Genesis is interpreted as "the world," God's account of creation itself no longer holds together.

## Summary

Trees, mountains, seas, and beasts are all used in the Bible with **a variety of meanings**, depending on context. Assigning each one a single fixed meaning creates contradictions in countless other passages. The Bible guides readers to grasp meaning within context; it does not ask them to apply an outside formula.

**The meaning of a symbol is determined by the text, not by a table of formulas.**
selfCheckQuestions: Are the four beasts of Daniel 7 "false pastors" or worldly empires? What does the text itself say they are?
How does the creation account change if "Seas" in Genesis 1:9-10 is changed to "the world"?
Does Acts 5:30 make sense if the "tree" is interpreted as "a person"?
Is it consistent interpretation to give a symbol a fixed meaning but make exceptions for some verses?
Where in the Bible is the table of parable-interpretation formulas written down?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Psalm 92:12; Genesis 2:9; Acts 5:30; Daniel 2:35; Matthew 17:20; Zechariah 4:7; Isaiah 57:20; Genesis 1:9-10; Revelation 21:1, 13:1; Daniel 7:3; Isaiah 43:20

01-06.title: How to Tell Whether a Parable Interpretation Is Wrong
01-06.description: A practical guide to testing whether a given parable interpretation is sound, with three checks that use the biblical text as the standard.
01-06.content:
## A Question to Ask First

When someone offers a figurative interpretation of a Bible verse, how can we tell whether it comes from the text or has been imposed on it from outside?

## Why We Need a Way to Test

Anyone can interpret a parable. The trouble is that almost any interpretation can sound convincing. When you hear "tree = person," it feels right, because in some verses a tree really does refer to a person. That is why we need concrete ways to check whether an interpretation is valid.

## Test 1: Check whether the text supplies its own interpretation

When a parable appears in the Bible, the text itself often explains what it means.

>! He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one;
>! — Matthew 13:37-38 (KJV)

Jesus Himself spelled out the meaning of each element. In a case like this, no outside formula is needed.

**Question to check**: Is the meaning of the parable already explained in the surrounding context? Does the proposed interpretation agree with the text's own explanation?

In Matthew 13:38, "the good seed" is not "the word" but **"the children of the kingdom"** (people). Even within a single chapter, the meaning of the seed changes from parable to parable.

## Test 2: Apply the same formula to other passages

When an interpretive formula is proposed, try applying it to other passages in the Bible.

For example, apply the formula "sea = world" to the following verse.

>! and there was no more sea.
>! — Revelation 21:1 (KJV)

With "sea = world," this becomes "and there was no more world." Yet the same verse speaks of "a new earth." A new earth with no world is a contradiction.

>! And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
>! — Matthew 14:25 (KJV)

With "sea = world," this becomes "walking on the world." But this verse is a historical account of one of Jesus' miracles.

**Question to check**: When the proposed formula is applied to ten other passages in the Bible, do they all read naturally? If even one produces a contradiction, it is not a universal formula.

## Test 3: Check whether the interpretation presupposes its conclusion

This is the most important test. Check whether the interpretation was built to support a particular conclusion.

If a parable-interpretation formula leads to the conclusion that a particular group is legitimate, we need to ask:

- Does the formula stand independently of the conclusion?
- If the same formula is applied to another group, does it justify that group as well?
- Which came first, the formula or the conclusion?

If changing the formula makes the conclusion collapse, then the formula is not a tool for interpreting the Bible but a device for reaching a particular conclusion.

## A Worked Example

Suppose someone interprets "Babylon in Revelation 18" as a particular denomination in Korea.

1. **Check the text**: How does Revelation 18 itself describe Babylon? "Babylon the great," and "all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication" (Revelation 18:2-3). Is there any direct basis for saying it refers to a particular Korean denomination?
2. **Apply it to other passages**: By the same method, do the Old Testament passages about Babylon (Isaiah 13, Jeremiah 50–51) also refer to a Korean denomination?
3. **Check for a presupposed conclusion**: Was this interpretation constructed to establish the legitimacy of a particular group?

## Summary

There are three ways to test a parable interpretation. First check the text's own explanation, then apply the same formula to other passages, and finally see whether the interpretation presupposes its conclusion. An interpretation that fails these three checks is more likely laid on top of the Bible than drawn out of it.

**A correct interpretation becomes clearer the more it is tested.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is the parable interpretation I was taught drawn directly from the surrounding context of the text?
When the same interpretive formula is applied to ten other passages in the Bible, are there no contradictions?
In Matthew 13:38, "seed = the children of the kingdom"; how does that fit with the formula "seed = word"?
Was the interpretation constructed to support a particular conclusion?
Could I reach the same conclusion by reading the text alone, without this interpretation?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Matthew 13:37-38; Revelation 21:1; Matthew 14:25; Revelation 18:2-3

01-07.title: Why Parable Interpretation Takes Priority Over Context
01-07.description: We look at the structural reason Shincheonji's system puts parable-interpretation formulas ahead of context, and compare it with biblical principles of interpretation.
01-07.content:
## A Question to Ask First

When we read the Bible, which should come first: following the context of the passage, or applying an outside interpretive formula?

## How Shincheonji's Interpretation Is Structured

As the previous articles showed, Shincheonji's parable-interpretation formulas are not applied consistently across the Bible. Yet there is a structural reason these formulas are kept in place.

Shincheonji's doctrinal system is built in the following sequence:

1. The whole Bible was written in parables (premise)
2. There are fixed formulas for unlocking the parables (tool)
3. Interpreting the Bible with these formulas leads to a specific conclusion (conclusion)
4. This conclusion can be known only through the promised pastor (authority)

In this structure, when **the context** shows a meaning different from the formula, the formula wins, not the context. Giving up the formula would bring down the conclusions in steps 3 and 4 along with it.

## What Becomes Possible When Context Is Ignored

Putting formulas ahead of context makes it possible to **steer any verse toward a desired conclusion**. That is the central problem with this system.

For example, given the formulas "seed = word, field = heart, bird = evil spirit," every verse containing one of those words can be connected to the same conclusion. What the text actually says becomes secondary.

At that point the Bible no longer speaks to the reader; it is made to say whatever the interpreter wants.

## The Principle of Interpretation the Bible Shows

The Bible shows that grasping meaning within context is the right method.

>! Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
>! — 2 Timothy 2:15 (KJV)

"Rightly dividing" means handling the word accurately. To handle the word accurately, we have to read what the text says as it stands.

>! All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
>! — 2 Timothy 3:16 (KJV)

For Scripture to be profitable for doctrine and instruction, its meaning must be graspable without an outside formula. A Bible that cannot be understood without a formula is hard to call "profitable."

## Historically, Contextual Interpretation Was the Norm

Throughout the history of biblical interpretation, putting context first has been the basic principle since the time of the early church. The fathers of the Antiochene school first established the historical and grammatical meaning of a text and only then looked for its spiritual meaning. That is fundamentally different from ignoring the text and applying an outside system.

There was, of course, also a stream that emphasized symbolic interpretation, such as the Alexandrian school. But even they did not deny the meaning of the text; they added a spiritual meaning on top of it. That is different from **replacing** the meaning of the text.

## The Problems When Formulas Override Context

1. **Testing becomes impossible**: because any verse can be converted into a desired meaning through the formula, there is no standard left by which to say, "this interpretation is wrong."
2. **The Bible becomes subordinate to the interpreter**: the meaning of Scripture no longer reaches readers directly, but only through the person who holds the formula.
3. **No comparison with other interpretations is possible**: when context is the standard, anyone can read the same text and discuss it; when a formula is the standard, only the side that holds the formula can interpret.

## Summary

Shincheonji's parable-interpretation formulas take priority over context not because of any hermeneutical principle, but in order to preserve a specific conclusion that cannot be reached without them. According to the Bible, sound interpretation means grasping meaning within context. Following context makes testing possible; following a formula makes it impossible.

**When context is the standard of interpretation, truth comes to light; when a formula is, authority is manufactured.**
selfCheckQuestions: Could I reach the same conclusion by reading the biblical text alone, without the parable-interpretation formulas?
When context and formula conflict, which was I taught to follow? Why?
If Scripture is "profitable" according to 2 Timothy 3:16, shouldn't it be understandable without an outside formula?
If another group uses the same formulas and reaches a different conclusion, how do I decide which one is right?
Which is testable: a system whose standard of interpretation is context, or one whose standard is a formula?

02-01.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Creation and Re-creation
02-01.title: Is Biblical History a Repeating Cycle of Creation and Re-creation?
02-01.description: Shincheonji teaches that biblical history is a cycle of creation, betrayal, and re-creation. We check how the Bible actually presents history.
02-01.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Does the Bible present history as a cycle that repeats itself, or as a movement toward a single purpose?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that biblical history repeats in a cycle of **creation → betrayal (fall) → destruction → re-creation**. It says this pattern recurs through the age of Adam, the age of Noah, the age of Moses, and the age of Jesus' first coming, up to the present age of the second coming, and that in each age a new chosen people and a new pastor are raised up.

This doctrine lays the foundation for the conclusion that "now is the age of re-creation, and a new pastor is needed."

## The Structure of History the Bible Shows

The Bible presents history not as a cycle but as **the gradual unfolding of a single plan of salvation**.

>! God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son,
>! — Hebrews 1:1-2 (KJV)

This passage shows the core structure of biblical history. God spoke **in many different ways**, and then **in these last days spoke by His Son**. This is not a cycle but **progressive revelation**, and it reaches its **climax** in Christ.

>! That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him:
>! — Ephesians 1:10 (KJV)

Paul says the purpose of history is **the gathering together of all things in Christ**. History does not go around in a repeating cycle; it moves toward one purpose.

## Creation, Fall, Redemption, Consummation: The Bible's Actual Storyline

The structure of the whole Bible can be summarized as follows:

1. **Creation** (Genesis 1–2): God makes the world, and it is "good"
2. **Fall** (Genesis 3): human disobedience
3. **The history of redemption** (Genesis 3:15 through Revelation 20): God's plan of salvation unfolds step by step
4. **Consummation** (Revelation 21–22): the new heaven and the new earth

Within step 3, the history of redemption, there are many eras, but each one is not "a cycle that starts over from creation"; they are **stages of a single plan of salvation**.

>! Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you: Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
>! — 1 Peter 1:10-11 (KJV)

The Old Testament prophets prophesied **with Christ in view**. The eras do not form separate cycles; all of them belong to one storyline that points to Christ.

## The Problems the Cyclical View Creates

Seeing history as a cycle creates the following problems:

1. **It weakens the uniqueness of Christ**: Hebrews 9:26 says that Christ "now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself." The word "once" does not fit a repeating cycle.

>! For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
>! — Hebrews 9:26 (KJV)

2. **It changes the meaning of the new covenant**: if the new covenant Jesus established were to fail again and require another re-creation, that would clash with the phrase "the everlasting covenant" (Hebrews 13:20).

3. **The conclusion is built into the premise**: once the premise "history repeats itself" is accepted, the conclusion that the present is also an age of re-creation follows automatically. The premise itself contains the conclusion.

## Summary

The Bible does not see history as cyclical repetition. It presents history as progressive revelation and the advance of a plan of salvation that points to Christ. Hebrews 1:1-2 makes this movement plain. The cyclical view weakens the meaning of Christ's once-for-all work and of the everlasting covenant, and it is structured so that the conclusion "the present is the age of re-creation" is already contained in the premise.

**Biblical history moves not toward repetition but toward completion.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is the structure of history shown in Hebrews 1:1-2 a cycle or progressive revelation?
If Christ's work was accomplished "once" (Hebrews 9:26), is another cycle of salvation needed after it?
If "the everlasting covenant" (Hebrews 13:20) failed and re-creation became necessary, what would "everlasting" mean?
Where does the Bible directly teach the cycle of creation, betrayal, and re-creation?
If the cyclical view is accepted as a premise, isn't the conclusion about the present age decided automatically?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Hebrews 1:1-2; Ephesians 1:10; 1 Peter 1:10-11; Hebrews 9:26

02-02.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Creation and Re-creation
02-02.title: Must the Chosen People Always Betray God?
02-02.description: Shincheonji teaches that the people God chooses inevitably betray Him in every age. We check what the Bible actually says about Israel and the church.
02-02.content:
## A Question to Ask First

If the people God has chosen must all inevitably betray Him, what does God's choosing actually mean?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that in every age the people God has chosen (the chosen people) eventually **all betray Him**, and that God therefore abandons them and raises up **a new chosen people**. Adam's world collapsed, Israel betrayed God, the early church fell away, and present-day Christianity has betrayed Him, so the argument goes, which makes Shincheonji the new chosen people.

The claim can be summed up as **"total betrayal" and "total replacement."**

## What the Bible Says About Israel's Betrayal and the Remnant

It is true that Israel repeatedly turned away from God. But the Bible does not say that **all** of Israel betrayed Him. There was always **a remnant**.

>! I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
>! — Romans 11:1 (KJV)

>! Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
>! — Romans 11:5 (KJV)

Paul makes two things clear. First, **God has not cast away His people**. Second, **there has always been a remnant**. The formula "total betrayal → total replacement" runs head-on into Romans 11.

## There Was Always a Remnant in the Old Testament, Too

>! Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him.
>! — 1 Kings 19:18 (KJV)

When Elijah said, "I, even I only, am left," God answered that seven thousand remained. Even in the time of the worst apostasy, there were people who followed God.

>! The remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity, nor speak lies;
>! — Zephaniah 3:13 (KJV)

The idea of "the remnant" is a key theme that runs through the entire Old Testament. It appears again and again in many of the prophets, including Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah, and Zephaniah.

## The Promises to the New Testament Church

>! upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
>! — Matthew 16:18 (KJV)

Jesus promised the church that **"the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."** The claim that the entire church has betrayed God collides with this promise.

>! and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.
>! — Matthew 28:20 (KJV)

The promise "I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world" is hard to reconcile with the claim that the church has betrayed God completely and a new chosen people is needed.

## Not "Total Betrayal" but "Partial Falling Away and a Remnant"

The pattern the Bible shows is this:

- Many people turn away from God (partial falling away)
- Yet there is always a remnant that follows God
- God **does not abandon His people completely**
- The history of salvation continues rather than breaking off

This is a fundamentally different structure from "total betrayal → total replacement."

## Summary

The Bible does not teach "total betrayal" or "total replacement" of the chosen people. Romans 11 states plainly that God has not cast away His people and that there has always been a remnant. Jesus promised the church that the gates of hell would not prevail against it. Partial falling away is real, but expanding it into "total betrayal" in order to argue for the need for a new chosen people departs from what the Bible testifies.

**God has not cast away His people.**
selfCheckQuestions: How do I understand Paul's words in Romans 11:1-5, "Hath God cast away his people? God forbid"?
How do the seven thousand in 1 Kings 19:18 fit with "total betrayal"?
Is the promise in Matthew 16:18 that "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" compatible with the entire church betraying God?
If the idea of "the remnant" appears throughout the Old Testament prophets, is it an exception or a principle?
Can I find direct support in the biblical text for the claim that the whole church has betrayed God?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Romans 11:1, 5; 1 Kings 19:18; Zephaniah 3:13; Matthew 16:18; Matthew 28:20

02-03.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Creation and Re-creation
02-03.title: Did Every Pastor of Earlier Ages Fail?
02-03.description: Shincheonji teaches that the pastors of earlier ages all failed, so a new pastor is needed. We check how the Bible assesses the believers of earlier ages.
02-03.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Can Abraham, Moses, and David be called "failed pastors"? How does the Bible assess them?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the pastors (leaders) of each age **all failed** in the end, and that because of this failure God opens a new age and raises up a new pastor. By this logic, today's Christian leaders have also failed, and so a new promised pastor is needed.

## Hebrews 11: How the Bible Assesses the Believers of Earlier Ages

Hebrews 11 is often called the "Hall of Faith." This chapter presents the believers of earlier ages **not as failures but as examples of faith**.

>! By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous,
>! — Hebrews 11:4 (KJV)

>! By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house;
>! — Hebrews 11:7 (KJV)

>! By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed;
>! — Hebrews 11:8 (KJV)

>! By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter;
>! — Hebrews 11:24 (KJV)

These people were not perfect. Abraham lied about his wife, Moses struck the rock in anger, and David committed grave sin. Even so, the Bible does not call them **"failed pastors"**; it records them as **"examples of faith."**

## The Difference Between "Failure" and "Imperfection"

There is a key confusion in Shincheonji's logic. **Imperfection** and **failure** are not the same.

- **Imperfection**: every human being has flaws. But those flaws do not cancel God's plan of salvation.
- **Failure**: the "failure" Shincheonji speaks of means that a pastor has become so completely corrupt that his entire age must be discarded.

The Bible clearly distinguishes the two.

>! For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself,
>! — Hebrews 6:13 (KJV)

>! Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:
>! — Hebrews 6:17 (KJV)

God's promise is not canceled by a pastor's imperfection, because God **confirmed it by an oath**.

## How the Bible Assesses David

David committed grave sin. But how does the Bible assess him?

>! Because David did that which was right in the eyes of the LORD, and turned not aside from any thing that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
>! — 1 Kings 15:5 (KJV)

>! I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.
>! — Acts 13:22 (KJV)

God called David "a man after mine own heart." He was imperfect, but he was **not a failed pastor**.

## The Purpose of the Claim That "Every Pastor Failed"

The premise that **every** pastor of earlier ages failed exists to support the conclusion that "a new pastor is needed now." If some of the earlier pastors were faithful, and if God's promise held firm despite their imperfection, then the argument that "everything has collapsed and must start over from the beginning" loses its footing.

Hebrews 11 is the counterevidence. **The people of faith in earlier ages were not failures but faithful witnesses within God's plan that points to Christ.**

>! And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.
>! — Hebrews 11:39-40 (KJV)

This passage says that the believers of earlier ages did not receive the promise not **because they failed**, but **because God had provided some better thing**. Their faith was valid, and they are made complete together with us in Christ.

## Summary

The Bible does not assess the pastors of earlier ages as people who "all failed." Hebrews 11 records them as witnesses of faith, and God's promise held firm despite their imperfection. Inflating imperfection into "total failure" in order to argue for the need for a new pastor departs from the Bible's own assessment.

**God's promise is not canceled by human imperfection.**
selfCheckQuestions: Can the people listed in Hebrews 11 be called "failed pastors"?
Am I distinguishing between "imperfection" and "failure"?
How do I understand God calling David "a man after mine own heart"?
According to Hebrews 11:39-40, why did the believers of earlier ages not receive the promise?
Could the current doctrine stand without the premise that "every pastor failed"?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Hebrews 11:4, 7, 8, 24, 39-40; Hebrews 6:13, 17; 1 Kings 15:5; Acts 13:22

02-04.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Creation and Re-creation
02-04.title: Is the New Heaven and New Earth the Shincheonji Organization?
02-04.description: Shincheonji claims that "a new heaven and a new earth" in Revelation 21:1 refers to its own organization. We check what the biblical text actually says.
02-04.content:
## A Question to Ask First

When you read "a new heaven and a new earth" in Revelation 21, is the text describing a particular organization, or a new creation on a cosmic scale?

## What Shincheonji Claims

The very name Shincheonji (新天地) means "new heaven and new earth." Shincheonji teaches that "a new heaven and a new earth" in Revelation 21:1 refers to its own organization. In this interpretation, the "new heaven" is a new spiritual leadership and the "new earth" is a new gathering of believers.

>! And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea.
>! — Revelation 21:1 (KJV)

## The Context of Revelation 21–22

Read in context, this verse clearly describes not a particular organization but **a new creation on a cosmic scale**.

>! And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new.
>! — Revelation 21:5 (KJV)

"I make all things new" refers to **the renewal of all things**, not the founding of a particular organization.

>! and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
>! — Revelation 21:4 (KJV)

In the new heaven and new earth there is **no death, no sorrow, no pain**. No organization on earth today can claim to be free of death and pain. This is an end-time promise that has not yet been fulfilled.

>! And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
>! — Revelation 21:23 (KJV)

The New Jerusalem is a place with no need of the sun or the moon. Applying this to an organization on earth does not fit the text's description.

## "New Heavens and a New Earth" in the Old Testament

This idea does not first appear in Revelation. It is already found in Isaiah.

>! For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
>! — Isaiah 65:17 (KJV)

Isaiah, too, describes the new heavens and new earth as **God's new creation**. The context is not a prophecy about the founding of a particular organization.

The same idea appears in Peter's letters.

>! Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
>! — 2 Peter 3:13 (KJV)

Peter describes the new heavens and new earth as the place **"wherein dwelleth righteousness."** It is a promise that has not yet arrived, and the words "look for" express a hope for the future. If it were an organization that already existed, there would be no reason to say we "look for" it.

## What the Text Describes vs. the Organizational Interpretation

| What the text describes | If interpreted as a particular organization |
|---|---|
| There is no death (21:4) | Do people not die within the organization? |
| All things are made new (21:5) | Is founding an organization the renewal of all things? |
| No need of the sun or moon (21:23) | Does the organization exist without the sun and moon? |
| There is no more sea (21:1) | Did the sea disappear when the organization was founded? |

Applying these descriptions to a particular earthly organization would mean claiming that things which have not come true at all "have already been fulfilled."

## Summary

In the Bible, "a new heaven and a new earth" consistently refers to **God's cosmic new creation**, in Isaiah, in Peter, and in Revelation. It is a place without death or pain, where all things are made new and the glory of God shines directly. Equating it with a particular organization on earth does not match the text's description.

**The new heaven and new earth are the final fulfillment God has promised, not the name of an earthly organization.**
selfCheckQuestions: In which organization on earth today is the description in Revelation 21:4, no more death and no more pain, being fulfilled?
Do "new heavens and a new earth" in Isaiah 65:17 and 2 Peter 3:13 refer to the same organization as well?
When Peter says we "look for" it, is he describing something that already exists, or a hope for the future?
Is it natural to apply "I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5) to the founding of an organization?
Is using "new heaven and new earth" as an organization's name the same thing as the Bible's promise being fulfilled in that organization?

02-05.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Creation and Re-creation
02-05.title: Can the Kingdom of God Be Identified with a Particular Organization?
02-05.description: Shincheonji claims that the kingdom of God is its own organization. We check how the Bible describes the kingdom of God.
02-05.content:
## A Question to Ask First

Does the "kingdom of God" Jesus spoke of refer to a particular, visible organization?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the kingdom of God (the kingdom of heaven) has been realized in its own organization. When the twelve tribes, made up of the 144,000 who are sealed, are complete, that is the kingdom of God. It follows from this logic that belonging to Shincheonji means entering the kingdom of God.

## The Kingdom of God as Jesus Described It

When the Pharisees asked Jesus about the kingdom of God, He answered:

>! The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
>! — Luke 17:20-21 (KJV)

Jesus made three things clear.

1. The kingdom of God **"cometh not with observation"** — it is not something identified as a visible organization.
2. **"Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there!"** — no one can point to a particular place or organization and say, "This is the kingdom of God."
3. **"The kingdom of God is within you"** — the kingdom of God is a spiritual reality.

These words collide directly with the claim that "our organization is the kingdom of God."

## Other Bible Passages About the Kingdom of God

>! Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
>! — John 18:36 (KJV)

Before Pilate, Jesus said, **"My kingdom is not of this world."** The kingdom of God cannot be reduced to an organization or institution of this world.

>! For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
>! — Romans 14:17 (KJV)

Paul defines the kingdom of God as **"righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost."** It is a spiritual reality, distinct from an organization's name or structure.

>! For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.
>! — 1 Corinthians 4:20 (KJV)

## The Difference Between the Kingdom of God and an Organization

The features of the kingdom of God as the Bible describes it can be summarized as follows:

- It does not come with observation (Luke 17:20)
- It is not of this world (John 18:36)
- No one can say, "Lo here! or, lo there!" (Luke 17:21)
- It is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17)
- It is in power (1 Corinthians 4:20)

Taken together, these features show that the kingdom of God **cannot be equated with any particular earthly organization**.

The church is, of course, the community that bears witness to and experiences the kingdom of God on this earth. But the church is not the **whole** of the kingdom of God. The kingdom of God is revealed through the church, yet it is not confined to the name or boundaries of any particular church or organization.

## Groups in History That Made the Same Claim

Shincheonji is not the only group in history to claim that "our organization is the kingdom of God." Jehovah's Witnesses and the Unification Church, among others, have made similar claims. If any one of them were right, the rest would be wrong, and the standard for deciding must be the biblical text. And the biblical text says that the kingdom of God cannot be identified with a particular organization.

## Summary

Jesus said that the kingdom of God "cometh not with observation" and that no one can say, "Lo here! or, lo there!" The kingdom of God is not of this world; it is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. This teaching does not allow any particular earthly organization to be equated with the kingdom of God.

**The kingdom of God is not the name of an organization but wherever God's reign comes.**
selfCheckQuestions: How do I understand Jesus' words in Luke 17:20-21 that the kingdom of God "cometh not with observation"?
How does "My kingdom is not of this world" in John 18:36 fit with a particular organization?
When several groups make the same claim, what is the standard for deciding which organization is "the real kingdom of God"?
According to the definition in Romans 14:17, is the essence of the kingdom of God an organization or a spiritual reality?
Can "Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there!" coexist with the claim that "our organization is the kingdom of God"?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Luke 17:20-21; John 18:36; Romans 14:17; 1 Corinthians 4:20

03-01.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-01.title: Does Every Age Need One Promised Pastor?
03-01.description: Examines Shincheonji's claim that each age must have one promised pastor sent by God, in light of Hebrews and 1 Timothy.
03-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

If every age after Jesus still needs a new "promised pastor," does that mean Jesus' saving work was left unfinished?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji divides biblical history into ages and teaches that in each age God sends **one promised pastor**. In Adam's age it was Noah, in Noah's age Abraham, in the Old Testament age Moses, and at the first coming Jesus. Today, they claim, the promised pastor is Chairman Lee Man-hee.

In this framework, the promised pastor is indispensable for salvation in his age, and God's will can be known only through him.

## Relevant Scripture

>! God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds.
>! — Hebrews 1:1-2 (KJV)

>! For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
>! — 1 Timothy 2:5 (KJV)

>! Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
>! — Hebrews 13:8 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Structure of Revelation in Hebrews

Hebrews 1:1-2 describes God's revelation in two stages. "In time past" he spoke through the prophets, at sundry times and in divers manners; "in these last days" he has spoken through his Son.

The key phrase here is **"in these last days."** The writer of Hebrews makes clear that revelation through the Son is final. The point is that the age of the prophets has given way to the age of the Son. Nothing in the passage suggests that another agent of revelation will follow the Son.

### 2. The Uniqueness of the Mediator

1 Timothy 2:5 states that there is **one** mediator between God and men. The verse sets no time limit. It does not say, "There is one mediator for now, but another will come later."

If the promised pastor Shincheonji describes functions as a mediator, that collides with the "one mediator" of 1 Timothy 2:5. If his role is something other than mediator, then we need to ask where in Scripture that role is defined.

### 3. Do the Old Testament Prophets and Jesus Share the Same Pattern?

Shincheonji lists Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus as instances of the same "promised pastor" pattern. Yet the whole argument of Hebrews runs the other way. Hebrews insists that Jesus is greater than Moses (3:3), greater than the Aaronic priesthood (7:11-28), and the mediator of a better covenant than the old one (8:6).

By that argument, Jesus is not **on the same level** as the figures of earlier ages; he is **different in kind**. Placing Jesus as one more example in a chain of prophets moves in the opposite direction from the central argument of Hebrews.

### 4. Is Another Pastor Needed After Jesus?

>! But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.
>! — Hebrews 7:24 (KJV)

Hebrews 7:24 declares that Jesus' priesthood is "unchangeable": it does not change and does not pass to anyone else. In context, the Levitical priests died and their office passed to others, but because Jesus lives forever, his office is permanent.

If yet another promised pastor is needed after Jesus, someone has to explain what this "unchangeable" priesthood means.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "Jesus was the promised pastor of the first coming. In the age of the second coming, another promised pastor is needed, one with whom the spirit of Jesus dwells. This is because the age has changed."

This objection rests on the premise that "the age has changed." But the "last days" in Hebrews cover the whole New Testament era, from Jesus' first coming to his return. Hebrews does not split the first and second comings into separate ages, each needing its own pastor.

The claim that "the spirit of Jesus dwells with him" also needs proof of its own. We have to ask what standard determines whether the spirit of Jesus is with a particular person, and whether that standard comes directly from the text of Scripture.

---

## Summary

Hebrews declares that God's revelation, after the age of the prophets, has been given finally through the Son. 1 Timothy says there is one mediator. Hebrews 7 says Jesus' office does not pass to anyone else. Taken together, these three passages make it hard to reconcile the claim that another promised pastor of the same kind is needed after Jesus.

**Treating Jesus as one case in a recurring pattern of prophets is the exact opposite of what Hebrews sets out to prove.**
selfCheckQuestions: In Hebrews 1:1-2, after the words "in these last days spoken unto us by his Son," is any further agent of revelation mentioned?
Does the declaration of "one mediator" in 1 Timothy 2:5 carry any time limit?
What does the "unchangeable priesthood" of Hebrews 7:24 mean?
Is listing Jesus on the same level as Noah and Moses consistent with the argument of Hebrews?
From which passage of Scripture is the concept of a promised pastor directly derived?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Hebrews 1:1-2, 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 7:24, Hebrews 13:8

03-02.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
