03-02.title: Can Jesus and the Promised Pastor Be Seen as the Same Pattern?
03-02.description: Examines, mainly through Hebrews and Colossians, Shincheonji's logic of setting Jesus and Chairman Lee Man-hee side by side as promised pastors of their respective ages.
03-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

Shincheonji explains that just as Jesus was the promised pastor of the first coming, Chairman Lee Man-hee is the promised pastor of the second coming. For this pattern to hold, Jesus and Chairman Lee would have to fill the same kind of role. Does the Bible teach such a pattern?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the promised pastor of each age ministers according to the same pattern. When God's chosen people of one age fall away, God sends a new promised pastor to open a new age. In this scheme, Jesus is the promised pastor of the Old Testament age, and Chairman Lee Man-hee is the promised pastor of the New Testament age (the age of the second coming).

This parallel rests on the premise that Jesus' role was limited to his own age, and that in a new age a new promised pastor ministers in the same way.

## Relevant Scripture

>! Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
>! — Colossians 1:15-17 (KJV)

>! And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
>! — Colossians 1:18 (KJV)

>! But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
>! — Hebrews 7:24-25 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. Jesus' Place According to Colossians

Colossians 1:15-18 proclaims who Jesus is. All things were created by him and for him; he is before all things; he is the head of the church; in all things he has the preeminence.

In this passage Jesus is not the pastor of one age but **the Lord of all things**. The phrase "in all things he might have the preeminence" carries no time limit. Following the argument of Colossians, there cannot be another preeminent one of the same kind after Jesus.

### 2. The Permanence of the Priesthood in Hebrews

Hebrews 7:24-25 says Jesus' priesthood is "unchangeable." The Greek word ἀπαράβατον (aparabaton) means "not transferable" or "unalterable." Hebrews argues that the Levitical priests needed successors because they died, but Jesus, who lives forever, needs no successor.

Shincheonji's promised-pastor scheme has a new figure in each age taking over the role of the previous one. That looks much more like the Levitical pattern of succession, which Hebrews explicitly sets aside.

### 3. Are Jesus and a Human Leader the Same Kind of Figure?

For Shincheonji's parallel to work, Jesus and Chairman Lee Man-hee must be the same kind of being. But Scripture testifies of Jesus as follows:

- The image of God (Colossians 1:15)
- The creator of all things (Colossians 1:16)
- Preeminent in all things (Colossians 1:18)
- The eternal priest (Hebrews 7:24)
- The one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5)

We need to ask whether even one of these attributes applies to a human being. If none does, then placing Jesus and the promised pastor side by side in the same pattern goes beyond what the text allows.

### 4. The Problem with the "Same Pattern" Premise

Shincheonji's scheme of pastors for each age places Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Lee Man-hee in the same pattern. Hebrews, however, argues that Jesus is the one who **brought this pattern to an end**.

>! Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
>! — Hebrews 7:27 (KJV)

The word "once" (ἐφάπαξ, once for all) means that no repetition is needed. It declares the pattern closed.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "We accept that Jesus is the Son of God, but Jesus also ministered as a promised pastor. For God's work to be carried out in each age, a pastor in the flesh is needed."

This objection starts from the idea that Jesus ministered as a promised pastor. But the moment Jesus is classified as one of several promised pastors, the uniqueness and permanence of Jesus that Colossians and Hebrews stress are weakened.

The Jesus whom Scripture presents is not "one among several promised pastors" but "the only Son of God and the eternal high priest." Consider for yourself whether both views can be held at the same time.

---

## Summary

Colossians proclaims Jesus as preeminent over all things and head of the church. Hebrews testifies that Jesus' priesthood does not pass to anyone else and that his work was accomplished once for all. Setting Jesus and a human leader side by side as "promised pastors" of the same kind collides with the core argument of these passages.

**Seeing Jesus as one case of a repeatable pattern and seeing him as the only one who brought the pattern to an end are fundamentally different interpretations.**
selfCheckQuestions: Does the phrase "in all things he might have the preeminence" in Colossians 1:18 carry any time limit?
Can the "unchangeable" priesthood of Hebrews 7:24 coexist with a scheme in which pastors are replaced age by age?
Can any of Jesus' attributes (creator of all things, the one mediator, the eternal priest) apply to a human being?
Does the word "once" in Hebrews 7:27 allow for repetition?
Does classifying Jesus as one of the promised pastors not weaken the argument of Colossians?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Colossians 1:15-18, Hebrews 7:24-25, Hebrews 7:27, 1 Timothy 2:5

03-03.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-03.title: Is the One Who Overcomes in Revelation a Single Person?
03-03.description: Examines, through the context and the Greek text, whether "the one who overcomes" in Revelation 2-3 refers to one specific individual or is a promise given to all believers.
03-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Revelation 2-3, are the promises to "the one who overcomes" in the seven churches meant for one particular individual, or are they an exhortation addressed to every believer in those churches?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that "the one who overcomes" (ὁ νικῶν), who appears again and again in Revelation 2-3, refers to **one specific person**: Chairman Lee Man-hee. All the promises given to the seven churches, they say, are fulfilled in this one man.

## Relevant Scripture

>! He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.
>! — Revelation 2:7 (KJV)

>! He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
>! — Revelation 2:11 (KJV)

>! To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
>! — Revelation 2:17 (KJV)

>! And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations.
>! — Revelation 2:26 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Structure of the Greek Text

The Greek behind "the one who overcomes" is ὁ νικῶν (ho nikōn). It is a present active participle with the article, literally "the one who is overcoming." Grammatically, this expression is not a proper name pointing to **one particular person**. It works as a **general condition**: "anyone who overcomes."

English Bibles render it "the one who overcomes" or "whoever overcomes," a promise open to everyone who meets the condition.

### 2. The Recipients and Context of Each Letter

The seven letters of Revelation 2-3 are each addressed to a particular church. Each contains praise, rebuke, and exhortation suited to that church's situation, and each closes with a promise to "the one who overcomes."

- Ephesus: "thou hast left thy first love" → the tree of life to the one who overcomes (2:4-7)
- Smyrna: "be thou faithful unto death" → the one who overcomes will not be hurt by the second death (2:10-11)
- Pergamos: "thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam" → hidden manna to the one who overcomes (2:14-17)
- Thyatira: "thou sufferest that woman Jezebel" → power over the nations to the one who overcomes (2:20-26)

In the context of each letter, "the one who overcomes" refers to **the believer who prevails** over that church's particular trials and difficulties. In Ephesus, overcoming means recovering their first love; in Smyrna, staying faithful under persecution; in Pergamos, rejecting false teaching.

### 3. Does One Person Fit Every Situation of the Seven Churches?

If, as Shincheonji teaches, "the one who overcomes" is one particular individual, then that one person must have experienced and overcome all of these: the Ephesian situation of "leaving the first love," the Smyrnan situation of persecution "unto death," the Pergamene problem of "the doctrine of Balaam," and the Thyatiran problem of "tolerating Jezebel."

But each letter deals with a different problem in a different church. The idea that one person experiences all seven churches' distinct problems at once does not fit the individual character of the letters.

### 4. Parallel Passages in 1 John

The same author, John, uses the verb "overcome" (νικάω) in another letter as well.

>! I have written unto you, young men, because ye are strong, and the word of God abideth in you, and ye have overcome the wicked one.
>! — 1 John 2:14 (KJV)

>! For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
>! — 1 John 5:4 (KJV)

In 1 John, those who overcome are plainly **all believers**. If the same author uses the same word, then reading it in Revelation alone as suddenly meaning one particular individual requires separate evidence.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "In Revelation 2:26, 'he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him...,' the word 'to him' (αὐτῷ) is singular, so it refers to one person."

In Greek, a singular pronoun is the natural choice in a general condition to refer to **each individual** who meets the condition. It is the same structure as "To any student who does well, I will give him a prize": "him" is singular, but it does not mean only one student.

English works the same way. In "whosoever believeth in him should not perish" (John 3:16), "whosoever" takes a singular verb, yet it applies to everyone who believes.

---

## Summary

Grammatically, "the one who overcomes" in Revelation 2-3 is a general condition, a promise open to any believer in each church. The different situations and exhortations of the seven letters are addressed to the believers of each church, not to one particular individual. In 1 John, by the same author, the same expression refers to all believers.

**Limiting "the one who overcomes" to one particular individual conflicts with the grammar, the context, and the author's other letter alike.**
selfCheckQuestions: Does the Greek expression ὁ νικῶν (the one who overcomes) grammatically point to only one particular person?
Can the different situations and exhortations of the seven churches all apply to a single person?
In 1 John 5:4, who is it that "overcometh the world"?
Is there any basis for saying that the same author uses the same word with a different meaning?
If "the promise to the one who overcomes" applies to only one person, what promise is left for the rest of the believers?

03-04.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-04.title: Is Lee Man-hee the One Who Overcomes in Revelation 2-3?
03-04.description: Looks one by one at the rewards promised to the one who overcomes in the seven churches, and asks whether they were fulfilled in one specific individual or promised to all believers.
03-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

The rewards promised in Revelation 2-3 to the one who overcomes (the tree of life, the hidden manna, the white stone, power over the nations, white raiment, the new Jerusalem): have they already been fulfilled in one person?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that every promise given to "the one who overcomes" in the seven churches of Revelation 2-3 has been fulfilled in Chairman Lee Man-hee. He is, they say, the promised pastor who overcame in the battle with the seven stars (the seven messengers), received the actual fulfillment (silsang) of Revelation, and testifies to it.

## Relevant Scripture: The Seven Rewards

### Ephesus: The Fruit of the Tree of Life (2:7)

>! To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.
>! — Revelation 2:7 (KJV)

The tree of life appears again in Revelation 22:2: "on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." This belongs to the scene of the new Jerusalem, the final salvation, and it is enjoyed by **all who are saved**.

### Smyrna: Exemption from the Second Death (2:11)

>! He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
>! — Revelation 2:11 (KJV)

Revelation 20:14 explains the second death as "the lake of fire." Escaping the second death is not one person's privilege; it is a promise for **everyone whose name is written in the book of life** (Revelation 20:15).

### Pergamos: The Hidden Manna and the White Stone (2:17)

The hidden manna symbolizes God's provision, and the new name on the white stone symbolizes a personal assurance of salvation. The words "which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it" show that this promise is given uniquely to **each individual**. The picture is not one white stone for one person, but a white stone of their own for each person who overcomes.

### Thyatira: Power over the Nations (2:26-27)

>! And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations: And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers.
>! — Revelation 2:26-27 (KJV)

This promise quotes Psalm 2:9 and was originally a promise about the Messiah. Its extension in Revelation to the one who overcomes means that the saints reign with Christ (Revelation 20:6). This is **a shared reign of all the saints**, not limited to one person.

### Sardis: White Raiment and the Book of Life (3:5)

>! He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.
>! — Revelation 3:5 (KJV)

White robes appear in Revelation 7:9, worn by a great multitude. The promise not to blot names out of the book of life is likewise a guarantee for **all** who overcome, not for one person.

### Philadelphia: The New Jerusalem and the New Name (3:12)

The promise to make the overcomer a pillar in the temple and to write on him the name of God, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Jesus' new name is an assurance of eternal belonging and identity. It is a future that awaits every faithful believer, not a privilege for one person alone.

### Laodicea: Sitting on the Throne Together (3:21)

>! To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.
>! — Revelation 3:21 (KJV)

Sitting with Christ on his throne means reigning together with him. The comparison "even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father" describes sharing in Jesus' victory, not holding the same status as Jesus.

## What Needs to Be Examined

### Have These Rewards Already Been Fulfilled?

If, as Shincheonji claims, the one who overcomes is Chairman Lee Man-hee, then all seven rewards above should already have been fulfilled. We need to ask whether the fruit of the tree of life, exemption from the second death, power over the nations, and a seat on the throne have actually come to pass in one person today.

Most of these rewards are eschatological in nature. The new Jerusalem, the tree of life, the throne: these appear in the scenes of final consummation in Revelation 21-22. If that final consummation has not yet come, we need to ask whether these rewards can be said to have already been fulfilled in one person.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "The promises to the one who overcomes have been fulfilled spiritually. By receiving and testifying to the actual fulfillment of Revelation, Chairman Lee Man-hee was given a spiritual tree of life, spiritual manna, and spiritual authority."

If these are read as spiritual fulfillments, the same standard must apply to the other verses. If the second death is spiritual and sitting on the throne is spiritual too, then every promise in Revelation shrinks to a spiritual dimension. We need to check whether this interpretive standard is applied consistently.

A claim of spiritual fulfillment is also hard to verify. Claiming a fulfillment that cannot be confirmed from outside amounts to the same structure as "it cannot be confirmed without Shincheonji's explanation."

---

## Summary

The seven rewards of Revelation 2-3 are promises given to the believers who overcome in each church. The new name on the white stone, the white raiment, the book of life, the shared reign on the throne: all of these are promises open to everyone who believes in Christ and overcomes, not to one particular individual.

**Concentrating the seven promises to the seven churches on one person ignores the basic structure of the text, which is speaking to the believers of those seven churches.**
selfCheckQuestions: Have all seven rewards (tree of life, manna, white stone, power, white raiment, new name, throne) already been fulfilled in one person?
Does the new name on the white stone, "which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it," apply to only one person?
If exemption from the second death and sitting on the throne have already come to pass, what is the evidence?
Is the standard of "spiritual fulfillment" being applied equally to the other promises in Revelation?
Is the great multitude in white robes in Revelation 7:9 one person or many people?

03-05.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-05.title: Who Ate the Book in Revelation 10?
03-05.description: Examines, through the context of the passage and an Old Testament parallel, whether the scene in Revelation 10 where the open book is eaten was fulfilled in Chairman Lee Man-hee.
03-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Revelation 10, who is the person who takes the open book from the angel and eats it? Does the text itself say who that person is?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the figure who eats the open book in Revelation 10 is Chairman Lee Man-hee. He is, they say, the only person who ate the book opened from heaven (the word of revelation) and was commissioned to prophesy its contents again before many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings.

## Relevant Scripture

>! And the voice which I heard from heaven spake unto me again, and said, Go and take the little book which is open in the hand of the angel which standeth upon the sea and upon the earth. And I went unto the angel, and said unto him, Give me the little book. And he said unto me, Take it, and eat it up; and it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey.
>! — Revelation 10:8-9 (KJV)

>! And I took the little book out of the angel's hand, and ate it up; and it was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter.
>! — Revelation 10:10 (KJV)

>! And he said unto me, Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings.
>! — Revelation 10:11 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Recipient Named by the Text

The speaker in Revelation 10 is **John** himself. In "I went unto the angel" (10:9) and "I took the little book out of the angel's hand, and ate it up" (10:10), the "I" is the apostle John, who is writing Revelation. Revelation 1:1 states plainly that this revelation was given "unto his servant John."

The text itself says that John is the one having this experience. Reading it as someone other than John requires bringing in separate grounds from outside the text.

### 2. An Old Testament Parallel: Ezekiel

The scene in Revelation 10 closely resembles Ezekiel 2-3.

>! Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel. So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat that roll.
>! — Ezekiel 3:1-2 (KJV)

>! Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.
>! — Ezekiel 3:3 (KJV)

Ezekiel also ate a scroll, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth. This is **a symbolic act of prophetic commissioning**, in which a prophet receives God's word in order to deliver it. Just as Ezekiel's eating of the scroll was Ezekiel's own experience, the eating of the scroll in Revelation is John's experience.

### 3. What "Thou Must Prophesy Again" Means

In Revelation 10:11, John is given a further prophetic task: "Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings." And in fact, from Revelation 11 onward John sees and records many more visions. This "prophesying again" ties directly to the writing of the rest of Revelation.

### 4. On What Grounds Is This Scene Applied to Someone Other Than John?

For Shincheonji to apply this passage to Chairman Lee Man-hee, one of the following would have to hold:

- Grounds showing that John had this experience on behalf of (as a representative of) a different person in the future
- Grounds showing that Revelation 10 is not John's actual experience but a foreshadowing of a future event
- Grammatical or contextual grounds showing that "I" refers to someone other than John

We need to distinguish whether these grounds come directly from the text, or whether this is an interpretation that has meaning only within Shincheonji's doctrinal system.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "Revelation is a book of prophecy that shows what will happen in the future. What John saw were future events, and John saw that scene on behalf of the future promised pastor."

For this interpretation to work, there would need to be a consistent standard for telling which parts of Revelation are John's own experience and which are a stand-in experience for a future figure.

If the "I" of Revelation 10 is not John but some other future figure, then by the same standard the other instances of "I" in Revelation (for example, 1:9, "I John, who also am your brother," and 1:17, "when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead") could also be someone else. We need to check whether this standard is applied consistently.

---

## Summary

The text of Revelation 10 says directly that John is the one who eats the scroll. In the Old Testament book of Ezekiel, the same symbolic act is recorded as the prophet's own experience. Applying this scene to a particular modern person rather than John requires a separate premise brought in from outside the text.

**If the text says "I (John)," then the grounds for changing that to someone else have to be found in the text itself.**
selfCheckQuestions: According to the text, who is the speaker who says "I" in Revelation 10?
In Ezekiel 3, is the one who eats the scroll Ezekiel himself or some future figure?
What is the standard for reading the "I" of Revelation as someone other than John, and is it applied consistently?
How does "Thou must prophesy again" connect with the rest of Revelation?

03-06.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-06.title: Who Is the Messenger of Revelation 22:16?
03-06.description: Examines Shincheonji's presentation of Chairman Lee Man-hee as the "messenger" (angel) of Revelation 22:16, in light of the context and the use of the word for angel throughout Revelation.
03-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Revelation 22:16, who is "mine angel," the messenger Jesus says he has sent? Does the conclusion that this messenger is a particular modern person come directly from the text?

## What Shincheonji Claims

On its [official website](https://www.shincheonji.org/ko/introduce/organization), Shincheonji presents Chairman Lee Man-hee as the messenger of Revelation 22:16. In "I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches," they say, "mine angel" is Chairman Lee Man-hee.

## Relevant Scripture

>! I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
>! — Revelation 22:16 (KJV)

>! The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John.
>! — Revelation 1:1 (KJV)

>! And he saith unto me, Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand.
>! — Revelation 22:10 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Meaning of ἄγγελος (Angelos)

The Greek word behind "angel" (messenger) in Revelation 22:16 is ἄγγελος (angelos). It means "messenger" or "angel," and depending on context it can refer either to a heavenly angel or to a human messenger.

Shincheonji argues that the word here means a human messenger, and that this human messenger is Chairman Lee Man-hee. But there is a wide logical gap between the possibility that ἄγγελος can mean a human being and the conclusion that this human being is one specific individual.

### 2. How ἄγγελος Is Used Throughout Revelation

ἄγγελος appears more than 70 times in Revelation, and most of those occurrences refer to heavenly angels.

- The seven angels who sound the trumpets (8:2)
- The seven angels who pour out the vials (15:1)
- The angel who shows the new Jerusalem (21:9)
- The angel who delivers the revelation to John (22:8)

In particular, the angel in Revelation 1:1, "he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John," is the same word ἄγγελος. The same word is used at the opening and the close of Revelation, and the angel of the opening (1:1) is generally understood to be a heavenly angel.

Reading only the ἄγγελος of 22:16 as a human being requires evidence that it differs from the ἄγγελος of 1:1.

### 3. The Context of Revelation 22

Consider the flow of Revelation 22:6-16:

- 22:6: "the Lord God of the holy prophets sent his angel"
- 22:8: "And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things."
- 22:9: The angel says, "See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God."
- 22:16: "I Jesus have sent mine angel"

In 22:8-9, the angel who showed John the revelation refuses worship and calls himself a "fellowservant." It is quite likely that this angel is the same being as the messenger of 22:16. In context, this angel is the one who showed John the visions, and he plays the role of mediator for the narrative of Revelation as a whole.

### 4. What "In the Churches" Means

The phrase "in the churches" in 22:16 means that the content of this revelation is delivered to the seven churches (or, more broadly, to all churches). In the structure of Revelation, the content of this testimony is the whole book, and the person who wrote it down is John.

The messenger's role is to deliver the revelation, and in Revelation the final recipient of that delivery is John. The text consistently keeps the structure in which this messenger is an angel sent to John.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "The messenger of Revelation 22:16 is the one who is to 'testify' to the churches, so he must be a human messenger who actually goes to the churches and testifies. An angel does not go to a church and testify in person."

This objection makes a fair point. The words "to testify unto you" assume an actual act of testimony. But in the structure of Revelation, the one who carries out this testimony is **John**, because John wrote down the revelation he received through the angel and sent it to the seven churches (Revelation 1:11).

The structure "messenger = angel → delivered to John → John writes it down and testifies to the churches" is already laid out at the opening of Revelation (1:1-4). Setting that structure aside and reading the messenger as a separate modern person requires additional grounds.

---

## Summary

The word ἄγγελος in Revelation 22:16 is used more than 70 times in Revelation, mostly for heavenly angels. The same word is used in the same role at the opening (1:1) and the close (22:16) of Revelation. In the context of chapter 22, this messenger is quite likely the same being as the angel who showed John the revelation.

The conclusion that this messenger is a particular modern person does not come directly from the text; it is an interpretation that has meaning only within Shincheonji's doctrinal system.

**That the phrase "mine angel" exists and that this messenger is a particular individual are two different claims.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is the same Greek word used for "his angel" in Revelation 1:1 and "mine angel" in 22:16?
How many times does ἄγγελος refer to a human being in Revelation, and what do most of its uses refer to?
Are the angel of Revelation 22:8-9 and the messenger of 22:16 the same being or different beings?
What argument is needed to get from "a messenger exists" to "the messenger is a particular individual"?
In Revelation's chain of testimony (God → Jesus → angel → John → churches), where would a modern individual fit?
sources: Shincheonji Church of Jesus, the Temple of the Tabernacle of the Testimony, official website, "Organization" page (accessed 2026-08-04)

03-07.seriesTitle: Saviors of Each Age and the Promised Pastor
03-07.title: Must We Believe in the Promised Pastor to Be Saved?
03-07.description: Examines Shincheonji's claim that believing in the promised pastor is a condition of salvation, in light of the teaching on salvation in Acts, John, and Romans.
03-07.content:
## A Question to Start With

What does the Bible say are the conditions of salvation? Must believing in a particular person be added to believing in Jesus Christ?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that salvation can be reached only through the promised pastor of each age. Believing in and following Chairman Lee Man-hee, the promised pastor of the present age, is said to be a necessary condition of salvation. The reasoning is that without the promised pastor no one can know the true meaning of Revelation, and without knowing its true meaning no one can be saved.

## Relevant Scripture

>! Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
>! — Acts 4:12 (KJV)

>! Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
>! — John 14:6 (KJV)

>! That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
>! — Romans 10:9 (KJV)

>! For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
>! — Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Conditions of Salvation in Scripture

The New Testament bears consistent witness to the conditions of salvation.

- **Acts 4:12**: There is "none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." The only saving name is Jesus Christ.
- **John 14:6**: Jesus is the only way to the Father. "But by me" leaves no room for any other stopover.
- **Romans 10:9**: The condition of salvation is to "confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus" and to believe in the resurrection.
- **Ephesians 2:8-9**: Salvation comes by grace through faith, not of works.

None of these verses adds "believing in the promised pastor" as a condition of salvation.

### 2. The Problem of Adding a Human Being to the Mediator

>! For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
>! — 1 Timothy 2:5 (KJV)

If there is one mediator between God and men, then the claim that salvation must pass through yet another human being effectively adds another mediator to the declaration of "one."

Even if Shincheonji describes the promised pastor not as a "mediator" but as a "teacher" or "witness," the moment that role is presented as a necessary condition of salvation, it in fact functions as a mediator.

### 3. The Problem with "You Must Know in Order to Be Saved"

Shincheonji's teaching on salvation is built like this:

1. You must know the true meaning of Revelation to be saved.
2. Only the promised pastor can teach the true meaning of Revelation.
3. Therefore you must learn from the promised pastor to be saved.

In this structure, the condition of salvation shifts from **believing in Jesus Christ** to **knowing a particular person's interpretation**. "Knowing the actual fulfillment (silsang) of Revelation" is not among the conditions of salvation in Romans 10:9.

This structure also leads to the conclusion that every Christian before the promised pastor appeared could not have been saved. We need to ask whether all the believers across two thousand years of church history who did not know the "true meaning" of Revelation are excluded from salvation.

### 4. What Did Paul Add to Salvation?

>! But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
>! — Galatians 1:8 (KJV)

Paul warns strongly against preaching **any other gospel** than the one he preached. By the words "or an angel from heaven," no being, whatever its authority, may add another condition to the gospel. Consider for yourself whether adding faith in a particular person to the conditions of salvation amounts to "another gospel."

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "In the Old Testament age, God's will could not be known except through Moses, and in the age of the first coming there was no salvation except through Jesus. In the same way, in the age of the second coming one must go through the promised pastor."

This objection assumes the scheme of ages. But that premise itself needs to be tested. Moses delivered the law; Jesus is the fulfiller of the law and the Savior (Matthew 5:17, Hebrews 9:12). The roles of Moses and Jesus are different in kind.

Above all, the claim that another path of salvation is needed after Jesus collides directly with the declaration of Hebrews 9:12 that he "entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us." If Jesus' salvation is complete, no further condition is needed; if a further condition is needed, then Jesus' salvation is not complete. The two cannot both stand.

---

## Summary

The Bible presents faith in Jesus Christ as the condition of salvation. Acts 4:12 declares that there is no salvation through any other name, and 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is one mediator. Galatians 1:8 warns against adding other conditions to the gospel.

Adding faith in a particular person to the conditions of salvation inserts something that is not found in the Bible's teaching on salvation. Whether this amounts to "another gospel" deserves careful consideration.

**If salvation is complete in Jesus Christ alone, no further condition is needed. If a further condition is needed, then the salvation of Jesus Christ is not complete.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any exception to the declaration in Acts 4:12 that there is "none other name"?
Does "knowing the actual fulfillment of Revelation" appear among the conditions of salvation in Romans 10:9?
Could the Christians of the two thousand years before the promised pastor not have been saved?
Does adding a particular person to the conditions of salvation not fall under the warning of Galatians 1:8?
If the "eternal redemption" obtained once for all in Hebrews 9:12 is complete, is any further condition needed?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Acts 4:12, John 14:6, Romans 10:9, Ephesians 2:8-9, 1 Timothy 2:5, Galatians 1:8, Hebrews 9:12

04-01.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-01.title: Is Betrayal, Destruction, Salvation the One Pattern of the Whole Bible?
04-01.description: Compares with Scripture Shincheonji's core doctrine that all of biblical history unfolds as a repeating pattern of betrayal, destruction, and salvation.
04-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

Is the claim that biblical history repeats a single pattern of "betrayal → destruction → salvation" something the Bible itself teaches, or an interpretive framework laid over the Bible?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that biblical history moves in a three-stage cycle of **betrayal, destruction, and salvation**. When the people God has chosen (the chosen people) betray him, a destroyer appears and brings them down; then God sends a new promised pastor to save. This pattern, they say, has repeated from the age of Adam until now, and it is "the one true order of the whole Bible."

## Relevant Scripture

>! God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
>! — Hebrews 1:1-2 (KJV)

>! For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
>! — John 3:16 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. Does the Bible Itself Teach This Pattern?

No verse anywhere in the Bible directly declares that "betrayal, destruction, and salvation is the repeating pattern of biblical history." The pattern is an **interpretive framework** that Shincheonji built by rearranging various events in the Bible.

An interpretive framework cannot be dismissed as wrong just because it is a framework. But to call it "the one true order of the whole Bible," the pattern would have to fit every major event in Scripture without exception.

### 2. Biblical Events That Do Not Fit the Pattern

Many events in the Bible are hard to explain with the betrayal-destruction-salvation pattern.

- **The death of Abel** (Genesis 4): Abel did not betray God, yet he was killed. The sequence of betrayal → destruction does not hold.
- **The suffering of Job** (Job): Job was a righteous man, yet he suffered. Destruction (suffering) came without betrayal.
- **The story of Joseph** (Genesis 37-50): It can be forced into a frame of the brothers' betrayal → Joseph's suffering → salvation, but that is not the "betrayal of the chosen people" the doctrine speaks of.
- **The story of Ruth** (Ruth): The account of Ruth, a foreign woman, joining an Israelite family does not fit the betrayal-destruction-salvation pattern.
- **The story of Daniel** (Daniel): Daniel was taken captive but stayed faithful to the end. There were chosen people who did not betray God.

### 3. Is "Betrayal" Defined Consistently?

We need to look at how Shincheonji's doctrine applies the term "betrayal."

- Age of Adam: Adam's fall = betrayal
- Age of Noah: the corruption of the world = betrayal
- Age of Moses: the golden calf = betrayal
- First coming: the Jewish religious leaders' rejection of Jesus = betrayal
- Present age: the betrayal of the Tabernacle Temple (Yoo Jae-yeol)

The nature of the "betrayal" differs in every case. Adam's fall was disobedience, Noah's age was general corruption, the golden calf was idolatry, and the Jewish leaders' act was rejection of the Messiah. To bind these into one pattern, "betrayal" has to be defined very broadly. The broader the definition, the more nearly any event can be squeezed into the pattern, and at that point the pattern loses its value as a tool of analysis.

### 4. The Structure of History in Hebrews

Hebrews 1:1-2 divides God's work into two stages: "in time past ... by the prophets" and "in these last days ... by his Son." The view of history in Hebrews is not a repeating cycle but a **progression** from the incomplete to the complete. Hebrews argues that with the coming of Jesus Christ a better covenant, a better sacrifice, and eternal redemption have been accomplished.

In this structure there is no room for the cycle of betrayal, destruction, and salvation to repeat after Jesus. The word "once" (ἐφάπαξ, Hebrews 9:12) in Hebrews means the cycle has ended.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "The repeating pattern of the Bible is something actually observed in human history. Israel betrayed God again and again, and each time God raised up a new leader."

It is true that Israel repeatedly left God and returned (the cycle in Judges). But that is not the same as the doctrinal pattern of "betrayal, destruction, salvation." The pattern in Judges recurs within the same chosen people; it is not a structure in which the chosen people are replaced. The New Testament also testifies that this Old Testament cycle came to an end with the coming of Jesus Christ.

---

## Summary

"Betrayal, destruction, salvation" is not a pattern the Bible itself declares; it is an interpretive framework built by selecting particular events from the Bible. Many events in Scripture do not fit it, and the definition of "betrayal" shifts from case to case. Hebrews testifies that the Old Testament cycle came to an end with the coming of Jesus Christ.

**Any interpretive framework can be made to fit if it is laid over the Bible. We have to distinguish whether a framework comes from the Bible itself or is brought in from outside and laid over it.**
selfCheckQuestions: Where does the Bible directly declare that "betrayal, destruction, and salvation is the repeating pattern of Scripture"?
Do the stories of Abel, Job, Ruth, and Daniel fit the betrayal-destruction-salvation pattern?
Is the "betrayal" of each age of the same nature, or are different events being bundled under one name?
Is the word "once" in Hebrews compatible with a repeating cycle?
Does a pattern that can be applied to almost any event have any value as a tool of analysis?

04-02.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-02.title: Was the Tabernacle Temple Really a Chosen People That Betrayed God?
04-02.description: Compares the historical record with Shincheonji's claims to examine whether Yoo Jae-yeol's Tabernacle Temple, which Shincheonji names as "the betrayer," was really a chosen people established by God.
04-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

For the betrayal-destruction-salvation pattern to work in Shincheonji's doctrine, those who betrayed God must first have been a "chosen people" established by God. Was Yoo Jae-yeol's Tabernacle Temple really a chosen people established by God?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the Tabernacle Temple founded by Yoo Jae-yeol (柳在烈), the Restored Gwacheon Tabernacle Temple, as the tabernacle of the seven golden candlesticks in Revelation. God, they say, established the Tabernacle Temple through Yoo Jae-yeol, and it served as the chosen people; but when Yoo Jae-yeol betrayed God, the betrayal in Revelation was fulfilled.

This claim is one of the starting points of Shincheonji doctrine. Without a betrayer there is no destroyer, and without a destroyer there is no need for a savior (the one who overcomes).

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. What Kind of Group Was the Tabernacle Temple?

Yoo Jae-yeol's Tabernacle Temple was a fringe Korean religious group active in the 1960s and 1970s. The established churches (the National Council of Churches in Korea, the Presbyterian Church in Korea, and others) never recognized it as an orthodox church.

The claim that the Tabernacle Temple was a chosen people established by God comes only from **Shincheonji's interpretation**. The Tabernacle Temple may well have claimed to be the chosen people of Revelation, but that claim has never been objectively confirmed.

### 2. Who Granted the Status of "Chosen People"?

In the Bible, the chosen people are the people God himself has chosen. In the Old Testament this is Israel; in the New Testament it is the church (those who believe in Christ).

>! But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people.
>! — 1 Peter 2:9 (KJV)

In 1 Peter 2:9, the "chosen generation" refers to everyone who believes in Christ. Designating one particular Korean religious group as the only chosen people of the age of Revelation goes beyond the scope of 1 Peter.

We need to ask what the grounds are for saying the Tabernacle Temple was a chosen people, and to distinguish whether that comes directly from the biblical text or from Shincheonji's interpretation of Revelation applied to the Tabernacle Temple.

### 3. Circular Logic in the Betrayal-Destruction-Salvation Structure

Shincheonji's line of reasoning can be laid out as follows:

1. Revelation records events of betrayal, destruction, and salvation.
2. The Tabernacle Temple is the chosen people of Revelation (the tabernacle of the seven golden candlesticks).
3. Because Yoo Jae-yeol betrayed God, the betrayal in Revelation was fulfilled.
4. Lee Man-hee, who saw this fulfillment, is the one who overcomes.

But how is proposition 2 (the Tabernacle Temple = the chosen people of Revelation) proven? It is supported by the reasoning that "because Lee Man-hee is the one who overcomes, the Tabernacle Temple he overcame must have been the chosen people." In other words, the conclusion (Lee Man-hee is the one who overcomes) proves the premise (the Tabernacle Temple was the chosen people), and the premise in turn proves the conclusion: a **circular structure**.

### 4. Independent Verification of the Tabernacle Temple

Whether the Tabernacle Temple was the chosen people of Revelation should be checkable independently, without Shincheonji's interpretation.

- Is there any objective assessment that the Tabernacle Temple's teaching was biblically sound?
- Is there any basis outside Shincheonji for saying the Tabernacle Temple corresponds to the seven churches of Revelation 1-3?
- Is there independent evidence confirming that Yoo Jae-yeol received a mission directly from God?

If the answers to all these questions begin with "according to Shincheonji's interpretation," then the Tabernacle Temple's status as chosen people is a premise that holds only within Shincheonji doctrine. (to be verified: further research needed on the Tabernacle Temple's exact teachings and record of activity)

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "That the Tabernacle Temple was the chosen people is something Chairman Lee Man-hee personally saw, heard, and testified to. The testimony of the one who witnessed the actual fulfillment of Revelation is the surest evidence."

This objection rests on "eyewitness testimony." But the claim that Chairman Lee Man-hee is an eyewitness is itself what needs to be tested. "I saw this myself" is a claim, not evidence. It has to be checked by whether it agrees with outside sources, whether its timeline is free of contradictions, and whether past and present accounts are consistent.

---

## Summary

The claim that the Tabernacle Temple was the chosen people of Revelation is a starting point of Shincheonji doctrine, but apart from Shincheonji's own interpretation it has no independent confirmation. If, in the betrayal-destruction-salvation structure, the identity of the betrayer depends on Shincheonji's conclusion, the argument is circular.

**If the premise a doctrine starts from can be proven only by the doctrine itself, that premise cannot be independently verified.**
selfCheckQuestions: Can the grounds for saying the Tabernacle Temple was the chosen people of Revelation be confirmed without Shincheonji's explanation?
Is there any record of established churches or outside bodies recognizing the Tabernacle Temple as an orthodox church?
Is the reasoning "it was the chosen people because it is what the one who overcomes overcame" not circular?
How could one independently confirm that Yoo Jae-yeol received a mission from God?
If the identity of the betrayer cannot be confirmed, do the identities of the destroyer and the savior not also become shaky?

04-03.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-03.title: Was the Steward Education Center the Destroyer?
04-03.description: Examines, through the historical record and the text of Revelation, Shincheonji's claim that the Steward Education Center (or its leader), which brought down the Tabernacle Temple, is the "destroyer" of Revelation.
04-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

What role did the party Shincheonji names as "the destroyer" actually play in history? Is it appropriate to map a dispute between Korean religious groups onto the cosmic war of Revelation?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the force that brought down the Tabernacle Temple (the betrayer) as the **destroyer** of Revelation (the beast, the dragon's forces). The Steward Education Center (or its leader) is usually named in this role. They infiltrated the Tabernacle Temple and brought it down from within, and this, Shincheonji says, is the actual fulfillment of the destruction recorded in Revelation.

(to be verified: the latest official Shincheonji materials on the specific people and group named as the destroyer, and the grounds given, need to be checked)

## Relevant Scripture

>! And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them.
>! — Revelation 13:7 (KJV)

>! And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.
>! — Revelation 12:9 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. The Scale of Revelation's Destroyer and of the Actual Events

The beast of Revelation 13 is described in terms like "power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations" (13:7), "all the world wondered after the beast" (13:3), and "they worshipped the beast" (13:4). These are events on a **worldwide scale**.

The dispute between the Tabernacle Temple and the Steward Education Center, by contrast, was a conflict between small religious groups in Korea. It is nowhere near the scale of "all kindreds, and tongues, and nations." We need to ask whether mapping Revelation's cosmic, worldwide language onto one particular Korean religious dispute fits the sense of scale in the text.

### 2. Has the Identity of the Destroyer Been Kept Consistent?

We need to check whether the party Shincheonji names as the destroyer has stayed the same throughout the group's history. The destroyer's name, role, and the timing of events should be compared between early teaching and current teaching.

If the account of the destroyer's identity has changed over time, the claim that Revelation's prophecy speaks precisely about specific events loses credibility. (to be verified: comparison of how early and current teaching materials describe the destroyer)

### 3. The Problem of Mapping Korean Religious Disputes onto Revelation

Revelation opens as a letter sent to seven churches in first-century Asia Minor. We have to consider what these words meant to John, its author, and to its original readers.

There are several traditions of interpreting Revelation:

- **Preterism**: reads the events as fulfilled in the first-century Roman Empire
- **Historicism**: reads the events as unfolding progressively across church history
- **Futurism**: reads the events as still to come
- **Idealism**: reads the book as symbolizing the spiritual struggle between good and evil

Shincheonji's reading, that the events of Revelation took place in a particular Korean religious group in the 1980s, belongs to none of these traditions; it is an interpretation of its own. That alone does not prove it wrong, but for it to stand it would need very strong grounds.

### 4. The Context of "Make War with the Saints, and Overcome Them"

>! And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations.
>! — Revelation 13:7 (KJV)

In this verse, those the beast overcomes are "the saints," and the scope is "all kindreds, and tongues, and nations." We need to examine whether the Steward Education Center's bringing down of the Tabernacle Temple matches this scale, and how the premise that the Tabernacle Temple's members were "the saints" is confirmed.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "The language of Revelation has a spiritual meaning, so it cannot be judged by physical scale. 'All kindreds and tongues' may mean each tribe of spiritual Israel."

This objection asks us to read Revelation's language spiritually. But if that standard is applied consistently, the other numbers and dimensions in Revelation must all be read down spiritually as well. Is 144,000 a literal number or a symbol? Is the size of the new Jerusalem literal or symbolic? If the standard shifts according to convenience, the interpretation has a consistency problem.

---

## Summary

Interpreting the Steward Education Center as the destroyer of Revelation means mapping Revelation's worldwide, cosmic scale onto a small religious dispute in Korea. For this interpretation to stand, it has to account for the difference in scale and show that the account of the destroyer's identity has stayed consistent. The premise that the Tabernacle Temple were "the saints" also has to be verified independently.

**Mapping the cosmic events of Revelation onto a small dispute at a particular time and place requires grounds for that mapping that come directly from the text.**
selfCheckQuestions: Does the scale of "all kindreds, and tongues, and nations" ruled by the beast in Revelation 13 match the scale of a Korean religious dispute?
Is the account of the party named as the destroyer consistent between early and current teaching?
How is the premise that the Tabernacle Temple's members were the "saints" of Revelation confirmed?
Is the standard of reading Revelation's language spiritually being applied consistently to other verses?
Could this interpretation be derived from the biblical text alone, without Shincheonji's explanation?

04-04.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-04.title: Were the Seven Messengers the Seven Stars of Revelation?
04-04.description: Examines, through the context of the passage and the historical facts, the claim that seven specific figures in Shincheonji's history are the seven stars (the angels of the seven churches) of Revelation 1.
04-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Revelation 1:20, the "seven stars" in Jesus' right hand are explained as "the angels of the seven churches." Shincheonji teaches that these seven angels, or messengers, were seven specific people in the Tabernacle Temple. Does this interpretation come directly from the text?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the seven stars of Revelation 1:20 were seven leaders (messengers) in the Tabernacle Temple. These seven messengers, they say, were the recipients of the letters addressed to the angels of the seven churches in Revelation 2-3, and when the Tabernacle Temple betrayed God and was destroyed, these seven betrayed God along with it. Chairman Lee Man-hee, as the one who witnessed their betrayal and overcame, is said to have opened a new age.

(to be verified: official materials on the specific list of people Shincheonji names as the seven messengers, and the grounds given, need to be checked)

## Relevant Scripture

>! The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
>! — Revelation 1:20 (KJV)

>! Unto the angel of the church of Ephesus write; These things saith he that holdeth the seven stars in his right hand, who walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks.
>! — Revelation 2:1 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. Who Is the "Angel" (ἄγγελος)?

In Revelation 2-3, each letter is sent to the "angel" of a church. There are several interpretations of who this angel, or messenger, is:

- **An angel**: a heavenly angel responsible for each church
- **A pastor or overseer**: the human leader of each church
- **A personification of the church**: a figure of speech for the church community itself

Shincheonji reads the messenger as a human leader and then narrows it to seven people in one particular Korean group at one particular time. Reading the messenger as human is a possible interpretation in itself, but the conclusion that this human was a specific person in twentieth-century Korea rather than first-century Asia Minor needs grounds of its own.

### 2. The Situations of the Seven Churches and Their Counterparts in the Tabernacle Temple

Each of the seven churches in Revelation 2-3 is in a situation of its own.

- **Ephesus**: has left its first love (2:4)
- **Smyrna**: tribulation and poverty (2:9)
- **Pergamos**: dwells where Satan's seat is (2:13)
- **Thyatira**: tolerates Jezebel (2:20)
- **Sardis**: has a name that it lives, but is dead (3:1)
- **Philadelphia**: has a little strength and has kept the word (3:8)
- **Laodicea**: neither cold nor hot (3:15-16)

We need to check whether these seven situations match, in concrete terms, the situations of each of the seven messengers in the Tabernacle Temple. For example, did one of the seven "dwell where Satan's seat is," another endure "tribulation and poverty," and another "tolerate Jezebel," each in a different situation?

If all seven messengers were in the same Tabernacle Temple, it needs to be explained how the seven churches' different situations could all hold at once in a single place.

### 3. The Problem of the Number Seven

It needs to be confirmed historically whether the Tabernacle Temple had exactly seven leaders, and whether those seven correspond one by one to the seven churches of Revelation.

- If there were more than seven leaders, who was selected, and by what standard?
- If there were fewer than seven, how was the number made to fit seven?
- Was the selection of the seven fixed in advance, or assigned after the fact?

This is a question of historical verification. Whether it was declared in advance that "these seven are the seven stars," or the seven were mapped onto the seven stars after the events, changes the nature of the interpretation.

### 4. The Relationship to Revelation's Original Readers

The seven churches of Revelation (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea) were **real churches in real cities**. Their existence is confirmed by first-century archaeological evidence and historical records.

For Revelation's original readers, the angels of the seven churches were their own church leaders (or the angels assigned to them). Reinterpreting them as specific people in twentieth-century Korea requires explaining why the original first-century meaning ceased to apply.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "Revelation is a book of prophecy, so it was fulfilled first in the first century and will be fulfilled finally at the end time. The seven churches spiritually symbolize seven sections of the Tabernacle Temple."

Double fulfillment (or multiple fulfillment) is one of the methods recognized in biblical interpretation. But to claim multiple fulfillment, the meaning in the original context has to match the new application. We need to check whether the distinct situation of each of the seven churches, such as Ephesus and Smyrna, corresponds concretely to the situation of the seven sections (or seven people) of the Tabernacle Temple.

---

## Summary

The seven stars of Revelation 1:20 are the angels of the seven churches, and those churches were real churches in first-century Asia Minor. Mapping them onto a particular group and particular people in twentieth-century Korea requires evidence that each church's distinct situation corresponds concretely to the situation of each of the seven people.

**A matching count of seven is not enough to conclude that the seven stars of Revelation are specific individuals.**
selfCheckQuestions: Does the distinct situation of each of the seven churches in Revelation correspond concretely to the situation of each of the seven people in the Tabernacle Temple?
Did the Tabernacle Temple have exactly seven leaders? By what standard were those seven chosen?
Was it announced in advance that these seven people were the seven stars, or was this mapped onto them after the fact?
On what grounds are letters to real churches in first-century Asia Minor applied to a particular Korean group?
Do the distinct problems of each church, such as Ephesus and Smyrna, also apply to each person in the Tabernacle Temple?

04-05.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-05.title: Which Came First, the Events or the Interpretation of Revelation?
04-05.description: Examines, by chronology and clear criteria, whether Shincheonji announced the events of Revelation in advance or linked events to Revelation after they had happened.
04-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

The fulfillment of Revelation that Shincheonji claims as its actual fulfillment (silsang), the events of betrayal, destruction, and salvation: were they specifically announced before they happened, or were they linked to Revelation after they happened?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the events of Revelation actually took place at a particular time and in a particular place. The betrayal of the Tabernacle Temple, the destroying work of the Steward Education Center, and Lee Man-hee's victory and salvation: all of these are said to be the actual fulfillment of what is written in Revelation.

## Relevant Scripture

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

>! And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.
>! — John 14:29 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. Telling Prophecy Apart from After-the-Fact Interpretation

True prophecy is declared specifically **before the event happens**. The Bible itself gives this standard.

- Deuteronomy 18:22: whether a prophet's word comes to pass is the test of a true prophet.
- John 14:29: Jesus spoke "before it come to pass."
- Isaiah 46:10: "Declaring the end from the beginning"

Above all, we have to look at **the order of events**. A prophecy is true prophecy only if it is declared before the event. If the event happens first and is linked to Scripture afterward, that is not the fulfillment of prophecy but **after-the-fact interpretation** (post-hoc interpretation).

### 2. Checking the Chronology of Shincheonji's History

The following need to be confirmed:

- Is there any record of Shincheonji (or Lee Man-hee) specifically announcing that "the Tabernacle Temple will betray God" **before** it did?
- Is there any record of a specific announcement that "a destroyer will come" **before** the Steward Education Center entered the Tabernacle Temple?
- Is there any record of an announcement that "the one who overcomes will come out of the Tabernacle Temple" **before** Lee Man-hee came forward as the one who overcomes?

If no such advance announcements are on record, then these events are not "the fulfillment of Revelation's prophecy" but "events that happened and were then mapped onto Revelation."

### 3. The Problems with After-the-Fact Interpretation

After-the-fact interpretation has these features:

- It links an event to a prophecy after the event has happened.
- The interpretation of the prophecy is adjusted to fit the event.
- The same prophecy can be applied to other events as well.
- It is not a testable prediction.

This does not mean that after-the-fact interpretation is necessarily false. But after-the-fact interpretation and advance prophecy have to be distinguished. If Shincheonji claims that the events of Revelation have been "fulfilled," it needs to make clear whether this is the fulfillment of an advance prophecy or an after-the-fact interpretation.

### 4. How Prophecy Is Fulfilled in Scripture

Consider how prophecies are fulfilled in the Bible:

- **Isaiah 7:14** → the virgin conception → fulfillment confirmed in Matthew 1:22-23
- **Micah 5:2** → birth in Bethlehem → fulfillment confirmed in Matthew 2:6
- **Psalm 22** → the suffering of the cross → fulfillment confirmed in the Gospels

These prophecies have several things in common: the prophecies themselves are specific, centuries separate the time of prophecy from the time of fulfillment, and the content of the prophecy was not altered after the fulfillment.

The same standard should be applied to Shincheonji's doctrine of actual fulfillment. We need to check which verse of Revelation prophesied the betrayal of the Tabernacle Temple, whether that verse pointed to the Tabernacle Temple before the event, and whether the interpretation was changed after the event.

### 5. If There Was an Advance Announcement, What Form Would It Take?

If Shincheonji claims to have prophesied before the events, the following conditions must be met:

- The content of the prophecy must survive in a record (a document, video, or similar with a verifiable date).
- The content of the prophecy must be specific enough (not at the level of "problems will arise in the future").
- The content of the prophecy must not have been revised afterward.

This question turns on whether any record meeting these conditions exists.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "Chairman Lee Man-hee personally witnessed these events at the Tabernacle Temple. He came to understand the actual fulfillment by comparing the words of Revelation with the actual events; it was not fitted together afterward."

This objection takes the form of "an eyewitness's realization." But it has two problems. First, "realization" and "advance prophecy" are different. Seeing an event and then realizing that it connects with Revelation is a form of after-the-fact interpretation. Second, to confirm whether an eyewitness's testimony is accurate, it has to be compared with independent sources.

In John 14:29, Jesus said, "I have told you **before** it come to pass." The standard of true prophecy is a declaration before the event; a realization after the event does not meet it.

---

## Summary

To claim the fulfillment of a prophecy, there must be a specific announcement before the event. The Bible itself gives this standard (Deuteronomy 18:22, John 14:29). Linking an event to Revelation after it has happened is after-the-fact interpretation and must be distinguished from the fulfillment of prophecy.

**The simplest way to tell prophecy from after-the-fact interpretation is to check the order of events. Check whether the prophecy was recorded before the event.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any Shincheonji record (with a verifiable date) that specifically announced the betrayal of the Tabernacle Temple in advance?
If the events were linked to Revelation after they happened, is that the fulfillment of prophecy or after-the-fact interpretation?
Do Shincheonji's claims of actual fulfillment have the same structure as the pattern of fulfilled prophecy in Scripture (Isaiah, Micah, and others)?
What does it mean that Jesus spoke "before it come to pass" in John 14:29?
Are "realization" and "advance prophecy" the same thing?

04-06.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of Betrayal, Destruction, and Salvation
04-06.title: Are the Accounts of the Betrayer and the Destroyer Consistent?
04-06.description: Examines whether the identities of the betrayer and the destroyer named by Shincheonji have changed over time, and considers what any such change would mean.
04-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

Have the identities of the betrayer and the destroyer that Shincheonji teaches stayed the same from the group's early days until now? And if they have changed, can the "actual fulfillment" of Revelation change?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the betrayer, the destroyer, and the savior (the one who overcomes) of Revelation each correspond to particular people and groups. It calls this the "actual fulfillment" (silsang) and says it consists of events that really happened as written in Revelation.

The doctrine of actual fulfillment is built around **naming specific people**. It teaches in concrete terms who the betrayer is, who the destroyer is, and who the one who overcomes is.

## Relevant Scripture

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken.
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

>! And Jesus answered and said unto them, Take heed that no man deceive you. For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many.
>! — Matthew 24:4-5 (KJV)

## What Needs to Be Examined

### 1. What It Means to Check for Changes

This article asks, "Have the accounts of the betrayer and the destroyer changed over time?" This is a question of **consistency**, separate from whether the doctrine itself is true.

If the actual fulfillment of Revelation consists of historical events that really happened, the main figures in those events cannot change, because historical facts are fixed. If the account of who the betrayer or destroyer is has changed over time, then one of the following must be true:

- The earlier account was wrong (the actual fulfillment was misidentified)
- The current account is an addition (it reveals something not disclosed before)
- Both accounts are right but from different angles (they are different aspects of the same event)

### 2. Specific Items That Need Checking

The following items should be compared between past and current teaching materials:

- **The betrayer's identity**: Is the person named early on the same as the person named now?
- **The destroyer's identity**: Is the person (or group) named early on the same as now?
- **The timing of the betrayal**: When is the betrayal said to have happened? Has that timing ever changed?
- **The manner of destruction**: How is the destroyer said to have brought down the Tabernacle Temple?
- **The list of the seven messengers**: Have the people corresponding to the seven stars stayed the same?

(to be verified: a concrete comparison of early Shincheonji teaching materials (1980s-90s) with current ones. This may be possible through the testimony of former members or leaked materials, but the authenticity of the original sources needs to be verified)

### 3. What a Confirmed Change Would Mean

If it is confirmed that the account of the betrayer or destroyer has changed, that is different from a simple change of wording.

- **A change of wording**: "The chosen people betrayed God" → "The people God chose turned away from him": the same content expressed differently
- **A change of content**: "The betrayer is A" → "The betrayer is B": a change in the core claim

If the key figures have changed, that is a change of content. If the actual fulfillment of Revelation is historical fact, the main figures in that fact cannot change.

### 4. The Explanation of "Food in Due Season"

When doctrinal changes are pointed out, Shincheonji sometimes explains them with the idea of "food in due season" (KJV: "meat in due season"). Because God gives the word that is needed at each time, they say, content not revealed before is newly disclosed.

>! Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?
>! — Matthew 24:45 (KJV)

But "food in due season" and "changing an earlier account" have to be distinguished. Telling people something new in addition is different from changing what was said before. Teaching "the betrayer is A" and then changing it to "the betrayer is B" is not adding food; it is throwing out the earlier food.

### 5. Ways to Check for Changes

Here are some ways readers can check for themselves:

- If you have notes from teaching you received in the past, compare them with what is taught now.
- Compare what you learned with people who completed the same course at a different time.
- Check whether past teaching materials or sermon videos are still publicly available.
- Check whether teaching materials have ever been recalled or had access restricted.

If the doctrine has not changed, there should be no problem in making past materials public.

## Possible Objections from Shincheonji

> "The doctrine did not change; when the time came, deeper content was opened. You cannot tell everything from the start; it is taught step by step according to the believers' level."

Teaching in stages can be reasonable. But teaching in stages and changing content are different things. Teaching "it is A" in stage one and then saying "now I will tell you more about A" in stage two is teaching in stages. Teaching "it is A" in stage one and then saying "actually, it is B" in stage two is a change.

And if access to past materials is restricted, we need to distinguish whether that is because of the needs of staged teaching or to keep changed content from coming to light.

---

## Summary

If the actual fulfillment of Revelation is historical fact, the account of that fact should stay consistent over time. If the identities of the betrayer and the destroyer have changed, that means the earlier account was wrong, and that affects the credibility of the doctrine of actual fulfillment.

The simplest way for readers to check for themselves is to compare past teaching materials with current ones.

**Historical facts do not change. If the account of them has changed, what changed is not the facts but the interpretation.**
selfCheckQuestions: Is the name of the betrayer you learned early in Shincheonji's teaching the same as the name taught now?
Has the account of the destroyer ever changed over time?
Are past teaching materials or sermon videos still accessible today? If access has been restricted, why?
How can "food in due season" be distinguished from "throwing out an earlier account"?
Did people who completed the same course at different times learn the same content?

05-01.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-01.title: Was Revelation Fulfilled in South Korea?
05-01.description: Shincheonji claims that the prophecies of Revelation were fulfilled in South Korea. This article looks at the original recipients and context the text of Revelation points to.
05-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

If Revelation is a prophecy fulfilled in one particular country, why was it sent to seven churches in first-century Asia Minor?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the prophecies recorded in Revelation were fulfilled as concrete events in South Korea. Particular Korean religious groups and people are said to be the real substance (實體) behind the figures that appear in Revelation, and Chairman Lee Man-hee is said to have personally witnessed all of these events.

## The Original Recipients of Revelation

Revelation names its recipients clearly at the outset.

>! John to the seven churches which are in Asia.
>! — Revelation 1:4 (KJV)

>! What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia; unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea.
>! — Revelation 1:11 (KJV)

These seven churches really existed in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey). Revelation 2-3 contains messages suited to the concrete situation of each church.

## The Recipients Had to Be Able to Understand It

Revelation says that those who read this message are blessed.

>! Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand.
>! — Revelation 1:3 (KJV)

The words "for the time is at hand" conveyed an imminent meaning to first-century readers. If this prophecy were to be fulfilled only in Korea two thousand years later, its original recipients could not have read and kept it.

## Can Events of Cosmic Scale Be Confined to One Country?

The prophecies of Revelation deal with events of cosmic scale that concern every people and nation.

>! Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him.
>! — Revelation 1:7 (KJV)

Expressions like "every eye" and "all kindreds of the earth" describe a universal scope that cannot be confined to one country. Narrowing them down to particular events in Korea requires separate grounds.

## Summary

Revelation is a document sent to seven churches in first-century Asia Minor, and it contains a message its original recipients could understand and keep. An interpretation that confines Revelation's prophecies to events in a particular country, a particular era, and a particular group stands in tension with what the text says about its recipients and with its universal scope. Accepting such a narrowed interpretation would require grounds drawn from the biblical text itself.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you confirmed directly from the text who the original recipients of Revelation were?
Is there any basis for taking "for the time is at hand" to refer to events two thousand years later?
Is there any textual basis for confining Revelation's "all kindreds of the earth" to one country?
Can you explain how a letter sent to seven churches in Asia Minor becomes a story about Korea?
Does the evidence for this interpretation come from the biblical text or from Shincheonji's explanation?

05-02.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-02.title: Is the Tabernacle of the Seven Golden Candlesticks the Tabernacle Temple?
05-02.description: Shincheonji interprets the seven golden candlesticks as the Tabernacle Temple (a religious group based in Gwacheon). This article looks at the explanation the text of Revelation itself gives.
05-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

If Revelation itself explains what the "seven golden candlesticks" are, why would another interpretation be needed?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the seven golden candlesticks of Revelation are the Tabernacle Temple that existed in Gwacheon (a religious group led by Yoo Jae-yeol). The core narrative of Shincheonji doctrine is that betrayal took place in this Tabernacle Temple, and that Chairman Lee Man-hee came out of it and set up a new tabernacle of truth.

## What the Text of Revelation Says Directly

Revelation explains the meaning of the seven golden candlesticks itself.

>! The mystery of ... the seven golden candlesticks ... the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
>! — Revelation 1:20 (KJV)
