The text of Revelation spells it out: "the seven candlesticks ... are the seven churches." These seven churches are named specifically in 1:11 as Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.

## The Seven Churches Were Real Historical Churches

Revelation 2-3 delivers a separate message to each of these seven churches. Each message reflects the concrete situation of that church.

- **Ephesus**: has left its first love (2:4)
- **Smyrna**: will have tribulation ten days (2:10)
- **Pergamos**: dwells where Satan's seat is (2:13)
- **Thyatira**: tolerates the woman Jezebel (2:20)

These concrete descriptions match the actual situation of first-century Asia Minor. Pergamum really did have an altar of Zeus (interpreted as Satan's seat), and the historical background of each city fits the content of its message.

## Can One Group Be Seen as Seven Churches?

If, as Shincheonji interprets it, the seven candlesticks are the Tabernacle Temple, it needs to be explained why seven different messages were sent to a single group. It also needs to be explained why the praise and rebuke for each church differ.

## Summary

Revelation 1:20 says directly that the seven golden candlesticks are seven churches. These churches are named in 1:11, and in chapters 2-3 each receives its own message suited to its situation. Reinterpreting a symbol the text has already explained requires presenting textual grounds of corresponding weight.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you confirmed what Revelation 1:20 directly says the seven candlesticks are?
Do the messages to the seven churches in Revelation 2-3 read as messages about a single group?
Is it justified to change an interpretation the text itself has given into a different meaning?
Have you ever looked into the historical background of real churches such as Ephesus and Smyrna?

05-03.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-03.title: Who Are the Seven Heads and Ten Horns?
05-03.description: Shincheonji identifies the seven heads and ten horns of Revelation as specific Korean individuals. This article looks at the context of the text and the history of its interpretation.
05-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

What level of evidence would be needed to identify the "seven heads and ten horns" of Revelation as specific people living today?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji identifies the beast with seven heads and ten horns in Revelation 13 and 17 as specific Korean religious leaders. It teaches that the pastors who betrayed God in the Tabernacle Temple are the real substance of this beast.

## The Context of the Text

Revelation 17 explains the seven heads directly.

>! The seven heads are seven mountains, on which the woman sitteth. And there are seven kings.
>! — Revelation 17:9 (KJV)

>! And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet; but receive power as kings one hour with the beast.
>! — Revelation 17:12 (KJV)

The "seven mountains" have widely been read as pointing to the Roman Empire, since Rome was a city built on seven hills. The "seven kings" have been understood as successive Roman emperors.

## A Variety of Historical Interpretations

Many interpretations of the seven heads and ten horns have been offered over the centuries. From the early church to the present, this passage has been read as the Roman Empire, as worldly power, as the Antichrist of the end times, and more. Each interpretation offers grounds of its own.

But an interpretation that identifies this passage with specific Korean people living today has to answer the following questions:

- Is there anything in the biblical text indicating that these figures are Korean?
- How can the "seven mountains" be explained in a Korean context?
- Is there historical evidence that the "ten kings" exercised royal power?

## Telling Claims Apart from Evidence

Shincheonji identifies the real substance of this passage in very specific terms. The more specific a claim, the more specific the evidence it needs. A claim like "this person is one of the seven heads" must be supported by the biblical text, historical facts, and independent confirmation. Relying only on Shincheonji's internal explanation makes the argument circular.

## Summary

Interpretations of the seven heads and ten horns of Revelation have varied throughout history. But any interpretation needs textual grounds and independent evidence to support it. Identifying specific people living today requires evidence in proportion to how specific the claim is.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you confirmed from the text what the "seven mountains" of Revelation 17:9 refer to?
Do the grounds for identifying the seven heads and ten horns as specific people come from the Bible or from Shincheonji's explanation?
If another religious leader used the same method of interpretation to identify different people, how would you refute it?
Have you ever looked at how this interpretation compares with other interpretations in history?
Do you agree with the principle that specific claims require specific evidence?

05-04.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-04.title: What Were the Fire, Hail, and Blood of Revelation?
05-04.description: Shincheonji interprets the fire, hail, and blood of Revelation as doctrinal attacks or spiritual warfare. This article examines whether that spiritualizing interpretation is consistent.
05-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

If the fire, hail, and blood of Revelation are read in a spiritual sense, is the same principle being applied to Revelation's other physical descriptions?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the plagues described in Revelation, such as fire, hail, and blood, not as physical phenomena but as doctrinal attacks or spiritual warfare. It explains the physical imagery of the trumpet and vial plagues as doctrinal disputes between particular religious groups.

## The Connection to the Old Testament Background

The plague imagery of Revelation is closely tied to the Old Testament, especially the ten plagues of Exodus.

>! The first angel sounded, and there followed hail and fire mingled with blood, and they were cast upon the earth: and the third part of trees was burnt up.
>! — Revelation 8:7 (KJV)

This description echoes the plague of Exodus 9:23-24.

>! And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground.
>! — Exodus 9:23 (KJV)

The plagues of Exodus were actual physical events. If Revelation borrows this imagery, it is hard to insist that it carries a purely spiritual meaning.

## Selective Spiritualizing

We need to examine whether Shincheonji applies its spiritualizing interpretation consistently.

- If fire, hail, and blood are read spiritually, why are other elements read literally?
- What is the standard for taking the number 144,000 literally while taking the physical plagues spiritually?
- Is the interpretive principle being applied selectively to support a conclusion decided in advance?

Any system of interpretation is trustworthy only if it applies the same principles consistently.

## The Nature of Apocalyptic Literature

Revelation belongs to the literary genre of apocalyptic literature. Apocalyptic literature uses symbols and visions to express God's sovereignty and his final judgment. The features of this genre have to be understood, but that does not mean every image may be matched one-to-one with a particular modern event.

## Summary

The fire, hail, and blood of Revelation are closely tied to the plague imagery of the Old Testament and must be understood within the features of apocalyptic literature. Reading them only as doctrinal attacks or spiritual warfare is one possible position, but it needs to be examined whether the same interpretive principle is applied consistently and whether it fits the Old Testament background.
selfCheckQuestions: Given that the plagues of Exodus were actual events, on what grounds is the same imagery in Revelation read only spiritually?
Is there a standard for reading fire and hail spiritually while reading 144,000 literally?
Is the interpretive principle being applied selectively depending on the conclusion?
Have you ever studied the features of apocalyptic literature as a genre?
What would result if the same spiritualizing principle were applied to every verse of Revelation?

05-05.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-05.title: Was the War in Revelation a Doctrinal Dispute?
05-05.description: Shincheonji interprets the wars of Revelation as doctrinal disputes between religious groups. This article looks at the scale and nature of the war the text of Revelation describes.
05-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

Can the scale and outcome of the war Revelation describes be explained as a doctrinal dispute?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the wars in Revelation as doctrinal disputes between religious groups. It teaches that the war in heaven in Revelation 12, the final battle in chapter 19, and others were in reality doctrinal clashes inside and around the Tabernacle Temple.

## The Scale of the War Revelation Describes

The war in Revelation 12 is described on a heavenly scale.

>! And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, and prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven.
>! — Revelation 12:7-8 (KJV)

This war, in which Michael and the angels fight the dragon (Satan), is a cosmic spiritual war. Revelation 19 describes the final battle together with the return of Christ.

>! And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war.
>! — Revelation 19:11 (KJV)

## What Is Lost When It Is Reduced to a Doctrinal Dispute

If this war is read as a doctrinal dispute, the following elements of the text go unexplained:

- Why Michael and the angels appear (12:7)
- The dragon being cast out of heaven (12:9)
- The scene of Christ appearing on a white horse (19:11)
- The ending in which the beast and the false prophet are cast alive into the lake of fire (19:20)
- The millennial kingdom and the final judgment of chapter 20

In a doctrinal dispute, no one is cast into a lake of fire, and angels do not physically join the battle. Shrinking a spiritual war of this scale down to a dispute between organizations blurs the meaning the text means to convey: God's ultimate victory and judgment.

## Continuity with the War Imagery of the Old Testament

The war imagery of Revelation connects to the Old Testament tradition of the LORD's wars. Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and others also describe an end-time war in which God fights against the forces of evil. In this tradition, war represents God's sovereign judgment, not a doctrinal dispute.

## Summary

The war of Revelation is described as an event of cosmic scale, involving Michael and the angels, the return of Christ, and the final judgment. Reducing it to a doctrinal dispute between religious groups leaves core elements of the text unexplained and breaks its continuity with the Old Testament tradition.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you confirmed from the text who takes part in the war of Revelation 12:7-8?
If the war of Michael and the angels is read as a doctrinal dispute, who does Michael become?
In a doctrinal dispute, what would correspond to the beast and the false prophet being cast into the lake of fire?
Have you considered how this interpretation connects with the Old Testament tradition of the LORD's wars?
How does shrinking the scale of the war affect the meaning of God's sovereignty and judgment?

05-06.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-06.title: Does the Order of Events in Revelation Match Actual History?
05-06.description: Examines whether the chronological order of Revelation's fulfillment claimed by Shincheonji matches the actual historical record.
05-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

When fulfillment of prophecy is claimed, why does the order of events matter?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the prophecies of Revelation were fulfilled in Korea in a specific chronological order. It explains that the sequence of betrayal (the fall of the Tabernacle Temple) → destruction (its ruin by the dragon's forces) → salvation (Chairman Lee Man-hee's founding of a new tabernacle) matches the flow of Revelation.

## Why Order Matters in the Fulfillment of Prophecy

In the Bible, not only the content but also the order of fulfillment matters. When Old Testament prophecies were fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the order and manner foretold could be confirmed. In the same way, a claim that Revelation has been fulfilled requires that the sequence of events Revelation presents match actual history.

## Points That Need Examining

In Shincheonji's claim that Revelation has been fulfilled, the following need to be checked:

- Does the order of events recorded in Revelation match exactly the order of the historical events Shincheonji points to?
- Can the dates of the events Shincheonji claims be confirmed by independent historical sources?
- Has the interpretation of the order of events in Revelation ever changed over time? (to be verified)

## The Danger of After-the-Fact Interpretation

Claims of fulfilled prophecy call for caution about after-the-fact interpretation (事後解釋). Anyone can let an event happen first and then match Bible verses to it. True fulfillment of prophecy means the prophecy comes first and the event then happens as it said.

>! And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.
>! — John 14:29 (KJV)

Jesus said the purpose of prophecy is "that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe." In other words, a prophecy must be clearly stated before the event.

## Checking the Historical Record

For the specific events Shincheonji claims (the betrayal in the Tabernacle Temple, the actions of particular people, and so on), we need to check whether participants at the time or independent records testify to the same facts. One side's account alone is hardly enough to establish historical fact.

## Summary

A claim of fulfilled prophecy requires that the content, order, and timing of events all match, and that they be confirmable by independent records. The heart of the test is whether this is the fulfillment of an advance prophecy rather than after-the-fact interpretation, and whether the historical record supports it.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever compared the order of the fulfillment events Shincheonji claims directly with the text of Revelation?
Can the dates of these events be confirmed by independent records?
Can you tell the difference between matching Bible verses to events after they happen and events happening as prophesied?
Is the interpretation of the order of Revelation's fulfillment the same now as it was in the past?

05-07.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-07.title: Who Actually Witnessed the Fulfillment of Revelation?
05-07.description: Shincheonji claims that Chairman Lee Man-hee personally witnessed every event in the fulfillment of Revelation. This article considers whether that witness can be independently verified.
05-07.content:
## A Question to Start With

Can the fulfillment of historical events be established on the testimony of one person alone?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that Chairman Lee Man-hee personally saw with his own eyes and heard with his own ears every event in the fulfillment of Revelation. He is said to be the only witness, and the actual fulfillment of Revelation can be known only through his testimony.

## The Biblical Principle of Witnesses

The Bible sets out a clear principle for confirming testimony.

>! In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.
>! — 2 Corinthians 13:1 (KJV)

>! At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
>! — Deuteronomy 19:15 (KJV)

The Bible does not establish a fact on one person's testimony alone. The principle that the agreeing testimony of two or three witnesses is required holds consistently across the Old and New Testaments.

## The Absence of Independent Witnesses

Many people were involved in the events Shincheonji claims as the fulfillment of Revelation. The events at the Tabernacle Temple involved its members and pastors at the time, as well as outsiders. Whether any independent witness testifies to these events as "the fulfillment of Revelation," however, needs to be checked.

In particular, the following need to be examined:

- How do others who belonged to the Tabernacle Temple at the time remember the same events?
- Apart from Chairman Lee Man-hee, is there any independent witness who interprets the same events as "the fulfillment of Revelation"?
- Do records of the events in question exist in sources outside Shincheonji? (to be verified)

## Distinguishing the Witness from the Interpreter

"Witnessing" an event and "interpreting" that event as "the fulfillment of Revelation" are two different things. The fact that there was conflict inside a religious group may itself be confirmable. But the interpretation that this conflict fulfilled the prophecy of Revelation requires a separate argument.

If the facts witnessed and the interpretation are not kept apart, it is easy to mistake the existence of an event for proof that the interpretation is valid.

## Summary

By the principle of two or three witnesses, the Bible does not establish a fact on one person's testimony alone. We need to check whether there are independent witnesses and outside records of Revelation's fulfillment, and we must distinguish witnessing an event from interpreting it theologically.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you applied the biblical principle of witnesses (two or three witnesses) to this claim?
Apart from Chairman Lee Man-hee, is there any independent witness who testifies to the same events in the same way?
Can you tell the difference between witnessing an event and interpreting it as the fulfillment of Revelation?
Have you ever heard the testimony of others who took part in the Tabernacle Temple at that time?
Have you considered the risks of relying on the testimony of only one person?

05-08.seriesTitle: The Doctrine of the Actual Fulfillment of Revelation
05-08.title: Why Can the Actual Fulfillment Be Seen Only Through Shincheonji's Explanation?
05-08.description: If the actual fulfillment of Revelation really took place, why can no one confirm it without Shincheonji's commentary? This article examines that question.
05-08.content:
## A Question to Start With

If a prophecy has truly been fulfilled, must one particular group's commentary be needed to confirm it?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji explains that the prophecies of Revelation have already been fulfilled, but that understanding this actual fulfillment requires receiving Shincheonji's teaching. Only Chairman Lee Man-hee personally saw the actual fulfillment of Revelation, they say, and the fulfillment can be confirmed only through his testimony.

## Features of Fulfilled Prophecy Recorded in Scripture

When prophecy was fulfilled in the Bible, the fulfillment could usually be confirmed.

>! And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
>! — Luke 2:12 (KJV)

The shepherds heard the angel's words and could go and see the baby Jesus for themselves. No separate interpreter was needed.

>! So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.
>! — Matthew 24:33 (KJV)

Jesus spoke of the signs of fulfillment with the words "when ye shall see." The premise is that the fulfillment can be seen directly.

## The Structure of Circular Reasoning

Shincheonji's doctrine of actual fulfillment has the following circular structure:

1. The prophecies of Revelation have been fulfilled → therefore Shincheonji is true
2. Shincheonji is true → therefore Shincheonji's interpretation of the actual fulfillment is correct
3. Shincheonji's interpretation of the actual fulfillment is correct → therefore Revelation has been fulfilled

In this argument, the premises and the conclusion prop each other up. Breaking out of this circle would require at least one piece of evidence that can be confirmed independently, without Shincheonji's explanation.

## The Problem of Verifiability

If the fulfillment of Revelation truly took place, at least one of the following should be possible:

- Outside records of the events at the time exist
- Independent witnesses can confirm the same facts
- The results of the fulfillment can be observed in reality

If none of these can be confirmed without Shincheonji's commentary, then what we have is not fulfillment but interpretation. The point is not that the interpretation itself is wrong. It is that interpretation and fulfillment have to be distinguished.

## Summary

When prophecy was fulfilled in the Bible, the fulfillment could be confirmed without a particular interpreter. If the evidence of fulfillment can be reached only through one group's explanation, the reasoning becomes circular. A true fulfillment should allow independent confirmation.
selfCheckQuestions: In the cases of fulfilled prophecy recorded in the Bible, could the fulfillment be confirmed without a particular interpreter?
Can you find a circular structure in Shincheonji's claims of actual fulfillment?
Is there even one piece of evidence of fulfillment that can be confirmed independently, without Shincheonji's explanation?
Can you tell the difference between "interpretation" and "fulfillment"?
If another religious group claimed in the same way that events in its own group fulfilled Revelation, how would you tell the two apart?

06-01.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-01.title: Is 144,000 a Literal Number?
06-01.description: Shincheonji reads the 144,000 as an exact, literal headcount. This article examines the biblical and symbolic meaning of the number.
06-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

Shincheonji reads some numbers literally and others symbolically. What decides which is which?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the 144,000 of Revelation 7:4 as an exact, literal number of people. It teaches that its registered membership must reach exactly 144,000, and that when this number is filled, God's work will be complete.

## What the Text of Revelation Says

>! And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
>! — Revelation 7:4 (KJV)

In this verse, the 144,000 come "of all the tribes of the children of Israel." Verses 5-8 then specify 12,000 from each of the twelve tribes.

## The Structure of the Number: 12 x 12 x 1,000

144,000 is made up of 12 x 12 x 1,000. In Scripture, each of these numbers carries symbolic weight.

- **12**: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles of Jesus — the number of completeness for God's people
- **1,000**: often used in Scripture to express the fullness of a great number (Ps. 50:10; 84:10)

The 12 x 12 x 1,000 structure can be read as a symbolic expression of the complete number of God's people. Many biblical scholars interpret it this way.

## What Decides Literal Versus Symbolic?

Within Shincheonji's own system of interpretation, several questions arise.

- If fire, hail, and blood are read symbolically, why is the 144,000 read literally?
- Is the precise distribution of "12,000 from each" of the twelve tribes also applied literally? Must each tribe have exactly 12,000 people?
- If "the children of Israel" is read symbolically, on what basis is the number alone taken literally?

If, within a single verse, "the children of Israel" is read symbolically while "144,000" is read literally, the consistency of that interpretive principle needs to be explained.

## Summary

The number 144,000 is built on a 12 x 12 x 1,000 structure and can reasonably be read as a symbol of the complete number of God's people. Taking the number literally while reading "the children of Israel" in the same verse symbolically creates a problem of interpretive consistency.
selfCheckQuestions: Were you aware that 144,000 has a 12 x 12 x 1,000 structure?
What is the criterion for reading "the children of Israel" symbolically but the number literally?
Is the requirement of exactly 12,000 from each tribe also being applied literally?
What is the criterion for reading fire and hail symbolically but the 144,000 literally?
Do you know of other places in Scripture where numbers are used symbolically?

06-02.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-02.title: Are the 144,000 Shincheonji Members?
06-02.description: Shincheonji claims that the sealed 144,000 are its registered members. This article looks at how the text of Revelation describes those who are sealed.
06-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

Have you checked for yourself whether the traits Revelation gives the 144,000 actually match the traits of Shincheonji members?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the sealed 144,000 of Revelation 7:4 are the members registered with Shincheonji. Anyone who completes the Shincheonji education center course and is formally registered is, by this teaching, one of the sealed.

## How Revelation Describes the 144,000

Revelation spells out the characteristics of the 144,000 in concrete terms.

>! there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
>! — Revelation 7:4 (KJV)

First, these people come "of all the tribes of the children of Israel." In 7:5-8, the tribes are named one by one: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, and so on.

Revelation 14 describes further characteristics.

>! These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, being the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb. And in their mouth was found no guile: for they are without fault before the throne of God.
>! — Revelation 14:4-5 (KJV)

## The Text's Description Compared with Shincheonji Members

According to Revelation, the 144,000:

- Come from each of the tribes of Israel (7:4-8)
- Are pure (14:4)
- Follow the Lamb (14:4)
- Have no guile in their mouths (14:5)
- Are without fault (14:5)

"In their mouth was found no guile" and "without fault" set a very high moral standard. It is worth asking whether this is a qualification met by registering with an organization, or a spiritual state recognized by the grace of God.

## Whose Act Is the Sealing?

>! Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads.
>! — Revelation 7:3 (KJV)

The one who seals is God, and the text presents the sealing as God's sovereign act. That is different in kind from a registration procedure carried out by a human organization.

## Summary

The 144,000 described in Revelation come from the tribes of Israel, have no guile in their mouths, are without fault, and are sealed by God. Anyone who equates them with the membership roll of a particular group needs to explain concretely how each of these conditions is met.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you read for yourself how Revelation 14:4-5 describes the 144,000?
Can the condition "no guile in their mouth, without fault" be met by completing a course and registering?
If God is the one who seals, can a human organization manage the sealing?
However you interpret "all the tribes of the children of Israel," is that interpretation applied consistently?
Have you ever checked yourself against the text's own qualifications for the 144,000?

06-03.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-03.title: Are Shincheonji's Twelve Tribes the Twelve Tribes of the Bible?
06-03.description: Shincheonji has organized itself into twelve tribes. This article compares them with the twelve tribes of the Bible.
06-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

On what basis were the twelve tribes of the Bible formed, and could they really be the same kind of thing as the organizational divisions of a modern group?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji divides its organization into twelve tribes and gives each one the name of a biblical tribe (Judah, Reuben, Gad, and so on). It teaches that these are the reality behind the twelve tribes listed in Revelation 7:5-8.

## The Nature of the Twelve Tribes in Scripture

In the Bible, the twelve tribes are a division by lineage and nationhood that began with the twelve sons of Jacob (Israel).

>! The sons of Leah; Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Zebulun: ... and Benjamin: ... Dan, and Naphtali: ... Gad, and Asher
>! — Genesis 35:23-26 (KJV, abridged)

The twelve tribes were national units, each with its own family line, allotted land, and historical identity. That is fundamentally different from a modern division assigned according to an organizational chart.

## Unusual Features of the Tribal List in Revelation 7

The list of twelve tribes in Revelation 7:5-8 differs from the Old Testament lists.

- **The tribe of Dan is missing**
- **Manasseh is listed separately** (Manasseh was a son of Joseph and is usually counted within the tribe of Joseph)
- **Levi is included** (in the Old Testament, Levi was the priestly tribe that received no allotment of land)

These differences show that Revelation does not simply reproduce an Old Testament tribal list and that it has a theological purpose of its own. One has to ask whether Shincheonji's twelve tribes match this list exactly, and how Shincheonji accounts for these differences.

## Administrative Divisions Versus Biblical Tribes

Shincheonji's twelve tribes are regional, administrative divisions. Members are assigned to a tribe based on where they live or when they joined. Biblical tribes, by contrast, were determined by descent and could not be changed by personal choice or by an organization's decision.

This difference matters, because the interpretation of Revelation 7 depends on whether "all the tribes of the children of Israel" refers to tribes by descent or to something else. Whichever reading one adopts, it has to be applied consistently.

## Summary

The twelve tribes of the Bible were units of lineage and nationhood descended from Jacob, and the tribal list in Revelation 7 differs even from the Old Testament lists. Giving biblical tribal names to the administrative divisions of a modern organization does not make that organization the tribes of the Bible.
selfCheckQuestions: Do you know how the twelve tribes of the Bible were formed (from the twelve sons of Jacob)?
Have you noticed that the tribe of Dan is missing from the list in Revelation 7:5-8?
Do you recognize the difference between how Shincheonji assigns tribes (by region and administration) and the biblical tribes (by descent)?
Have you ever considered whether using the same name means being the same thing?

06-04.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-04.title: Can People Keep the Roll of the Sealed?
06-04.description: Shincheonji keeps an organizational roll of those it considers sealed. This article looks at who does the sealing in Scripture and what kind of act it is.
06-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Scripture, whose act is the sealing, and is it the kind of thing whose roll people can keep?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that members are sealed when they complete its education program and are registered. The roll of the sealed 144,000 is managed by the organization, and the count is adjusted as people register or leave.

## Who Does the Sealing in Scripture

In Revelation, it is clear who does the sealing.

>! And I saw another angel ascending from the east, having the seal of the living God: ... and he cried with a loud voice ... Saying, Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads.
>! — Revelation 7:2-3 (KJV)

The sealing is done with "the seal of the living God" and carried out through an angel. It is a sovereign act of God.

In Paul's letters as well, the one who seals is God, through the Holy Spirit.

>! In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,
>! — Ephesians 1:13 (KJV)

>! And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
>! — Ephesians 4:30 (KJV)

Sealing is accomplished by the Holy Spirit, not by a human organization's registration process.

## The Problem with Human Management

When people keep the roll of the sealed, several problems follow.

- When someone leaves, is their sealing revoked? Can the sealing of the Holy Spirit be revoked?
- If sealing happens at registration, is someone who did not finish the course excluded from salvation?
- Can errors in record-keeping (administrative mistakes) affect a person's sealing?

Managing God's sovereign act through a human administrative system places God's sovereignty under human decisions.

## Summary

In Scripture, sealing is a sovereign act that God performs through the Holy Spirit. Managing it as an organization's registration roll fundamentally changes both the biblical meaning of sealing and who performs it. The claim that people can decide and manage God's sealing needs biblical support.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you checked who does the sealing in Revelation 7:2-3?
Have you checked what the sealing is accomplished by in Ephesians 1:13?
Is there any biblical basis for the claim that leaving cancels one's sealing?
What do you think of the claim that people can manage God's sovereign act?
Have you ever asked yourself whether administrative registration and the sealing of the Holy Spirit are the same thing?

06-05.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-05.title: Is God's Work Complete Once the 144,000 Are Filled?
06-05.description: Shincheonji teaches that God's work will be complete when its membership reaches 144,000. This article examines the biblical basis for that claim and whether it can be tested.
06-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

Is there any biblical basis for thinking that the completion of God's work depends on reaching a particular headcount?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that God's work will be complete when its registered membership reaches exactly 144,000. It presents the filling of this number as the central fulfillment of the prophecies of Revelation and stresses that members must work hard at evangelism to reach it.

## God's Work and Human Numbers

In Scripture, God's work of salvation does not depend on human numerical achievement.

>! The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
>! — 2 Peter 3:9 (KJV)

God is "not willing that any should perish." The idea that salvation closes once a specific number is reached sits uneasily with this text.

>! The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this.
>! — Isaiah 9:7 (KJV)

God's work is brought to completion by God's own "zeal." It is not accomplished by a human organization hitting a numerical target.

## A Claim That Can Be Tested

The claim that "God's work will be complete when the 144,000 are filled" is a testable prediction. If it is true, something concrete should change once that number is reached.

That raises the following questions.

- What specific event is predicted to happen when 144,000 is reached?
- If that event does not happen, how will it be explained?
- Does the same doctrinal system remain in place after the number is reached?

## The Danger of a Numbers-Driven Faith

When reaching a number becomes the goal of faith, the motive for evangelism can be distorted. The gospel is about proclaiming God's love and grace, not about meeting an organization's numerical targets.

>! For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
>! — John 3:16 (KJV)

"Whosoever believeth in him" carries no numerical limit.

## Summary

Scripture presents the completion of God's work as belonging to God's sovereignty. There is little biblical basis for making a specific headcount the condition for completing God's work, and because the claim is testable, it can be judged by what actually happens.
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any Bible verse saying that the completion of God's work depends on reaching a human headcount?
Does the phrase "whosoever believeth in him" carry any numerical limit?
What specific event were you taught would happen when 144,000 is reached?
Is your motive for evangelism spreading the gospel, or reaching a number?
If this claim is testable, what is the standard for testing it?

06-06.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-06.title: Membership Passed 144,000. Why Hasn't the Promise Been Fulfilled?
06-06.description: Shincheonji's membership has reportedly passed 144,000, yet the promised completion has not happened. This article examines that situation.
06-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

If Shincheonji's membership has already passed 144,000, what became of the promised completion of God's work?

## Shincheonji's Claim and the Reality

Shincheonji has long taught that God's work will be complete when its registered membership reaches 144,000. Yet according to multiple reports, its membership has already passed several hundred thousand. (to be verified — Shincheonji's official figures and outside estimates may differ)

## The Problem of an Unfulfilled Prediction

If the promised change has not appeared even after the number was reached, there are a few possibilities.

1. The original claim was wrong
2. The standard for when the number counts as reached was changed
3. The meaning of "completion" was redefined
4. The method of counting was changed (for example, by excluding those who left)

Options 2, 3, and 4 all mean that the original doctrine was revised. If doctrine was revised, the fact and the reasons for it should be disclosed openly.

## How Scripture Says Prophecy Is Tested

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken,
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

Scripture gives a clear standard for testing prophecy. If something spoken in the name of the LORD does not come to pass, the LORD did not speak it. The standard is strict, but it is clear.

## What Still Needs to Be Verified

On this subject, the following points need to be checked objectively.

- Has Shincheonji ever officially documented that "when 144,000 is reached, these specific things will happen"? (to be verified)
- How has the doctrine been changed or reinterpreted since the number was reached? (to be verified)
- How does Shincheonji currently explain the 144,000? (to be verified)

## Summary

When a group presents reaching a specific number as the condition for the completion of God's work, the natural test is whether the promise was kept once that number was reached. If it was not, the claim needs to be reexamined by the standard Scripture gives for testing prophecy (Deut. 18:22).
selfCheckQuestions: Do you know that Shincheonji's current membership has passed 144,000?
Did the promised events actually happen after the number was reached?
If the doctrine was changed, were you given a transparent explanation of the change and why it was made?
Have you applied the test for prophecy in Deuteronomy 18:22 to this claim?
What explanation have you been given for why the promise was not fulfilled?

06-07.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-07.title: Does the Great Multitude in White Come After the 144,000?
06-07.description: Shincheonji interprets the great multitude in white as people who join after the 144,000. This article looks at the context of the passage in Revelation.
06-07.content:
## A Question to Start With

How does Revelation 7 describe the relationship between the 144,000 and the great multitude?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the great multitude clothed in white in Revelation 7:9 as people who join after the 144,000 has been completed. It teaches that if the 144,000 are the "priests," the multitude in white occupy the position of "the people."

## The Structure of Revelation 7

Revelation 7 consists of two scenes.

**The first scene (7:1-8)**: the sealed 144,000

>! And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
>! — Revelation 7:4 (KJV)

**The second scene (7:9-17)**: a great multitude that no one could number

>! After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
>! — Revelation 7:9 (KJV)

## Who the Great Multitude Are

The text of Revelation itself explains who the great multitude are.

>! And one of the elders answered, saying unto me, What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they? And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
>! — Revelation 7:13-14 (KJV)

According to the text, the great multitude have these characteristics:

- They come **"of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues"** (7:9)
- They are **"they which came out of great tribulation"** (7:14)
- They **washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb** (7:14)
- Their number is one **"which no man could number"** (7:9)

The description of people coming "of all nations, and kindreds" belongs to a different context from a particular group's internal classification (priests versus people). Likewise, "they which came out of great tribulation" is a long way from the reading that they are "people who signed up later," after the 144,000.

## What "After This" Means

Interpreters differ on whether "After this" (7:9) indicates chronological sequence or simply the order in which the visions are narrated. In Revelation, "after this" is often used as a literary device marking the transition to the next vision (see 4:1).

## Summary

The great multitude of Revelation 7 is described as people "of all nations, and kindreds" who "came out of great tribulation." What the text says belongs to a different context from a particular group's organizational category (people who join after the 144,000). The place to start is the information the text itself provides.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you read for yourself how Revelation 7:13-14 explains who the great multitude are?
How does the phrase "of all nations, and kindreds" fit with a particular group's internal classification?
Is there any textual basis for reading "they which came out of great tribulation" as people who join after the 144,000?
Have you considered whether "after this" marks chronological sequence or the order in which the visions are narrated?
Have you ever heard other interpretations of the relationship between the 144,000 and the great multitude?

06-08.seriesTitle: The 144,000 and the Great Multitude in White
06-08.title: Is Salvation Divided into Priests and People?
06-08.description: Shincheonji divides salvation into priests (the 144,000) and people (the multitude in white). This article looks at what Scripture says about the priesthood of believers.
06-08.content:
## A Question to Start With

Does Scripture set up ranks of salvation among believers, with priests on one level and people on another?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that salvation comes in two tiers. The 144,000 receive the position of "priests," while the multitude in white who join later hold the position of "the people." To become a priest, one must complete Shincheonji's education program from the beginning, and this means greater blessing and higher status.

## The Priesthood of All Believers in Scripture

The New Testament plainly declares that every believer is a priest.

>! But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people;
>! — 1 Peter 2:9 (KJV)

The "ye" in this verse does not refer to an elite group; it refers to all the believers receiving the letter. "A royal priesthood" applies to every believer.

Revelation declares the same principle.

>! Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
>! — Revelation 1:5-6 (KJV)

>! And hast made us unto our God kings and priests: and we shall reign on the earth.
>! — Revelation 5:10 (KJV)

In "hath made us kings and priests," the "us" means everyone redeemed by the blood of Christ, and all of them become priests.

## How the Priesthood Changed from the Old Testament to the New

In the Old Testament, only the tribe of Levi served as priests. After the cross of Jesus Christ, however, the priesthood underwent a fundamental change.

>! For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.
>! — Hebrews 7:12 (KJV)

Because Jesus Christ became the eternal High Priest (Heb. 7:24-25), every believer has become a priest who can approach God directly. This is the principle of the priesthood of all believers.

## Are Ranks of Salvation Biblical?

Placing ranks on salvation is at odds with the heart of the gospel.

>! There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
>! — Galatians 3:28 (KJV)

The core of the gospel is that in Christ every distinction falls away and believers become "one." If one's rank in salvation depends on whether one completed an education program, salvation can be distorted from something received by grace into something earned by works (completing a course).

## Summary

Scripture declares every believer to be "a royal priesthood" (1 Pet. 2:9; Rev. 1:5-6; 5:10). A two-tier structure that divides salvation into priests and people collides with the priesthood of all believers and is at odds with the heart of the gospel: that believers are one in Christ (Gal. 3:28).
selfCheckQuestions: Have you checked whom "a royal priesthood" refers to in 1 Peter 2:9?
Have you checked who the "us" is in "hath made us kings and priests" in Revelation 1:5-6?
If one's rank in salvation is decided by completing a course, is that salvation by grace?
Have you ever been taught the principle of the priesthood of all believers?
Can the "one" of Galatians 3:28 coexist with a two-tier structure of priests and people?

07-01.title: Will Chairman Lee Man-hee Live Forever?
07-01.description: This article looks at whether Shincheonji taught that Chairman Lee Man-hee would never die, and whether the Bible verses offered in support actually mean that.
07-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

Chairman Lee Man-hee was born in 1931 and is now in his nineties. If it was taught that he would never die physically, where in the Bible is the basis for that?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Within Shincheonji, the belief that Chairman Lee Man-hee, as the promised pastor, would not die was widespread. John 21:22-23 is sometimes cited in support.

>! Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.
>! — John 21:22 (KJV)

John 11:26, "whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die," is also used to support the idea of physical immortality.

## Reading the Text in Context

If you read John 21:22-23 through the very next verse, the Bible corrects the misunderstanding itself.

>! Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?
>! — John 21:23 (KJV)

Verse 23 states plainly that the reading "he shall not die" was a **misunderstanding**. Jesus was not speaking about John's death; he was telling Peter, in effect, "That is not your concern. You follow me."

In context, "shall never die" in John 11:26 also refers to **spiritual life**. When Jesus said these words, Lazarus had already died physically, and Jesus raised him back to life. Physical death and spiritual life are distinct.

## What Scripture Says About Physical Death

Scripture clearly teaches that every person dies physically.

>! And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
>! — Hebrews 9:27 (KJV)

Paul, too, speaks of his own death matter-of-factly in Philippians.

>! For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
>! — Philippians 1:23 (KJV)

Even the apostles knew they could not escape physical death.

## The Doctrinal Problem

If Chairman Lee Man-hee dies physically, a question remains: what happens to the faith of the members who followed the teaching that he would not die? When a prediction about the central figure of a doctrine fails, the credibility of the whole doctrine has to be reexamined.

## Summary

John 21:22-23 is a passage in which the Bible itself corrects the idea that someone "shall not die." Hebrews 9:27 declares that death is appointed for every person. The claim that the promised pastor will live forever in the body does not fit the context of the biblical text.
selfCheckQuestions: When you read John 21:22-23 through verse 23, does the reading "he shall not die" hold up?
Have you checked the context of John 11:26 to see whether "shall never die" means physical immortality or spiritual life?
Does Hebrews 9:27 make any exceptions?
If Chairman Lee Man-hee dies, how should the teaching up to that point be understood?
Was there any apostle who did not die physically?

07-02.title: Did Shincheonji Never Teach Physical Immortality?
07-02.description: Shincheonji denies ever officially teaching physical immortality. Yet if many members believed it, this article asks where that belief came from.
07-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

If Shincheonji never taught physical immortality, why did so many members believe that Chairman Lee Man-hee, and they themselves, would never die?

## Shincheonji's Official Position

Shincheonji has stated that it never officially taught physical immortality as doctrine. Chairman Lee Man-hee has also testified in court that he never claimed physical immortality (to be verified — specific trial records).

## So Why Did So Many Members Believe It?

If it was never officially taught, the following questions remain.

- Why do so many former members testify, "We were taught that we would not die"?
- Were there remarks in internal meetings or sermons that hinted at physical immortality?
- Were members ever led to read "shall never die" (John 11:26) in a physical sense?

Even if it was not official doctrine, if there was an environment that led members to understand it that way, the responsibility lies with those who did the teaching.

## If It Wasn't Taught, It Should Have Been Corrected

If the leadership was aware of this belief, it should have actively corrected it. Yet according to the testimony of many former members, the belief in physical immortality went uncorrected for a long time (to be verified — specific evidence of when and how it was corrected).

Leaving it uncorrected may have been convenient because the belief worked in the organization's favor. The belief that "we will not die" strengthens members' devotion and loyalty.

## The Biblical Principle

>! Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
>! — Ephesians 4:25 (KJV)

Those responsible for teaching must clearly correct misunderstandings so that they do not spread. An official denial that "we never taught it" does not, by itself, discharge responsibility for a belief that has already spread.

## Summary

There is a gap between the official position, "we never taught it," and the testimony of many who say, "we were taught it." If it truly was never taught, an explanation is needed for why so many members came to believe the same thing, and why the misunderstanding went uncorrected for so long.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever personally heard in Shincheonji that "we will not die"?
If it was not official doctrine, how did so many people come to believe the same thing?
If the leadership knew about this misunderstanding and did not correct it, what might the reason be?
Is the denial "we never taught it" a sufficient explanation?
In light of Ephesians 4:25, what does it mean to leave a misunderstanding uncorrected?

07-03.title: How Did the Promise of Never Dying Change?
07-03.description: This article traces how Shincheonji's position on physical immortality has shifted over time and considers what that shift itself means.
07-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

If something is truth revealed directly by God, is there any reason its core content should change over time?

## How the Position Has Shifted

The atmosphere within Shincheonji regarding physical immortality has varied from period to period (to be verified — specific materials and statements for each period).

- **Early period**: Many testify that the belief that Chairman Lee Man-hee and Shincheonji members would not die was widespread within the group.
- **Middle period**: Observers note that as the Chairman grew older, the meaning of "eternal life" gradually moved from physical to spiritual.
- **Present**: Shincheonji officially denies physical immortality and explains that "will never die" has a spiritual meaning.

## What the Change Itself Tells Us

If the core of a doctrine has changed, it may not have been God's revelation in the first place. If it were God's word, there would be no reason for it to change over time.

>! And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
>! — Hebrews 9:27 (KJV)

>! The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
>! — Isaiah 40:8 (KJV)

Scripture says that the word of God stands forever. But if the teaching "you will not die" has turned into "it actually had a spiritual meaning," then either the original teaching was not God's word, or the explanation has been changed after the fact.

## One of Two Possibilities

Logically, only two scenarios are possible.

1. **If physical immortality was taught from the start**: that teaching was wrong, which calls the credibility of the whole doctrine into question.
2. **If a spiritual meaning was intended from the start**: the leadership bears responsibility for allowing countless members to misunderstand it.

Either way, an explanation is needed.

## Summary

Many testimonies and observations confirm that the position on physical immortality has shifted over time. Isaiah 40:8 declares that God's word stands forever, unchanging. If a core doctrine has changed, one must seriously reconsider whether it was God's revelation in the first place.
selfCheckQuestions: Is the teaching on physical immortality the same now as when you joined?
If the teaching changed, have you ever heard an official explanation for that change?
If it is God's revelation, why would its core content need to be revised?
How can changes in doctrine be reconciled with Isaiah 40:8, "the word of our God shall stand for ever"?
If the original teaching was wrong, couldn't other teachings also change later?

07-04.title: Did Chairman Lee Man-hee Personally See Every Event in Revelation?
07-04.description: Shincheonji claims that Chairman Lee Man-hee personally witnessed every event in Revelation. This article examines the basis for that claim and whether it can be verified.
07-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

If one person claims to have personally seen every event in Revelation, shouldn't it be possible to confirm when, where, and in front of whom those events took place?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that Chairman Lee Man-hee personally witnessed every event of Revelation, from chapter 1 through chapter 22, as it was actually fulfilled. It explains that this is why he, as "the promised pastor" and "the one who overcomes," is the sole witness.

Revelation 22:16 is cited in support.

>! I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches.
>! — Revelation 22:16 (KJV)

## The Problem of Verification

A claim to have "seen it personally" has to be verifiable. It should be able to answer the following questions.

- **Exactly when** did each event in Revelation take place?
- **Where** did it take place? Can the location be identified?
- Were there **other witnesses**?
- Is there a record of the event being announced **before** it happened, or was it interpreted after the fact?

If verifiable answers to these questions cannot be given, the claim to have "seen it personally" rests on his own statement alone.

## The Difference Between a Claim and Proof

Saying "I saw it" is not the same as it being proven that he saw it. In Scripture, too, testimony requires confirmation.

>! In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.
>! — 2 Corinthians 13:1 (KJV)

Jesus' resurrection was confirmed by more than five hundred people (1 Cor. 15:6). The events of Acts were recorded alongside many eyewitnesses. The major events of Scripture do not rest on the testimony of a single person.

## The Possibility of After-the-Fact Interpretation

Anyone can take events that have already happened and map them onto Revelation afterward. What matters is whether, **before** an event happened, it was specifically identified as the fulfillment of a particular part of Revelation. Fitting an interpretation after the fact is fundamentally different from announcing something in advance.

## Summary

The claim to have "personally seen every event" must be verifiable through specific dates, places, other witnesses, and records of advance announcement. Second Corinthians 13:1 says every matter is to be established by two or three witnesses. Testimony that rests on one person's statement alone falls short of the biblical standard of evidence.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever confirmed when and where the specific events of Revelation took place?
Is there any witness other than Chairman Lee Man-hee who saw the same events?
Is there any record announcing, before an event happened, that it would be the fulfillment of Revelation?
Does the "two or three witnesses" principle of 2 Corinthians 13:1 not apply in this case?
How does this compare with Jesus' resurrection being confirmed by more than five hundred people?

07-05.title: Can Only One Person Testify to the Fulfillment of Revelation?
07-05.description: Shincheonji teaches that only Chairman Lee Man-hee can testify to the actual fulfillment of Revelation. This article compares that claim with the biblical principle of testimony.
07-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

Does Scripture entrust important truths to the testimony of a single person, or does it require multiple witnesses?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that Chairman Lee Man-hee is the only person who can see and testify to the actual fulfillment (silsang) of Revelation, that is, the real-world fulfillment of the events recorded in it. The reason given is that he is the "angel" of Revelation 22:16.

## The Biblical Principle of Witnesses

Both the Old and New Testaments require multiple witnesses in important matters.

>! One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
>! — Deuteronomy 19:15 (KJV)

>! that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
>! — Matthew 18:16 (KJV)

This principle was laid down in the Old Testament law, quoted by Jesus himself, and repeated by Paul (2 Cor. 13:1). Scripture does not settle a matter on the testimony of one person alone.

## Examples from Scripture

The major events of Scripture always had multiple witnesses.

- **The resurrection of Jesus**: witnessed by Mary Magdalene (John 20:11-18), and by Cephas (Peter), the twelve, and more than five hundred brethren (1 Cor. 15:5-8)
- **The Transfiguration**: witnessed together by three disciples, Peter, James, and John (Matt. 17:1-3)
- **The coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost**: about 120 disciples were gathered together (Acts 1:15; 2:1-4), and about 3,000 people were baptized that day (Acts 2:41)
- **The martyrdom of Stephen**: took place publicly in front of many people (Acts 7:54-60)

God did not entrust important events to one person's private experience.

## If the Fulfillment Really Happened

If the events of Revelation really took place, others who were there would have seen the same things. If the events happened publicly, the claim that only one person can testify to them actually weakens the case that they happened at all.

## Summary

Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16 state explicitly that important matters are to be established by two or three witnesses. The major events of Scripture all had multiple eyewitnesses. The claim that "only one person can testify" does not fit the biblical principle of witnesses; instead, it creates a structure that makes verification impossible.
selfCheckQuestions: If the multiple-witness principle of Deuteronomy 19:15 does not apply to the fulfillment of Revelation, why not?
If only one person had testified to Jesus' resurrection, could we believe it?
If the events of Revelation really happened, why are there no other eyewitnesses?
Doesn't a structure that depends on one person's testimony make verification difficult?
Why did Jesus take three disciples with him at the Transfiguration?
sources: Bible (KJV): Deuteronomy 19:15, Matthew 18:16, 2 Corinthians 13:1, 1 Corinthians 15:5-8, Matthew 17:1-3, John 20:11-18, Acts 1:15, 2:1-4, 2:41

07-06.title: Can Someone Who Made False Predictions Be the Promised Pastor?
07-06.description: This article looks at the biblical standard for a true prophet and how to judge a prophecy that fails.
07-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

What does Scripture tell us to do when a prophet's words do not come to pass?

## The Biblical Standard: Deuteronomy 18:20-22

>! But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die. And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the LORD hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
>! — Deuteronomy 18:20-22 (KJV)

The biblical standard is clear. If what is spoken in the name of the LORD does not come to pass, it is not the word of God.

## Have There Been Predictions That Did Not Come to Pass?

We need to examine whether Chairman Lee Man-hee or the Shincheonji leadership ever announced a specific time or event that did not come to pass (to be verified — the specific content and timing of predictions, with official materials or recordings).

According to the testimony of many former members, remarks were made that led people to hold specific expectations about when the 144,000 would be completed, when "manguk soseong" (the restoration of all nations) would come, and so on. A distinction should be made between official predictions and implied expectations, but if in the end they did not come to pass, they should be examined by the standard of Deuteronomy 18.

## Responses When a Prediction Fails

When a prediction does not come to pass, the usual responses are:

- "The time has not yet come."
- "It was delayed because the members' faith was lacking."
- "We misunderstood what it meant."

Deuteronomy 18:22, however, makes no such exceptions. "If the thing follow not, nor come to pass" — that is the only standard.

## True Prophets and False Prophets

In Scripture, the predictions of true prophets were fulfilled regardless of how much faith the people had.

- Jeremiah's prophecy of Jerusalem's destruction: the people did not believe it, but it came to pass just as he said (Jer. 25:11-12).
- Isaiah's prophecy of Babylon's fall: it was fulfilled precisely, even centuries later.

True prophecy does not depend on how people respond.

## Summary

Deuteronomy 18:20-22 gives a clear standard for discerning a prophet. If what is spoken in the name of the LORD does not come to pass, it is not the word of God. This standard allows no exceptions. To find out whether the claim to be the promised pastor is true, the biblical approach is to examine whether his predictions actually came to pass.
selfCheckQuestions: Can the standard of Deuteronomy 18:20-22 be applied equally to Chairman Lee Man-hee?
What explanation have you been given for predictions that did not come to pass?
Jeremiah's prophecy came to pass despite the people's unbelief. Why, then, would Shincheonji's predictions depend on the members' faith?
Is there any time limit on the explanation that "the time has not yet come"?
If another religious leader offered the same excuse, would you accept it?

07-07.title: Is Testing the Promised Pastor a Betrayal?
07-07.description: This article looks at how questioning the promised pastor is treated as betrayal in Shincheonji and compares it with the biblical principle of discernment.
07-07.content:
## A Question to Start With

Were the Bereans, who checked Paul's teaching against the Scriptures, guilty of betrayal?

## Shincheonji's Position

Within Shincheonji, there is an atmosphere in which raising questions about Chairman Lee Man-hee, the promised pastor, or trying to test his teaching is regarded as betrayal or unbelief. The reasoning is that "doubting the promised pastor is doubting God."

## Scripture Commands Us to Test

Scripture does not tell us to accept teaching unconditionally. On the contrary, it commands us to exercise discernment actively.

>! Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
>! — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)

>! These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:11 (KJV)

The Bereans checked **even Paul's words** against the Scriptures, and Scripture commends this as **"more noble."** Paul did not call it betrayal.

## The Danger of a System That Blocks Testing

When testing the leader is itself forbidden, these problems follow.

- Even when the leader makes mistakes, there is no way to correct them.
- Members lose the right to check the Scriptures for themselves.
- It becomes impossible to keep Scripture's command to discern.
- In the end, one person's interpretation becomes the final authority, above Scripture.

## Even Jesus Was Open to Being Tested

>! If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not. But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.
>! — John 10:37-38 (KJV)

Jesus said, in effect, "Judge me by my works." He did not call testing him a betrayal. Instead, he invited people to judge by fruit and by deeds.

## Summary

First John 4:1 commands us to try the spirits, and Acts 17:11 commends checking even an apostle's teaching against the Scriptures. Even Jesus told people to judge him by his works. Calling such testing betrayal runs contrary to Scripture and suppresses what is in fact an expression of healthy faith.
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any exception to the command in 1 John 4:1, "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits"?
Was it betrayal for the Bereans to test Paul's words?
If the promised pastor must not be tested, how can a false pastor be distinguished from a true one?
Why did Jesus say, in effect, "Judge me by my works"?
In a system where testing is impossible, how can members confirm the truth?

08-01.title: Has Shincheonji Never Predicted a Specific Time?
08-01.description: Shincheonji officially denies ever predicting a specific date. This article looks at how a sense of urgency was nonetheless created within the group, and with what results.
08-01.content:
## A Question to Start With

Even without naming a specific date, if expectations about timing were created with words like "it will be fulfilled soon," how is that different from predicting a time?

## Shincheonji's Official Position

Shincheonji officially states that it has never made a prediction specifying a particular year or date. In other words, it says it never made predictions of the kind "such-and-such will be fulfilled in this month of this year."

## But a Sense of Urgency Was Created

According to the testimony of many former members, even though no explicit date was given, expressions like these were used (to be verified — specific internal materials).

- "It will be fulfilled shortly."
- "The time is near."
- "It will surely be completed in this generation."
- "If you don't come in now, it will be too late."

Expressions like these lead members to expect a particular time and put pressure on them to evangelize and commit themselves urgently.

## The Problem with Undated Predictions of Time

Not naming a specific date can actually be the more subtle approach. When a date is named, failure becomes obvious once that day passes; but "soon" has no deadline, so it can always be explained that "the time has not yet come."

Even so, "soon" cannot be extended indefinitely. A "soon" that remains unfulfilled after decades has effectively lost its meaning.

## The Warning of Scripture

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

The standard in Deuteronomy is clear: date or no date, if what is spoken in the name of the LORD does not come to pass, it is not the word of God.

## Summary

Even without naming a specific date, if a sense of urgency led members to expect a particular time, responsibility remains when that expectation goes unfulfilled. "We never named a date" may be a mere technicality. What really needs explaining is the creation of expectations that were never fulfilled.
selfCheckQuestions: When you joined, did you ever feel a sense of urgency that "it will be fulfilled soon"?
Has what you felt was so urgent back then come to pass even now?
Does not naming a date free someone from responsibility for a failed prediction?
Can the word "soon" go on for decades?
If another religious leader used the same approach, how would you judge it?

08-02.title: What Did "Shortly Come to Pass" Mean?
08-02.description: This article looks at how Shincheonji has used the phrase "things which must shortly come to pass" from Revelation, and what it means in its original context.
08-02.content:
## A Question to Start With

Can we tell from the text whether Revelation's phrase "things which must shortly come to pass" signals urgency for one particular era, or whether it means something else?

## How Shincheonji Uses the Phrase

Shincheonji quotes the phrase "things which must shortly come to pass" from Revelation 1:1 and 22:6 to stress the urgency of its claim that every event in Revelation is being fulfilled in our present age.

>! The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:
>! — Revelation 1:1 (KJV)

On the basis of this verse, it delivers messages such as "If you don't come in now, it will be too late" and "It will surely be completed in this generation."

## What "Shortly" Means

The Greek expression for "shortly" (en tachei, ἐν τάχει) does not necessarily mean "immediately" or "within a few years." It can also mean "swiftly, once it begins."

In Scripture, expressions of time may differ from the human sense of time.

>! But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
>! — 2 Peter 3:8 (KJV)

This verse states plainly that God's sense of time differs from ours. Confining "shortly" to a human timetable does not fit the perspective of Scripture itself.

## The Fact That 2,000 Years Have Passed

About 2,000 years have passed since Revelation was written. If "shortly" meant "immediately," everything should already have been fulfilled in the first century. Shincheonji interprets this as "fulfilled not in the first century but in our present age," but that amounts to applying the word "shortly" selectively.

In other words, an interpretation in which "shortly" did not apply from the first century through the twentieth, but suddenly applies from the moment Shincheonji appeared, sets the timing according to its own position rather than the text.

## Summary

The phrase "things which must shortly come to pass" includes the sense of "swiftly, once it begins," and 2 Peter 3:8 states explicitly that God's sense of time differs from ours. Using this phrase as a claim of urgency for one particular era in order to pressure members goes beyond what the text means.
selfCheckQuestions: Does the word "shortly" necessarily mean "within a few years"?
How does the interpretation change if you apply the view of time in 2 Peter 3:8 to this verse?
What is the basis for saying "shortly" did not apply for the 2,000 years since Revelation was written, but applies only now?
Has the urgency of "it will be fulfilled soon" ever functioned as pressure on you to evangelize and commit?
If another group used the same phrase, how would you judge it?

08-03.title: How Has the Explanation of the 144,000 and the Great Multitude Changed?
08-03.description: This article traces how Shincheonji's interpretation of the 144,000 and the great multitude in white has changed over time and considers what those changes mean.
08-03.content:
## A Question to Start With

If this is revelation given directly by God, is there any reason the meaning of its core numbers and concepts should change from one period to another?

## Shincheonji's Basic Doctrine

Shincheonji interprets the 144,000 of Revelation 7 and 14 as a literal number, teaching that it is the number of members registered in Shincheonji's twelve tribes. It explains the great multitude in white (Rev. 7:9) as a separate group that comes after the 144,000.

## What Has Changed

According to the testimony of many former members and outside observation, the explanation of the 144,000 and the great multitude has changed over time (to be verified — comparison of specific textbook content by period).

- **When the 144,000 would be completed**: At first it was expected to be completed by a certain time, but as target dates passed, the explanation was adjusted.
- **The status of the great multitude**: The explanation shifted on whether the multitude are priests or people, and whether they receive a different rank of salvation.
- **Tribal assignment and transfers**: There have been cases in which members' tribal assignments were changed, or the tribal structure itself was reorganized.

## What the Changes Mean

Details of a doctrine may change. But the meaning of the number 144,000, the identity of the great multitude, and the tribal structure are the **core** of Shincheonji's doctrine. These are not details.

>! Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
>! — Hebrews 13:8 (KJV)

If God's truth remains the same, then the core interpretation of someone who claims to have received that truth by revelation should also remain consistent.

## The Pattern of Change

A common pattern can be seen in how these changes have unfolded.

1. A specific time or goal is set.
2. The time passes, or the goal is not reached.
3. The interpretation is revised, or a new explanation is offered.
4. The earlier explanation is filed away as "our understanding at the time."

If this pattern keeps repeating, one has to consider the possibility that it was human interpretation rather than God's revelation from the start.

## Summary

The 144,000 and the great multitude are core elements of Shincheonji's doctrine. If the interpretation of this core content has changed over time, one has to ask how that fits with the truth of God, who according to Hebrews 13:8 is the same forever. The surest way to check is to compare past and present textbooks directly.
selfCheckQuestions: Is the explanation of the 144,000 you were taught when you joined the same as the current one?
Has the interpretation of the great multitude ever changed? If so, why?
Have you ever experienced a change in tribal assignment or a reorganization of the tribal structure?
If a core doctrine has changed, can it still be called "revelation"?
Can you check past textbooks for yourself?

08-04.title: Have World Peace and Manguk Soseong Been Achieved?
08-04.description: This article examines whether the world peace and manguk soseong (萬國所成) promised by Shincheonji have actually come about, looking at the results of HWPL's activities.
08-04.content:
## A Question to Start With

Shincheonji promised that it would bring about world peace. Is the world today any closer to that promise?

## Shincheonji's Promise

Shincheonji has taught that world peace will be realized through HWPL (Heavenly Culture, World Peace, Restoration of Light), led by Chairman Lee Man-hee. It set the goal of submitting the DPCW (Declaration of Peace and Cessation of War) to the United Nations and turning it into international law.

The expression "manguk soseong" is used to mean that every nation in the world will be brought to completion through Shincheonji's word.

## Where Things Stand

Even after the DPCW was proposed, wars and conflicts have continued around the world. There is no verifiable record that the DPCW has been adopted as international law or formally accepted by the United Nations (to be verified — the current status of the DPCW under international law).

As for manguk soseong, there is likewise no evidence that the whole world has been united under Shincheonji's teaching.

## The Gap Between the Promise of Peace and Reality

Pursuing peace is, in itself, worthwhile. The problem is that this promise is used to support Shincheonji's doctrinal legitimacy, namely the claim that Chairman Lee Man-hee is the promised pastor.

If the promise has not been fulfilled, the doctrinal claims that lean on it need to be reexamined as well.

## What Scripture Says About Peace

>! They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
>! — Jeremiah 6:14 (KJV)
