In Jeremiah's day, false prophets also proclaimed "Peace," but in reality there was no peace. Declaring peace is not the same as peace actually being achieved.

>! For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.
>! — 1 Thessalonians 5:3 (KJV)

If anything, Scripture warns us to be wary of declarations that world peace will be achieved by human effort.

## Summary

The promise of world peace through HWPL and the DPCW has yet to be borne out by any visible results. The same is true of manguk soseong. If these promises were used to support the doctrinal claim about the promised pastor, the fact that they have not been fulfilled means that this doctrinal support has been weakened.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever checked for yourself whether the DPCW has been adopted as international law?
Have you ever seen concrete evidence that manguk soseong is actually underway?
What explanation have you been given for why the promise of world peace has not been fulfilled?
What similarities do you see when you compare this with the false declarations of peace in Jeremiah 6:14?
If the promise has not been fulfilled, is the doctrine built on that promise still valid?

08-05.title: Was COVID-19 a Prophesied Event?
08-05.description: This article looks at the relationship between COVID-19 and Shincheonji, and whether the claim that the outbreak fulfilled prophecy holds up.
08-05.content:
## A Question to Start With

If COVID-19 was a prophesied event, is there any record of it being specifically announced before it happened?

## COVID-19 and Shincheonji

In early 2020, COVID-19 spread on a large scale, centered on the Shincheonji church in Daegu. The outbreak drew public attention and criticism toward Shincheonji.

Some Shincheonji-related claims interpreted this event as part of the fulfillment of the prophecies of Revelation, or explained it as part of a persecution of Shincheonji (to be verified — the specifics of the official position and internal interpretations).

## Prophecy or After-the-Fact Interpretation?

To judge whether an event fulfills a prophecy, there must be a record of it being specifically announced **before** it happened.

- Before COVID-19 broke out, is there any record announcing that "an epidemic will spread in Daegu"?
- Before it broke out, is there any record identifying which verse of Revelation it would fulfill?

Interpreting an event after it happens as "the fulfillment of Revelation" is not prophecy. It is after-the-fact interpretation. Because after-the-fact interpretation can be applied to any event, it cannot serve as evidence of prophecy.

## Persecution or Public Health Measures?

After COVID-19 spread, some viewed the health authorities' measures against Shincheonji as "persecution." But disease-control measures are a public health response aimed at stopping the spread of infection, regardless of religion. At the time, the same measures were applied to other religious facilities and to other venues where large numbers of people gather.

The causes and the consequences of the event need to be kept carefully distinct.

## The Biblical Principle

>! Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
>! — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV)

Scripture tells us to prove all things. Before interpreting an event to fit a doctrine, we must first check whether that interpretation matches the objective facts.

## Summary

To claim that COVID-19 fulfilled prophecy, there would need to be a record of it being specifically announced before it happened. Mapping it onto Revelation afterward is interpretation, not prophecy. Equating public health measures with persecution is also something to judge only after the facts have been carefully checked.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever seen a record showing that this event was prophesied before COVID-19 broke out?
Can mapping an event onto Revelation after it happens be called prophecy?
How can public health measures be distinguished from religious persecution?
Are you aware that the same disease-control measures were applied to other religious facilities?
What conclusion do you reach if you apply 1 Thessalonians 5:21, "Prove all things," to this situation?

08-06.title: Why Are Members' Faith Blamed When Prophecies Fail?
08-06.description: This article looks at the pattern of blaming members' lack of faith when prophecies go unfulfilled, and compares it with the biblical principles of prophecy.
08-06.content:
## A Question to Start With

In Scripture, did the prophecies of true prophets sometimes come to pass and sometimes fail depending on the faith of those who heard them?

## A Recurring Pattern

There are testimonies that whenever something expected in Shincheonji failed to happen, explanations like these were repeated.

- "It was delayed because the members' faith was lacking."
- "The time was pushed back because we didn't meet our evangelism goals."
- "It's because we aren't ready yet."

All of these explanations place **the blame for the failed prophecy on the members, not on the one who made it**.

## In Scripture, Prophecy Does Not Depend on How People Respond

The true prophecies of Scripture were fulfilled regardless of the faith of those who heard them.

>! Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
>! — Jeremiah 23:5 (KJV)

Jeremiah's prophecies came to pass precisely, even though most of the people of Israel did not believe them. When he prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem, the people persecuted and imprisoned him. Yet the prophecy was fulfilled just as he had said.

Jonah's prophecy of Nineveh's destruction was withdrawn because the people of Nineveh repented. Even in this case, though, whether the prophecy was fulfilled or withdrawn was God's sovereign decision, not Jonah's failure.

## The Problem of Shifting the Blame

Blaming members' faith for unfulfilled prophecy creates the following problems.

- **It cannot be tested**: Since "faith was lacking" can always be offered as the explanation, the very possibility that the prophecy was wrong disappears.
- **It shifts the guilt**: Members end up carrying guilt for the failed prophecy and are pressured to evangelize and commit themselves even harder.
- **It shields the leader**: The structure ensures that the one who made the prophecy is never held responsible, no matter what.

## The Standard of Deuteronomy

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken,
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

Deuteronomy makes no exception for "because the members' faith was lacking." If it does not come to pass, it is not the word of God. That is the only standard Scripture gives.

## Summary

There is no biblical basis for blaming members when a prophecy fails. The true prophecies of Scripture were fulfilled regardless of how much faith people had. Deuteronomy 18:22 declares, without exception, that "if it does not come to pass, it is not the word of God."
selfCheckQuestions: When a prophecy was not fulfilled, have you ever felt that it was your own faith's fault?
Jeremiah's prophecy came to pass despite the people's unbelief. Why, then, would Shincheonji's prophecies depend on the members' faith?
Does Deuteronomy 18:22 include any condition such as "except when the members' faith is lacking"?
In a structure where the blame for failed prophecy always falls on the members, when does the prophet ever take responsibility?
Has this structure ever functioned as a way to demand greater commitment?

08-07.title: Are Changed Doctrines "Meat in Due Season"?
08-07.description: Shincheonji explains doctrinal changes as "meat in due season." This article examines whether that explanation is biblically sound and whether it can apply to changes in core doctrine.
08-07.content:
## A Question to Start With

Can the idea of "meat in due season" justify even changes to core doctrine?

## Shincheonji's Explanation

When Shincheonji is told that its doctrines have changed, it explains this with the idea of "meat in due season," that is, food given at the proper time. The basis is Matthew 24:45, where the "faithful and wise servant" is responsible for giving the household their food in due season.

>! Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?
>! — Matthew 24:45 (KJV)

On this basis, it explains that the content of its teaching may vary according to the time.

## A Change in Food Is Not a Change in Truth

"Meat in due season" can mean delivering the same truth in a way that suits the situation. For example, teaching the basics to new believers and deeper things to mature believers.

>! I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
>! — 1 Corinthians 3:2 (KJV)

But this is **adjusting the depth of the same truth**, not **reversing earlier teaching as wrong**. When someone moves from milk to meat, the milk does not become "the wrong food."

## The Problem with Changing Core Doctrine

Changes like the following are hard to explain as "meat in due season."

- "You will not die" turning into "it means spiritual eternal life"
- The meaning of the 144,000, or the time of its completion, changing
- The interpretation of particular people or events changing

Changes like these are not adjustments in food; they are **revisions of the truth itself**. If it is truth revealed by God, there is no reason for its core content to be revised.

>! The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
>! — Isaiah 40:8 (KJV)

## The Direction of Change

Genuine teaching moves from the basics to greater depth, from the simple to the rich. Earlier stages are not repudiated. Shincheonji's doctrinal changes, however, often move in the direction of denying or replacing earlier teaching. That is not "the development of food" but "the reversal of interpretation."

## Summary

"Meat in due season" means delivering the same truth at different depths; it cannot serve as grounds for revising core doctrine. Isaiah 40:8 says that the word of God stands forever. If a core doctrine has changed, we must ask again whether it was the word of God in the first place.
selfCheckQuestions: Can "meat in due season" include changes to core doctrine?
Have you ever been told that something you were taught earlier was "wrong"?
How is adjusting the depth of the same truth different from changing the truth itself?
In the milk-and-meat analogy of 1 Corinthians 3:2, does the milk become "the wrong food"?
Why would truth revealed by God need to be revised?

08-08.title: Why Are Members Kept from Checking Earlier Textbooks and Sermons?
08-08.description: There are reports that access to past textbooks and sermon materials is restricted within Shincheonji. This article considers the reasons and what they mean.
08-08.content:
## A Question to Start With

If the teaching has not changed, why would checking past textbooks be a problem?

## What Has Been Reported

According to the testimony of many former members, access to past textbooks and sermon recordings is restricted or discouraged within Shincheonji (to be verified — official policy on managing materials).

- Testimony that members were instructed to return or discard earlier editions of textbooks
- Guidance not to share past sermon recordings or videos
- The explanation that "the old has passed; receive the new food"

## The Problem of Transparency

If the teaching had been consistent from the start, checking past materials would actually be an opportunity to prove the doctrine's consistency. If past materials are restricted, three things can be inferred.

1. There may be differences between past and present teaching.
2. There is a desire to keep those differences from coming to light.
3. There is an effort to keep members from comparing for themselves and reaching their own judgment.

## The Biblical Principle: Openness

The teaching in Scripture was open and transparent.

>! Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.
>! — John 18:20 (KJV)

Jesus said, "In secret have I said nothing." His teaching was public, and anyone could check it.

>! For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God.
>! — John 3:20-21 (KJV)

Those who follow the truth come to the light. If a teaching is true, there is no reason to fear disclosure.

## Information Control and Faith

Restricting access to past materials robs members of the chance to judge for themselves. That is not healthy faith; it is information control. The Bereans could "search the scriptures daily" because the materials they needed to check were open to them.

## Summary

If the teaching has not changed, making past materials available would only increase trust. Restricting access to them may be an attempt to hide the fact that things have changed. In John 18:20, Jesus said, "In secret have I said nothing." True teaching does not fear transparency.
selfCheckQuestions: Do you still have the textbooks you received in the past?
Have you ever compared past textbooks with the current ones?
Have you ever been told not to look at earlier materials?
If the teaching has not changed, why restrict past materials?
Was Jesus' teaching secret or public?

08-09.title: How Have Shincheonji's Textbooks Changed from Edition to Edition?
08-09.description: This article summarizes reports of changes across editions of Shincheonji's textbooks and considers what those changes mean doctrinally.
08-09.content:
## A Question to Start With

If a textbook was written by someone who received God's revelation, is there any reason its content should differ from one edition to the next?

## Reports of Textbook Changes

There are reports that Shincheonji's educational textbooks have been revised over time (to be verified — a specific comparison of editions requires obtaining the original materials).

Taken together, the testimonies of former members report changes of the following kinds.

- Interpretations of particular people or organizations were changed
- The timing or the subjects of the fulfillment of events in Revelation were revised
- Content emphasized in earlier editions was deleted or scaled back
- New interpretations were added

## Why Do the Textbooks Change?

The following are thought to be possible reasons for the revisions.

1. **Unfulfilled predictions**: when something taught to happen at a particular time did not come to pass
2. **Changes in who was identified**: when the people or organizations identified as betrayers or destroyers changed
3. **Responses to outside criticism**: when outsiders pointed out contradictions in the doctrine
4. **Organizational changes**: when the internal structure or the makeup of the tribes changed

## A Comparison with the Bible

The Bible was written by some forty authors over about 1,500 years, yet its core message is consistent. Copying errors and the like did occur as the manuscripts were transmitted, but that is fundamentally different from **deliberate revision of the content**.

>! For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book: And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.
>! — Revelation 22:18-19 (KJV)

Shincheonji applies this passage to established churches, accusing them of "adding to and taking away from Revelation." But if the same standard is applied to its own textbooks, how can adding to and taking away from their content be explained?

## How to Check

The surest way to check is to **compare past and present editions directly**. If you still have an earlier textbook, set it side by side with the current one and see what has changed.

## Summary

There are many reports that the textbooks have differed from edition to edition. A specific comparison requires obtaining the original materials. If they were written by someone who received God's revelation, there is no reason for their core content to be revised, and comparing past and present editions directly is the surest way to verify this.
selfCheckQuestions: Is the content of the textbooks you received in the past the same as that of the current ones?
Have you ever heard an official explanation of why the textbooks were revised?
Can the standard of Revelation 22:18-19 be applied equally to Shincheonji's textbooks?
If they record God's revelation, why would they need revision?
If you have kept an earlier edition, have you compared it with the current one?

09-01.title: Who Is Jesus?
09-01.description: A look at how Shincheonji understands Jesus, compared with what the Bible says about the identity of Jesus Christ.
09-01.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is Jesus merely a pastor for one era, or is He the eternal Son of God? How we answer this question determines the core of the Christian faith.

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that Jesus completed His role at His first coming and that a new era now needs a new pastor. In other words, Jesus was the promised pastor for the age of 2,000 years ago, and today the promised pastor of the new era (Chairman Lee Man-hee) has taken over that role.

By this logic, the authority and role of Jesus are limited to a particular era and have now been transferred to someone else.

## What the Bible Says About Jesus

The Bible does not confine the identity of Jesus to any one era.

>! Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
>! — Hebrews 13:8 (KJV)

Jesus does not change. That runs directly against the idea that yesterday's pastor is replaced by someone else today.

>! For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
>! — Colossians 2:9 (KJV)

If all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Jesus, we have to ask whether any other human being could possibly take over His role.

>! In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. ... And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us
>! — John 1:1, 14 (KJV)

The Gospel of John declares that Jesus is not simply a prophet or a pastor for one era. He is God Himself, who was with God from the beginning.

## The Problem with an Era-by-Era Theory of Pastors

Shincheonji's era-by-era theory of pastors puts Jesus on the same level as Moses and Joshua. Hebrews, however, states plainly that Jesus is greater than Moses.

>! For this man was counted worthy of more glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house.
>! — Hebrews 3:3 (KJV)

Jesus is not one pastor among equals. Reducing Him to a figure who served a single era does not fit the testimony of Scripture as a whole.

## Summary

The Bible testifies that Jesus Christ is the same forever, that the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Him, and that He has been God from the beginning. The claim that His role passes to other people as the eras change is not consistent with the evidence of the biblical text.
selfCheckQuestions: Can the meaning of "the same ... for ever" in Hebrews 13:8 coexist with the claim that the pastor changes from era to era?
Colossians 2:9 says that "all the fulness of the Godhead" dwells in Him "bodily." Could this apply to any other human being?
John 1:1 declares that Jesus is "God." Can He be limited to being a pastor for one era?
Why does Hebrews 3:3 say that Jesus is greater than Moses?
Is there any biblical basis for the claim that the role of Jesus is transferred to someone else?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Hebrews 13:8, Colossians 2:9, John 1:1, 14, Hebrews 3:3

09-02.title: Was Salvation Completed on the Cross of Jesus?
09-02.description: A look at how Shincheonji treats the meaning of the cross, and at what the Bible says about the finished work of salvation on the cross.
09-02.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Was the death of Jesus on the cross the completion of salvation, or is there still some further process to go through?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji does not deny the cross of Jesus, but it tends to shrink its meaning. In Shincheonji's doctrine of salvation, the key is to understand the actual fulfillment (silsang) of Revelation, receive the truth through the promised pastor, and have one's name registered in the book of life. In this framework, the cross is treated as one part of the process rather than the completion of salvation.

## What the Bible Says About the Finished Work of the Cross

On the cross, Jesus made an unmistakable declaration.

>! When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
>! — John 19:30 (KJV)

"It is finished" (τετέλεσται, tetelestai) is in the perfect tense and means "completely finished." It was also the word used when a debt had been paid in full. In other words, it is a declaration that the work of salvation was done.

>! By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. ... For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
>! — Hebrews 10:10, 14 (KJV)

Hebrews uses the phrases "once for all," "by one offering," and "perfected for ever." The point is that no further sacrifice or process is needed.

>! For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood,
>! — Romans 3:23-25 (KJV)

Paul says clearly that salvation was accomplished through "his blood," the blood of Christ.

## The Problem with Shrinking the Cross

If the cross is not the completion of salvation, we are left asking what Jesus meant when He declared, "It is finished." And the phrases "once for all" and "perfected for ever" in Hebrews are hard to reconcile with a salvation that requires additional conditions.

## Summary

The Bible declares that the death of Jesus on the cross was the event that completed salvation. The words "It is finished," the "offering ... once for all," and "perfected for ever" clash with any system that demands further conditions for salvation. Shrinking the meaning of the cross weakens the central message of the New Testament.
selfCheckQuestions: Do you understand the significance of "It is finished" (John 19:30) being in the perfect tense?
Why does Hebrews 10:10, 14 use the expressions "once for all" and "for ever"?
If additional conditions for salvation are needed beyond the cross, what does "It is finished" mean?
According to Romans 3:23-25, what is the basis of salvation?

09-03.title: Is the Second Coming of Jesus a Spiritual Coming Upon One Man?
09-03.description: A look at Shincheonji's teaching of a spiritual second coming, and at how the Bible describes the manner of Christ's return.
09-03.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is the second coming of Jesus a spirit coming upon one person's body, or an event that everyone will be able to see?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the second coming of Jesus takes place in a spiritual way. Specifically, it says the second coming is the spirit of Jesus coming upon the promised pastor, Chairman Lee Man-hee. According to this teaching, the second coming the Bible speaks of is not a physical return on the clouds but a spiritual presence within one person.

## What the Bible Says About the Manner of His Return

After Jesus ascended, angels spoke to the disciples.

>! Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.
>! — Acts 1:11 (KJV)

The key phrase is "in like manner as ye have seen him go." The disciples watched with their own eyes as Jesus was taken up into heaven, and a cloud received Him. His return will take place in the same way.

>! For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God:
>! — 1 Thessalonians 4:16 (KJV)

Paul says that "the Lord himself" will descend from heaven. This is not a spirit coming upon one man; it is the Lord Himself coming in person.

>! And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
>! — Matthew 24:30 (KJV)

Since "all the tribes of the earth ... shall see" Him, the second coming is not a hidden event taking place inside one person.

## The Problem with the Spiritual Second Coming Theory

If we apply the spiritual-coming interpretation, we have to reinterpret every one of these phrases as a figure of speech: "in like manner as ye have seen him go," "the Lord himself shall descend from heaven," and "all the tribes of the earth ... shall see." Yet these verses do not appear in figurative contexts. They appear in contexts of direct explanation and promise.

Furthermore, if the spirit of Jesus coming upon one person is the second coming, Shincheonji needs to explain how that differs from the Holy Spirit coming upon all believers at Pentecost (Acts 2).

## Summary

The Bible describes the return of Jesus as a visible event that everyone will be able to recognize. "In like manner as ye have seen," "himself," and "all the tribes of the earth ... shall see" point to an event quite different from a spirit coming upon one person's body.
selfCheckQuestions: What kind of return does "shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go" in Acts 1:11 describe?
Can "the Lord himself shall descend from heaven" in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 be interpreted as a spiritual coming?
Can the statement in Matthew 24:30 that "all the tribes of the earth ... shall see" Him coexist with a hidden spiritual event?
How is a spiritual second coming to be distinguished from the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost?
How many verses would have to be reinterpreted as figurative in order to read the second coming as spiritual?

09-04.title: Who Is the Holy Spirit, and How Does He Work?
09-04.description: A comparison of Shincheonji's understanding of the Holy Spirit with historic Christian teaching, and a look at the Spirit's work as the Bible describes it.
09-04.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Does the Holy Spirit work only through one person, or does He come directly upon every believer?

## What Shincheonji Claims

In Shincheonji's framework, the key is receiving the truth through the promised pastor. The work of the Holy Spirit is also understood within this framework. The reasoning is that receiving the revelation passed on by the promised pastor is how one experiences the work of the Spirit. In other words, the Spirit's work is mediated through one central person.

## What the Bible Says About the Holy Spirit

Jesus introduced the Holy Spirit as "another Comforter."

>! And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth;
>! — John 14:16-17 (KJV)

The words "abide with you for ever" show that the Spirit is not limited to a particular era or a particular person. Jesus also said "you" in the plural.

The coming of the Spirit at Pentecost shows this concretely.

>! And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. ... And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
>! — Acts 2:1, 4 (KJV)

The Spirit did not come upon just one person; He came upon "all" who were gathered there. Peter explained that this was the fulfillment of the prophecy of Joel.

>! And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh:
>! — Acts 2:17 (KJV)

The phrase "upon all flesh" declares that the Spirit is poured out directly on all believers, without passing through a single mediator.

## The Problem with a Framework That Mediates the Spirit's Work

If the Holy Spirit works only through one person, then the promise in John 14:16-17 that He will "abide with you for ever" takes on a limited meaning. It also does not fit the prophecy in Acts 2, "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh."

Paul says that every believer is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

>! Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
>! — 1 Corinthians 3:16 (KJV)

## Summary

The Bible teaches that the Holy Spirit comes directly upon every believer, abides with them forever, and dwells within each of them. A framework in which the Spirit's work can be experienced only through one person's mediation differs from the Bible's teaching on the Holy Spirit.
selfCheckQuestions: In John 14:16-17, upon whom does the Holy Spirit come?
In Acts 2, did the Holy Spirit come upon one person only, or upon everyone who was gathered?
Is Joel's prophecy, "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh," compatible with a framework centered on a mediator?
Does "the temple of God" in 1 Corinthians 3:16 refer only to one particular person?
What doctrinal problems arise when the work of the Holy Spirit is concentrated in one person?

09-05.title: Do the Spirits of the Dead Become One with the Bodies of the Living?
09-05.description: A look at Shincheonji's doctrine of the union of spirit and flesh, and at what the Bible says about the spirits of the dead and their relation to the living.
09-05.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is there any biblical basis for the claim that the spirits of biblical figures (for example, Moses, Elijah, or the apostle John) become one with the bodies of particular people living today?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches a doctrine called "union of spirit and flesh" (靈肉合一). According to this teaching, the spirits of figures in the Bible enter the bodies of Shincheonji leaders who are alive today and become one with them. For example, the spirit of a certain Old Testament figure is said to come upon a certain Shincheonji tribe leader. (To be verified: the specific list of who is matched with whom may have changed over time.)

## What the Bible Says About What Happens After Death

The Bible speaks plainly about a person's state after death.

>! And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
>! — Hebrews 9:27 (KJV)

It says that after death comes "the judgment," not that a person enters someone else's body.

The Bible strictly forbids contact with the spirits of the dead.

>! There shall not be found among you ... a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD
>! — Deuteronomy 18:10-12 (KJV, abridged)

Summoning or communicating with the spirits of the dead is something the Bible explicitly forbids. If, as the union of spirit and flesh doctrine claims, the spirits of dead biblical figures come upon living people, that moves close to the very territory the Bible warns against.

## Examining an Apparently Similar Case in the Bible

Someone might point to the spirit of Elijah resting on Elisha (2 Kings 2:9-15) as support. In that passage, however, "the spirit of Elijah" means the Spirit of God that had been at work in Elijah, the power of the Holy Spirit. Elijah's own individual soul did not enter Elisha. Even after Elijah was taken up to heaven, he remained a being distinct from Elisha.

## Summary

The Bible teaches that people face judgment after death, and it forbids contact with the spirits of the dead. The doctrine that the spirits of dead biblical figures enter the bodies of living people and become one with them has no direct basis in Scripture. If anything, its structure resembles the very practices the Bible warns against.
selfCheckQuestions: According to Hebrews 9:27, what comes after death?
Are there similarities between the practices forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10-12 and the doctrine of the union of spirit and flesh?
Can the spirit of Elijah resting on Elisha serve as a basis for the union of spirit and flesh?
Is there any direct verse of Scripture for the claim that the spirit of a dead biblical figure comes upon a particular person?
If one accepts the doctrine of the union of spirit and flesh, how should the Bible's warnings about contact with the dead be understood?

09-06.title: Is the Resurrection a Spiritual Change or a Real Resurrection?
09-06.description: An examination of whether Shincheonji's reading of the resurrection as spiritual enlightenment agrees with the Bible's teaching on the resurrection.
09-06.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is the resurrection the Bible speaks of a spiritual change in which a person comes to understand the truth, or is it an event in which dead bodies actually come back to life?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji interprets the resurrection spiritually. Death, it says, means a state of spiritual ignorance, and resurrection means coming to understand the truth through Shincheonji's teaching. So joining Shincheonji and learning the word is itself the resurrection, not a physical event in which someone rises from the grave.

## What the Bible Says About the Resurrection

Paul presents the reality of the resurrection together with historical evidence.

>! how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once;
>! — 1 Corinthians 15:3-6 (KJV)

The resurrection Paul records is not spiritual enlightenment. "He was buried, and ... he rose again ... and ... he was seen" describes a physical death and a physical resurrection. His mention of more than five hundred eyewitnesses is also meant to stress that this was a historical event.

Paul also spells out what would follow if there were no bodily resurrection.

>! But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.
>! — 1 Corinthians 15:13-14 (KJV)

If the resurrection were merely a spiritual change, Paul would have had no reason to go so far as to say "your faith is also vain." He argues this forcefully precisely because the resurrection is a real event.

Jesus Himself also spoke of the future resurrection.

>! the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.
>! — John 5:28-29 (KJV)

"All that are in the graves ... shall come forth" speaks of a bodily resurrection, not spiritual enlightenment.

## Summary

The resurrection in the Bible is a historical event, backed by the testimony of eyewitnesses. Paul declares that without the bodily resurrection, faith itself is vain. Reducing the resurrection to spiritual enlightenment clashes with the entire argument of 1 Corinthians 15.
selfCheckQuestions: Why does Paul mention five hundred eyewitnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-6?
If the resurrection is spiritual enlightenment, can you explain why Paul said "your faith is also vain"?
What does "all that are in the graves ... shall come forth" in John 5:28-29 mean?
Is "he was buried, and ... he rose again" a way of describing a spiritual change?

09-07.title: Is Salvation Decided by Membership in Shincheonji and Registration in the Book of Life?
09-07.description: An examination of whether the registration in the book of life and organizational membership that Shincheonji speaks of are conditions of salvation, and of what the Bible says salvation rests on.
09-07.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is salvation decided by belonging to a particular organization and having one's name entered on that organization's roll?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that its organization is the kingdom of God described in Revelation, and that being registered with Shincheonji is the same as having one's name written in "the book of life." The logic that follows is that anyone who does not belong to Shincheonji cannot be saved.

## What the Bible Says Salvation Rests On

>! For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
>! — Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV)

Salvation is given by grace through faith. It does not come from works or from membership in an organization.

>! That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
>! — Romans 10:9 (KJV)

The conditions of salvation Paul gives are to "confess ... the Lord Jesus" and to believe in His resurrection. Joining a particular organization or being entered on a roll is never mentioned.

## Whose Is "the Book of Life"?

In Revelation, the book of life clearly belongs to God and to the Lamb.

>! And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.
>! — Revelation 20:15 (KJV)

The book of life is under God's sovereignty. It is not a roll kept by some organization on earth. When a human organization claims, "Our roll is the book of life," it is in effect putting its own organization in the place of God's sovereignty.

## The Problem with Salvation by Organizational Membership

If salvation were decided by membership in a particular organization, that would clash with Ephesians 2:8-9, which says we are saved "by grace ... through faith." It would also call into question the salvation of every believer who lived before Jesus and before Shincheonji was founded.

The thief on the cross was not registered with any organization, yet Jesus said to him:

>! And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
>! — Luke 23:43 (KJV)

## Summary

The Bible says clearly that salvation is received by grace through faith. The book of life belongs to God; it is not the roll of a human organization. The claim that one must belong to a particular organization to be saved does not fit the Bible's teaching on salvation.
selfCheckQuestions: What does Ephesians 2:8-9 present as the basis of salvation?
Does joining an organization appear among the conditions of salvation in Romans 10:9?
Under whose sovereignty is the book of life in Revelation?
What question does the case of the thief on the cross raise for the idea of salvation by organizational membership?
Is there any biblical basis for equating a particular organization's roll with the book of life?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Ephesians 2:8-9, Romans 10:9, Revelation 20:15, Luke 23:43

09-08.title: Is There No Salvation in the Established Churches?
09-08.description: A look at the grounds for Shincheonji's claim that there is no salvation in the established churches, and at what the Bible says about the church.
09-08.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Are the established churches spiritually dead, with Shincheonji the only place of salvation?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that the established churches correspond to Babylon or the harlot in Revelation, that they have fallen spiritually, and that there is no salvation in them. So, it says, a person can be saved only by leaving the established churches and coming into Shincheonji.

## What the Bible Says About the Church

Jesus made a powerful promise to the church.

>! upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
>! — Matthew 16:18 (KJV)

The promise that "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" declares that the church of Christ will never be wiped out or lose its role in salvation. If the established churches as a whole had fallen into a state with no salvation, this promise would have failed.

Paul speaks of the security of those who are in Christ.

>! For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
>! — Romans 8:38-39 (KJV)

For those who are in Christ, nothing can separate them from the love of God. That clashes with the claim that people in the established churches who follow Christ in genuine faith are shut out of salvation.

## The Marks of an Exclusive Claim to Salvation

The claim that "only our organization is the place of salvation" is a feature common to many groups that have historically been classified as heretical. Jehovah's Witnesses, the Unification Church, and the World Mission Society Church of God (Ahnsahnghong) make similar claims.

Such claims serve to keep an organization intact by cutting off contact with outsiders, controlling information, and instilling fear of leaving.

## While Acknowledging the Church's Problems

It is true that the established churches have problems, and the Bible itself deals with problems within the church (the letters to the seven churches in Revelation 2-3). But saying there are problems and saying there is no salvation are completely different claims. Jesus gave even troubled churches the opportunity to repent; He did not tell them to move to a different organization.

## Summary

The Bible promises that the church of Christ will never be brought down by the gates of hell. Nothing can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God. The exclusive claim that "only we are saved" is a feature historically shared by heretical groups.
selfCheckQuestions: If the promise in Matthew 16:18 that "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" had failed, what would that mean?
According to Romans 8:38-39, what can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God?
What do Shincheonji's claims have in common with those of other groups that claim exclusive salvation?
In Revelation 2-3, what remedy did Jesus offer to troubled churches?
What function does the claim "only we are saved" serve in running an organization?

10-01.title: Does Passing an Exam Mean Mastering the Bible?
10-01.description: An examination of whether passing the Shincheonji Bible exam really means mastering the Bible, with a look at the structure and limits of the exam.
10-01.content:
## The Question to Ask First

If someone passes an exam written by a particular organization, does that prove they have mastered the whole Bible?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji runs its own Bible exams and presents passing them as proof of mastering the Bible. It argues that the large number of members who pass is evidence that Shincheonji's teaching is true.

## Looking at How the Exam Is Built

The Shincheonji Bible exam is written entirely within Shincheonji's own interpretive system. For a question such as "What are the seven stars in Revelation?" the correct answer is the interpretation Shincheonji has settled on. What the exam measures is not understanding of the Bible as a whole but how accurately someone has memorized Shincheonji's interpretive system.

It is like getting a perfect score on a test written using only one tutoring school's methods for solving problems. That shows you have learned that school's methods, not that you have mastered mathematics.

## The Problem with the Word "Mastery"

The Bible is a vast collection of sixty-six books. It spans many genres, including history, poetry, prophecy, letters, and the Gospels. Understanding it takes work on many levels: the nuances of the original languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), historical background, literary structure, and more.

Being able to answer every question from within one organization's interpretive system hardly amounts to "mastering" the Bible. Even Paul says this:

>! For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
>! — 1 Corinthians 13:12 (KJV)

Even the apostle Paul confessed, "I know in part." The very claim to have completely mastered the Bible in this life does not fit what the Bible teaches.

## What It Would Take for Passing an Exam to Prove the Truth

For an exam to serve as evidence of truth, its answers would have to be independently verifiable, apart from the body that wrote it. If the answers are accepted as correct only inside Shincheonji, they show the results of internal training and nothing more. They do not prove objective truth.

## Summary

The Shincheonji Bible exam measures how well someone has memorized Shincheonji's interpretive system. Mastering one interpretive system is not the same as mastering the Bible. Claiming complete mastery of a Bible about which even the apostle Paul confessed "I know in part" does not fit the Bible's own teaching.
selfCheckQuestions: Does the Shincheonji Bible exam measure understanding of the Bible, or memorization of Shincheonji's interpretive system?
In 1 Corinthians 13:12, how does Paul assess his own knowledge?
If the answers on an exam are correct only within the body that wrote it, what does that signify?
What conditions would have to be met before anyone could claim mastery of the Bible?
Does a large number of people passing prove that a doctrine is true?

10-02.title: Is Memorizing Fixed Answers Evidence of Truth?
10-02.description: A look at what it means for testing the truth that the answers on the Shincheonji exam are fixed in advance.
10-02.content:
## The Question to Ask First

If the examiners settle the correct answers in advance and the candidates must memorize them, what does passing actually prove?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji uses its own Bible exams to check how well members understand the Bible. Passing, it says, means a person has understood the Bible correctly, and that is evidence that Shincheonji's teaching is the true truth.

## How Fixed Answers Work

The Shincheonji Bible exam includes multiple-choice and written-answer questions. Every answer, however, is exactly what was taught in the Shincheonji curriculum. For a question such as "What are the sun, moon, and stars in Revelation?" only the answer Shincheonji has settled on counts as correct.

In this setup, what the exam proves is not "this person has understood the Bible" but "this person has accurately memorized what Shincheonji teaches."

## The Internal Consistency of a Closed System

Any interpretive system can produce answers that are consistent on their own terms. The Quran in Islam also comes with an internally consistent interpretive system, so an exam written within that system would have fixed correct answers, and candidates could pass it. Yet passing a Quran exam does not prove that Islam is the truth.

In the same way, passing an exam taken within Shincheonji's interpretive system does not prove whether Shincheonji's doctrine is true. Internal consistency may be a necessary condition for truth, but it is not a sufficient one.

## How the Bible Says to Test the Truth

>! Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God:
>! — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)

John tells us not to accept things unquestioningly but to "try the spirits." Discernment is not memorizing fixed answers; it is the ability to judge for yourself.

>! These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:11 (KJV)

The Bereans checked the Scriptures independently, asking "whether those things were so," even about Paul's teaching. That is the Bible's own model for testing the truth.

## Summary

Memorizing fixed answers and passing an exam proves that someone has completed a course of instruction, not that the content is true. Any closed system can produce an internally consistent exam. The Bible calls for independent discernment and searching of the Scriptures.
selfCheckQuestions: Does the Shincheonji exam measure understanding of the Bible, or memorization of what was taught?
Is a high degree of internal consistency in itself evidence of truth?
Is there any structural difference between the exam systems of other religions and Shincheonji's exam system?
How did the Bereans in Acts 17:11 test the truth?
What does the command to "try the spirits" in 1 John 4:1 require?

10-03.title: Can the Shincheonji Bible Exam Be Verified from the Outside?
10-03.description: A look at whether the answers on the Shincheonji exam can be independently verified by anyone outside Shincheonji.
10-03.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Could someone who has never been taught by Shincheonji arrive at the same answers on the Shincheonji Bible exam using the Bible alone?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji says that because its answers are grounded in the Bible, anyone can confirm them from the Bible. The reasoning is that anyone who reads the Bible correctly will inevitably arrive at Shincheonji's interpretation.

## The Standard for Outside Verification

If a claim is objectively true, it should be possible to verify it independently of the person making it. In science, experimental results are trusted because other researchers can repeat the same experiment and get the same results.

If the answers on the Shincheonji exam are the truth, a Bible scholar who has never been taught by Shincheonji should be able to reach the same answers from the Bible alone. In practice, however, Shincheonji's particular interpretations (for example, its table matching each symbol in Revelation to its meaning) cannot be derived without Shincheonji's instruction.

## The Problem of Circular Reasoning

Saying "If you read the Bible correctly, you will reach Shincheonji's answers," and then saying "If you don't reach Shincheonji's answers, you haven't read it correctly," is circular reasoning.

- Premise: Our interpretation is correct
- Evidence: The Bible supports our interpretation
- Response to objections: Anyone who disagrees has not read it correctly

Within this structure of logic, refutation is impossible. Whatever objection is raised, the answer always comes back to "you haven't read it correctly."

>! Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
>! — 1 Corinthians 11:1 (KJV)

Paul did tell people to follow him, but his grounds were that he himself was following Christ. Paul's teaching could also be tested by whether it agreed with Christ, and the Bereans did exactly that (Acts 17:11).

## The Conditions for a Verifiable Interpretation

Healthy interpretation of the Bible allows for:
- Independent confirmation through analysis of the original languages
- Checking the context against the historical background
- Cross-checking with other passages of Scripture
- Questions and discussion about the interpretation

It is worth checking for yourself whether Shincheonji's answers can pass this kind of independent verification.

## Summary

Objective truth must be independently verifiable. If no one can reach the same answers without Shincheonji's instruction, those answers are most likely Shincheonji's own interpretation rather than the objective meaning of the Bible. To avoid being trapped in circular reasoning, outside verification is necessary.
selfCheckQuestions: Can the answers on the Shincheonji exam be derived from the Bible alone, without Shincheonji's instruction?
Why is the claim "If you read correctly, you will reach our answers" an example of circular reasoning?
If even Paul's teaching was subject to testing, can Shincheonji's teaching be an exception?
Can answers that cannot be verified from the outside be called objective truth?

10-04.title: Who Decides That Someone Has Added to or Taken from Revelation?
10-04.description: A look at the grounds on which Shincheonji labels the established churches as "those who have added to or taken from Revelation," and at whether its standard of judgment holds up.
10-04.content:
## The Question to Ask First

To whom does the warning against adding to or taking from Revelation apply, and by what standard do we decide whether someone has done so?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji quotes Revelation 22:18-19 and accuses the established churches of adding to and taking from the words of Revelation. Its reasoning is that failing to interpret Revelation correctly is itself adding and taking away.

>! For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book: And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.
>! — Revelation 22:18-19 (KJV)

## What "Adding and Taking Away" Originally Meant

In this passage, to "add" and to "take away" mean tampering with the text of Revelation itself. In the ancient world it was common practice to put a warning at the end of a document saying that its contents must not be altered. Deuteronomy 4:2 contains the same kind of warning.

>! Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
>! — Deuteronomy 4:2 (KJV)

"Interpreting differently" and "adding to or taking from the text" have to be kept distinct. The established churches have never tampered with the text of Revelation.

## Who Is Doing the Judging?

Who decides that "the established churches have added to and taken from it"? Shincheonji does. Yet Shincheonji's own interpretation is not the literal meaning of Revelation either; it is a symbolic reinterpretation. For example, Shincheonji interprets the heaven, earth, sun, moon, and stars of Revelation as particular people or organizations.

If "interpreting differently is adding and taking away," then Shincheonji's symbolic interpretation has itself "added" meanings that are not in the text. Applied consistently, this standard leaves Shincheonji open to exactly the same criticism.

## Summary

The warning in Revelation 22:18-19 against adding and taking away is about tampering with the text, not a ban on differing interpretations. If differences of interpretation are to be labeled "adding and taking away," that standard must apply equally to Shincheonji's own interpretation.
selfCheckQuestions: In Revelation 22:18-19, does "adding and taking away" mean tampering with the text, or differences of interpretation?
In what context was the similar warning in Deuteronomy 4:2 given?
Have the established churches ever tampered with the text of Revelation itself?
Could Shincheonji's symbolic interpretation also fall under the standard of "adding and taking away"?
If the standard for judging that someone has "added or taken away" is one's own interpretation, is that a fair judgment?

10-05.title: Are the Existing Churches Really Unable to Explain Revelation?
10-05.description: A historical and scholarly check on the claim that only Shincheonji can explain Revelation.
10-05.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Are the established churches and the world of theology really unable to explain the book of Revelation at all?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji claims that the established churches cannot explain Revelation. Only the promised pastor, Chairman Lee Man-hee, it says, has seen and can deliver the actual fulfillment (silsang) of Revelation, and this is why Shincheonji is true.

## Checking the Historical Facts

Revelation has been studied in depth throughout the whole history of Christianity. From Irenaeus in the second century to scholars today, a vast body of commentary and research has built up.

There are four main schools of interpretation of Revelation.

- **Preterism**: sees Revelation as dealing with events of the first century
- **Historicism**: sees it as unfolding across the whole history of the church
- **Futurism**: sees most of its contents as events that will happen in the future
- **Idealism**: sees it as setting out the principles of the timeless struggle between good and evil

Each school interprets Revelation systematically, with its own grounds and reasoning. The claim that "no one can explain it" is simply not true.

## "Explaining" Versus "Interpreting the Shincheonji Way"

When Shincheonji says others "cannot explain" Revelation, what it really means is that they "explain it differently from Shincheonji." Interpreting differently and being unable to explain are entirely different things.

The Bible itself allows for some diversity of interpretation. Peter says this about Paul's letters:

>! in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
>! — 2 Peter 3:16 (KJV)

Peter acknowledges that there are "some things hard to be understood" in Paul's writings. It is natural for the Bible to have difficult parts, and that does not justify one organization claiming an exclusive right to interpret it.

## Summary

The established churches and scholars have studied Revelation through a variety of methods for 2,000 years. The claim that "no one can explain it" is an exaggerated way of saying "they interpret it differently from us." The fact that Revelation has difficult parts is no basis for one organization holding an exclusive right of interpretation.
selfCheckQuestions: Have you ever heard of the four schools of interpretation of Revelation?
Can you tell the difference between "cannot explain it" and "interprets it differently"?
What does Peter acknowledge in 2 Peter 3:16?
What assumption lies behind the claim that only one organization can interpret Revelation correctly?
What evidence would be needed to invalidate 2,000 years of study of Revelation?

10-06.title: Is Everyone Who Interprets Differently a False Pastor?
10-06.description: An examination of whether the claim that anyone who interprets the Bible differently from Shincheonji is a false pastor holds up biblically.
10-06.content:
## The Question to Ask First

If someone understands the Bible differently from Shincheonji's interpretation, does that automatically make them a false pastor?

## What Shincheonji Claims

Shincheonji teaches that only its own interpretation is correct and that pastors who interpret differently are false pastors. Since Shincheonji is the only place where the Bible is interpreted correctly, the reasoning goes, following teaching from anywhere else leads to destruction.

## The Early Church Had Differences of Interpretation Too

In the Bible we see differences of opinion even among the apostles.

>! But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
>! — Galatians 2:11 (KJV)

When Peter (Cephas) acted wrongly, Paul opposed him to his face. At the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15, too, there was "no small dissension and disputation" (Acts 15:2) over whether Gentiles had to keep the law.

The fact that the apostles differed did not make one side false pastors. They discussed the matter and reached agreement.

## The Biblical Standard for a False Pastor

The Bible's standard for a false pastor, or false prophet, is not "interpreting differently."

>! And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the LORD hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken,
>! — Deuteronomy 18:21-22 (KJV)

The key mark of a false prophet is that "the thing follow not, nor come to pass." Jesus also told us to discern false prophets by their "fruits."

>! Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
>! — Matthew 7:16 (KJV)

Here "fruits" means the character of a person's life and the results of their doctrine, not the size of their organization.

## Telling Diversity of Interpretation Apart from Core Truth

Throughout the history of Christianity, a distinction has been drawn between core doctrines (the deity of Jesus, atonement on the cross, the resurrection, the second coming) and non-core interpretations (how to read the symbols of Revelation, the timing of the millennium, and so on). Departing from core doctrine is a serious problem, but differences of interpretation in non-core areas are natural.

If every difference of interpretation is labeled the work of "false pastors," we can no longer account for the differences among the apostles themselves.

## Summary

Even the apostles of the early church differed in interpretation and practice, and that did not make one side false pastors. The Bible's standard for a false prophet is not "a difference of interpretation" but "prophecy that does not come to pass" and "fruits." Labeling every difference of interpretation as false departs from the Bible's own standard.
selfCheckQuestions: In Galatians 2:11, was the conflict between Paul and Peter caused by one of them being a false pastor?
Is the Bible's standard for a false prophet "a difference of interpretation" or "prophecy that does not come to pass"?
Do the "fruits" in Matthew 7:16 mean the size of an organization?
Why is the distinction between core doctrine and non-core interpretation important?
In Acts 15, how were the apostles' differences of opinion resolved?
sources: The Bible (KJV): Galatians 2:11, Acts 15:2, Deuteronomy 18:21-22, Matthew 7:16

11-01.title: "Refute Us Using the Bible Alone"
11-01.description: An analysis of what the demand to "refute us from the Bible" assumes, and a look at what testing a claim by the Bible actually means.
11-01.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is the demand to "refute us using the Bible alone" a fair one? What does it assume?

## Shincheonji's Objection

People on the Shincheonji side often challenge critics: "Refute us using the Bible alone." In other words, respond only with the text of Scripture, not with human ideas or theological theories. On the surface, this demand sounds entirely reasonable.

## The Hidden Assumption Behind the Demand

But this demand hides an important assumption. "Refute us using the Bible alone" may in fact mean "refute us from within Shincheonji's system of biblical interpretation."

It is a bit like being asked to refute a move in the game of go using the rules of chess. Both seem to be played on the same kind of board, but if the rules themselves differ, no real communication takes place. The heart of the issue is not whether we use the Bible but **how we read** it.

## We Do Use the Bible

The established churches also base their criticism on the Bible. Every article in this series offers Bible verses as its evidence. Both sides use the Bible; the difference lies in how they interpret it.

>! Understandest thou what thou readest?
>! — Acts 8:30 (KJV)

Philip's question to the Ethiopian eunuch puts its finger on exactly this point. People can read the same Bible and understand it differently. That is why the method and principles of interpretation matter.

## Interpretive Method Is the Key

Healthy interpretation of the Bible follows a few principles.
- **Context**: Read each verse within the passage around it
- **Original languages**: Check the meaning of the Hebrew and Greek
- **Historical background**: Take into account the situation at the time of writing
- **Harmony with the whole Bible**: Bring each verse into harmony with the rest of Scripture

These principles do not belong to any particular denomination. They are universal tools for reading the Bible honestly. The answer to the demand to "refute us using the Bible alone" is simple: we do use the Bible. We simply take its context, original languages, and historical background into account as well.

## Summary

The demand to "refute us using the Bible alone" sounds reasonable, but in practice it may mean "refute us within our own interpretive framework." The key is not whether the Bible is used but the method of interpretation. Reading the Bible with attention to context, original languages, and historical background is the most honest way to use it.
selfCheckQuestions: What does the demand to "refute us using the Bible alone" assume?
Why can people read the same Bible and still interpret it differently?
What are some of the principles of healthy biblical interpretation?
What problems arise if one ignores differences in interpretive method and simply insists on "the Bible alone"?
What does Philip's question in Acts 8:30 suggest?

11-02.title: "How Can You Know If You Have Never Even Been to Shincheonji?"
11-02.description: A look at whether the objection "You can't know unless you come and see for yourself" holds up logically.
11-02.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Does a person have to join a group in order to evaluate its doctrine?

## Shincheonji's Objection

People on the Shincheonji side push back: "How can you judge without coming and hearing it for yourself?" The claim is that you cannot know without experiencing it, and that judgments from outsiders are unfair.

## The Problem with This Objection

What happens if we apply this logic consistently? If we could judge a religion or group only by joining it, we could in practice judge nothing at all. By the same standard, Shincheonji should not be able to say anything about the doctrines of Islam, Buddhism, or Hinduism without having joined them.

This logic can also lead to dangerous results. You do not have to eat a food to find out whether it causes food poisoning. An analysis of its ingredients is enough to tell.

## Shincheonji's Teaching Is Publicly Available

Shincheonji's doctrine can be checked thoroughly through publicly available material.
- Chairman Lee Man-hee's public sermons and books
- Doctrinal explanations on Shincheonji's official website
- Testimony and teaching materials from former members
- Textbooks published by Shincheonji itself

Doctrine exists in written form, and written texts can be read and analyzed. "Experience" is not a prerequisite for judging whether a doctrine is true.

## The Bible's Way of Testing

>! Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
>! — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV)

Paul says to "prove all things." This testing does not assume that one has joined anything. It tests things in light of biblical principles.

>! Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
>! — Matthew 7:15 (KJV)

Jesus told us to beware of false prophets, not to go and join their following to see for ourselves.

## Summary

Whether a doctrine is true can be judged from public material and biblical principles. Joining is not a requirement for judging. Applied consistently, this logic would require joining every group, which would make any judgment impossible. The Bible calls for testing that does not presuppose membership.
selfCheckQuestions: Can the logic of "you have to come and see to know" be applied to other religions as well?
Is there material from outside sources that can be used to check Shincheonji's doctrine?
Does the "proving" in 1 Thessalonians 5:21 presuppose joining?
In Matthew 7:15, how did Jesus tell us to respond to false prophets?
Are there cases in which the truth of a doctrine cannot be judged by textual analysis alone?

11-03.title: "Don't the Established Churches Have Plenty of Problems Too?"
11-03.description: An examination of whether the objection that "the established churches have problems too" proves that Shincheonji's doctrine is legitimate.
11-03.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is the fact that the established churches have problems evidence that Shincheonji's doctrine is true?

## Shincheonji's Objection

When criticized, people on the Shincheonji side shoot back, "Don't the established churches have plenty of problems too?" They point to misconduct by pastors, church disputes, the handing down of pulpits from father to son, and so on, and ask whether churches like that have any right to criticize Shincheonji.

## A Logical Fallacy: Tu Quoque

This is a logical fallacy known as the "tu quoque fallacy" (Latin for "you too"). It tries to neutralize criticism of oneself by pointing out the other side's weaknesses.

For example, saying "You've sped before, so don't call me out for speeding" is no evidence that speeding is right. The critic's weaknesses are a separate matter from whether the criticism is true.

## We Acknowledge the Problems of the Established Churches

It is a fact that the established churches have problems, and we have no intention of denying it. The Bible itself faces the problems of the church squarely.

>! thou hast left thy first love. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works;
>! — Revelation 2:4-5 (KJV)

Jesus pointed out the problems in the church at Ephesus. But His remedy was not "move to a different organization." It was "repent."

## Each Claim Must Be Tested on Its Own

The fact that the established churches have problems does not automatically lead to these conclusions:
- Shincheonji's doctrine is true
- Chairman Lee Man-hee is the promised pastor
- Revelation is being fulfilled in Shincheonji

Each of these claims must be tested on its own. The problems of the established churches are the established churches' problems, and whether Shincheonji's doctrine is true is a separate question.

## Summary

It is true that the established churches have problems, but that does not prove Shincheonji's doctrine is true. Pointing out the other side's weaknesses to neutralize criticism of oneself is a logical fallacy. Each claim must be tested on its own.
selfCheckQuestions: Are the problems of the established churches logically related to whether Shincheonji's doctrine is true?
What is the "tu quoque fallacy," and how does it apply to this objection?
What remedy did Jesus offer in Revelation 2:4-5?
Is it possible to acknowledge the problems of the established churches and still test Shincheonji's doctrine?
Do a critic's weaknesses affect whether the criticism is true?

11-04.title: "Look at the Fruit and You Will See That Shincheonji Is Real"
11-04.description: An examination of whether Shincheonji's presentation of its organizational growth as "fruit" agrees with what the Bible means by fruit.
11-04.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Are an organization's growth and its members' devotion the kind of "fruit" that proves its doctrine is true?

## Shincheonji's Objection

Shincheonji points to its rapid growth, its members' passionate devotion, the number of people passing its Bible exams, and so on as its "fruit." Since Jesus said in Matthew 7 that we would know people "by their fruits," it argues, this good fruit is evidence that Shincheonji is the true church.

## The "Fruit" Jesus Spoke Of

>! Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Ye shall know them by their fruits.
>! — Matthew 7:15-16 (KJV)

In this context, "fruits" are the standard for discerning false prophets. And the words that follow make the meaning of fruit even clearer.

>! Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
>! — Matthew 7:21-22 (KJV)

Remarkably, even people who prophesied, cast out devils, and did wonderful works are turned away. Outward activity and results are not the essence of fruit.

## Growth Is Not Evidence of Truth

If rapid growth were evidence of truth, then every religion and movement in history that grew quickly would have to be true. Islam grew explosively in the seventh century, and Mormonism also has a history of rapid growth. The speed of growth has nothing to do with whether a doctrine is true.

The fruit of the Spirit that Paul speaks of points to something else.

>! But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance:
>! — Galatians 5:22-23 (KJV)

The fruit of the Spirit is personal character, not the size of an organization.

## Summary

The "fruit" the Bible speaks of is character in one's life and obedience to God's will. It does not refer to organizational growth or outward results. In fact, Matthew 7 warns that even people with outward results can be turned away. The reasoning that growth equals evidence of truth has no support in the Bible.
selfCheckQuestions: In what context are "fruits" mentioned in Matthew 7:15-16?
In Matthew 7:21-22, why were people with outward results turned away?
What does the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23 refer to?
If rapid growth is evidence of truth, are other fast-growing religions true as well?
Is there a necessary connection between the size of an organization and the truth of its doctrine?

11-05.title: "Being Persecuted Is Proof That We Are True"
11-05.description: An examination of whether being persecuted proves that a doctrine is true, and of what the Bible means by persecution.
11-05.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Does the mere fact of being persecuted prove that a doctrine is true?

## Shincheonji's Objection

Shincheonji interprets public criticism and being labeled a heresy as "persecution," and claims that this is evidence of the true church. Jesus and the early church were persecuted too, the reasoning goes, so Shincheonji, which is persecuted, must be the true church.

## The Relationship Between Persecution and Truth

Persecution is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for truth.

Paul says that a godly life brings persecution with it.

>! Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
>! — 2 Timothy 3:12 (KJV)

But this verse does not mean that "everyone who is persecuted is in the truth." You cannot flip the statement that the godly are persecuted and conclude that everyone who is persecuted is godly. In logic, "If A, then B" does not mean "If B, then A."

## Many Groups Are Persecuted

Throughout history, a great many religious groups have been persecuted.
- Jehovah's Witnesses are persecuted in various countries
- The Unification Church has faced public criticism since its founding
- Scientology faces sanctions in a number of countries

If persecution were evidence of the true church, all of these groups would have to be true. But their doctrines contradict one another, so persecution alone cannot identify the truth.

## The Causes of Persecution Must Be Distinguished

Persecution has many causes. There is persecution suffered for the sake of the truth, and there is criticism received because of wrongdoing. Peter draws this distinction too.

>! But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed;
>! — 1 Peter 4:15-16 (KJV)

Criticism received for wrongdoing is not persecution. We need to distinguish whether the criticism Shincheonji receives is because of its doctrine, or because of its recruiting methods and deceptive approaches (such as recruiting while concealing its identity).

## Summary

Being persecuted does not automatically prove that a doctrine is true. Many groups are persecuted, and persecution has many causes. The Bible also distinguishes between suffering for the truth and criticism received for wrongdoing.
selfCheckQuestions: Can the logic of 2 Timothy 3:12 be applied in reverse? (Does being persecuted mean one is godly?)
Are all the other religious groups that are persecuted also true?
What are the two kinds of suffering that Peter distinguishes in 1 Peter 4:15-16?
Is the main cause of the criticism Shincheonji receives its doctrine, or its recruiting methods?

11-06.title: "Even Jesus Was Called a Heretic in His Day"
11-06.description: A look at whether the comparison with Jesus being called a heretic holds up logically, and whether Jesus' situation and Shincheonji's are really the same.
11-06.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Does the fact that Jesus was rejected by the religious leaders of His day justify every group that is called a heresy today?

## Shincheonji's Objection

Shincheonji says, "Even Jesus was called a heretic in His day and was crucified," and claims that being called a heresy puts it in the same situation as Jesus. The reasoning is that the real truth is always opposed by established religion.

## What This Comparison Would Need

To put Jesus and Shincheonji on the same level, Shincheonji would need the same kind of evidence that Jesus had.

In the case of Jesus:
- Specific fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy (the place, time, and manner of His birth, and more)
- Visible miracles (healing the sick, raising the dead, miracles over nature)
- Bodily resurrection after death, with more than five hundred eyewitnesses

>! If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not. But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works:
>! — John 10:37-38 (KJV)

Jesus offered evidence to back up His claims. He did not say, "Just take My word for it." He said, "Look at the works and judge for yourselves."

## The Comparison Assumes What It Needs to Prove

The comparison "Jesus was called a heretic too, so we are true" already assumes, logically, that "we stand in the same position as Jesus." But that is the very claim that needs to be proved.

Any group called a heresy can use this reasoning. The leader of a cult can say, "Jesus was rejected too," and so can the founder of an entirely different religion. This reasoning on its own justifies no group at all.

## The Key Question

What matters is not "Is it called a heresy?" but "Is there evidence to back up its claims?" Jesus offered the evidence of fulfilled prophecy, miracles, and the resurrection. The question that remains is whether Shincheonji can offer evidence of equal weight.

## Summary

The fact that Jesus was called a heretic does not justify every group that is called a heresy today. This comparison already assumes that "we are like Jesus," and that is precisely the point that needs to be proved. Jesus offered objective evidence to back up His claims.
selfCheckQuestions: What evidence did Jesus offer to back up His claims?
What does the comparison "Even Jesus was called a heretic" assume?
Could this reasoning be applied to other groups as well?
In John 10:37-38, what standard of judgment did Jesus ask for?
Is there a necessary connection between being rejected and a doctrine being true?

11-07.title: "Shincheonji's Teaching Is the Most Biblical"
11-07.description: A look at whether the claim to be "the most biblical" is circular reasoning, and whether there is any standard by which the claim can be tested.
11-07.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Does the claim "Our interpretation is the most biblical" prove anything in and of itself?

## Shincheonji's Objection
