Shincheonji claims that its teaching is more biblical than that of any other church. It says it interprets the parables of the Bible one by one with perfect clarity and delivers a word that cannot be heard anywhere else.

## The Structure of Circular Reasoning

When this claim is analyzed, the following structure emerges.

1. "Our interpretation is the most biblical."
2. On what grounds? "Because the Bible says so."
3. Who decided that the Bible says so? "We did."

This is circular reasoning: a structure in which one's own interpretation is offered as the grounds for one's own interpretation. Any group can claim that its own interpretation is the most correct and use exactly the same structure of reasoning.

## A Standard for Testing Is Needed

To find out whether a claim is true, we need a standard for testing it from the outside.

>! searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
>! — Acts 17:11 (KJV)

The Bereans searched the Scriptures to see "whether those things were so" in Paul's teaching. They tested it against the text of Scripture itself, not against Paul's interpretive framework.

Questions for testing:
- Is this interpretation natural within its context?
- Does it agree with the meaning of the original languages?
- Does it avoid contradicting other parts of the Bible?
- How many assumptions are needed to arrive at this interpretation?
- Could someone reach the same conclusion without Shincheonji's instruction?

## The Trap of "Clarity"

It is understandable that Shincheonji's interpretation feels "clear." When every symbol is matched to an exact counterpart, it feels as though one has a sure answer. But clarity is not the same as accuracy. A wrong answer can be perfectly clear too.

## Summary

Any group can claim to be "the most biblical," and the claim proves nothing by itself. To escape circular reasoning, an independent standard for testing is needed. A clear answer is not necessarily a correct one.
selfCheckQuestions: If the grounds for the claim "Our interpretation is the most biblical" turn out to be the same interpretation, is this circular reasoning?
Could other groups make the same claim?
By what standard did the Bereans in Acts 17:11 test what they heard?
Is a clear interpretation necessarily an accurate one?
Can truth be established through internal claims alone, without outside testing?

11-08.title: "People Who Leave Had Problems to Begin With"
11-08.description: A look at whether personal attacks on former members hold up logically, and whether this approach reflects a healthy community.
11-08.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is labeling people who have left Shincheonji as "people who had problems to begin with" a legitimate rebuttal?

## Shincheonji's Objection

Within Shincheonji there is a tendency to characterize those who leave as people who "never had enough faith," "had something wrong in their hearts," or "still clung to worldly things." The claim is that former members' testimony cannot be trusted and that their criticism stems from personal grievances.

## The Ad Hominem Fallacy

This is the "ad hominem fallacy." Instead of answering the substance of someone's argument, it tries to neutralize the argument by attacking the person's character or condition.

What kind of person a former member was and whether their criticism is valid are two separate questions. Saying "This person had problems" does nothing to refute the substance of the criticism.

## A Structure That Discourages Leaving

When former members are labeled negatively, current members receive a powerful message. The fear that "if I leave, I'll be talked about like that too" discourages them from raising questions or leaving.

A healthy community does not threaten or slander people who leave. Decisions of faith are made according to each person's conscience and deserve respect.

>! Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
>! — Romans 14:1 (KJV)

## The Reality of Former Members

Among those who have left Shincheonji are senior figures who served devotedly for many years, including leaders, instructors, and people at the level of tribe leader. It is hard to label all of them as people who "had problems to begin with." If they did have problems, Shincheonji would need to explain how they were able to rise to high positions within it.

If a consistent pattern shows up across the testimony of former members, that is a sign of a structural problem rather than an individual one.

## Summary

Attacking former members personally does not refute the substance of their criticism. This approach plants a fear of leaving in current members. A healthy community does not slander those who leave; it answers the substance of the criticism raised.
selfCheckQuestions: Does attacking a former member's character count as a rebuttal of their criticism?
What effect does portraying former members negatively have on current members?
If someone who held a high position leaves, is "they had problems to begin with" an adequate explanation?
How does a healthy community treat people who leave?
What attitude does Paul urge in Romans 14:1?

11-09.title: "The Doctrine Didn't Change; It Was Opened"
11-09.description: A look at whether explaining doctrinal changes as an "opening" holds up logically, and whether this explanation can ever be falsified.
11-09.content:
## The Question to Ask First

When Shincheonji's doctrine changes, is the explanation "It didn't change; it was opened" one that can be tested?

## Shincheonji's Objection

When doctrinal changes are pointed out, Shincheonji explains that "what had not yet been opened has now been opened." Using the idea of "progressive revelation," or "a word opened when the time came," it argues that the earlier teaching was not wrong; it simply had not yet been fully revealed.

## The Problem of Unfalsifiability

The biggest problem is that this explanation can justify any change at all.

- If doctrine A was taught and then changed to B: "A was in a state of not yet being opened, and now B has been opened."
- If B is later changed to C: "B had not been fully opened either, and now C has been opened."

Within this structure, no change can ever be an error. Whatever change happens in the future, it can always be explained as something "opened." As the philosopher of science Karl Popper argued, a claim that cannot be falsified is not a meaningful claim.

## The Status of Earlier Teaching

If the earlier teaching was something "not yet opened," then at the time it was given, an incomplete teaching was being delivered as settled truth. The faith of the members who believed and followed the earlier doctrine was, in effect, built on something incomplete.

And if the doctrine taught now could also be "opened" further in the future, we are left asking how confidently anyone can follow the present teaching.

## The Nature of Truth According to the Bible

>! Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life:
>! — John 14:6 (KJV)

Jesus declared that He Himself is the truth. The truth does not change.

>! Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
>! — Hebrews 13:8 (KJV)

If truth grounded in Christ were something changeable that "opens and closes," it would be hard to reconcile with the words "the same ... for ever."

## Summary

The explanation "It didn't change; it was opened" is an unfalsifiable structure that can justify any change. If the earlier teaching was incomplete, the foundation of the faith of members at the time is shaken, and the current doctrine is not safe from being "opened" again in the future either.
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any change that could not be justified by the explanation that it was "opened"?
If the earlier doctrine was taught as settled truth, what does a change mean?
If the current doctrine could also be "opened" in the future, what is today's confidence based on?
Is "the same ... for ever" in Hebrews 13:8 compatible with doctrinal change?
Why is an unfalsifiable claim a problem?

11-10.title: "We Didn't Say It Because the Time Had Not Yet Come"
11-10.description: A look at what logical function the explanation "We didn't say it because the time had not yet come" serves, and at how the Bible describes the way God reveals Himself.
11-10.content:
## The Question to Ask First

Is it a testable explanation to say that something was not taught, or was taught differently, in the past "because the time had not yet come"?

## Shincheonji's Objection

When past and present teachings differ, Shincheonji explains that "we didn't say it because the time had not yet come." Since God opens His word according to His timing, it argues, anything not made known earlier was simply not yet due.

## How Convenient This Explanation Is

This is an extremely convenient line of reasoning that can justify any inconsistency in the past.

- If A was said in the past but B is correct: "When we said A, the time had not yet come."
- If something never mentioned before is now being taught: "The time came, and it was opened."
- If a past prophecy proved wrong: "It was not yet the time."

Within this structure of reasoning, no mistake by the leader can ever count as a mistake. Everything is explained by "God's timetable."

## How the Bible Says God Reveals Himself

The Bible says that God makes things known before He acts.

>! Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
>! — Amos 3:7 (KJV)

God, it says, reveals His plans to the prophets before He acts. The explanation "we didn't say it because the time had not yet come" stands in tension with this principle. If the promised pastor were a true prophet, God would have made the important matters known to him in advance.

## Explaining After the Fact Versus Prophesying Beforehand

True prophecy makes something known specifically before it happens. Explaining after an event that "it was always meant to turn out that way" is not prophecy; it is after-the-fact interpretation.

>! And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.
>! — John 14:29 (KJV)

Jesus said, "I have told you before it come to pass." Telling beforehand and explaining afterward are fundamentally different.

## Summary

The explanation "we didn't say it because the time had not yet come" is a structure that can justify every past inconsistency after the fact. The Bible says that God makes things known before He acts. Prophecy given beforehand and explanation offered afterward must be kept distinct.
selfCheckQuestions: Is there any inconsistency that could not be justified by saying "the time had not yet come"?
What is the principle of God's revelation in Amos 3:7?
What is the difference between prophecy given beforehand and explanation offered afterward?
What did Jesus mean in John 14:29 when He said, "I have told you before it come to pass"?
Within this structure of explanation, is there any case in which a mistake by the leader could be admitted?

11-11.title: "Dates and People May Have Changed, but the Reality Was There"
11-11.description: An examination, in light of why things were changed and of the standard of Scripture, of the claim that it does not matter if specific dates and people changed, because the reality behind the actual fulfillment of Revelation was there.
11-11.content:
## The Question to Ask First

When it is pointed out that the dates or people in the actual fulfillment (silsang) have changed, Shincheonji answers, "The small details don't matter. What matters is that the reality was there." That raises a question. Does the mere fact that something real existed allow us to say it was fulfilled according to the Bible?

## Shincheonji's Objection

When doctrinal changes or discrepancies in dates are pointed out, the explanation commonly heard from the Shincheonji side goes roughly like this:

- Details such as dates and people can shift a little over time.
- Just as no one remembers every lunch they ate a week ago, the dates of things that happened long ago can get mixed up.
- What matters is that the events of Revelation actually took place on this earth, in other words, that **there was a reality behind them**.

> The points above summarize explanations heard repeatedly in counseling. The original wording in official Shincheonji materials is **(to be verified)**.

This objection should not be brushed aside. "The details may be wrong, but the big picture is right" sounds reasonable, and human memory really does have its limits. So we will check two things in turn: what changed and why, and what the existence of a reality actually proves.

## 1. Were the Changes Really "Small Details"?

### Was It a Date Anyone Could Forget?

The lunch analogy fits the small memories of everyday life. But the dates Shincheonji speaks of are of a different kind. They are days that mark the starting point of the faith, such as the day the little book of Revelation 10 was received. People rarely forget the days that changed their lives, like a birthday or a wedding anniversary. That is all the more true of a day on which someone professes to have received revelation directly from God.

### When and Why Did It Change?

In counseling, people explain that this date was changed after it was pointed out that it did not fit the calculation of the seventy weeks in Daniel 9.

> The dates before and after the change, when the change was made, and the material in which the problem was pointed out are **(to be verified)**. If the editions of the textbooks and the dates of the sermons can be compared, this section will be supplemented with documentation.

If this account is true, the date did not change because memory faded. It was corrected to answer an outside objection that the calculation did not add up. In that case, the "lunch" analogy fails to explain why the change was made.

### Can Content Received by Revelation Be Corrected?

Shincheonji explains that this content was received by revelation, not through human study. There is also an account that Chairman Lee Man-hee heard it directly, as if in a question-and-answer exchange with the Holy Spirit (original source **to be verified**).

That raises a question. When the first explanation and the revised one differ, which of the two was the revelation?

- If the first date was the revelation, Shincheonji needs to explain why it was changed.
- If the revised date was the revelation, Shincheonji needs to explain where the first date came from.
- Shincheonji regards the objections of cult counseling centers as words that do not belong to God. If the revelation was corrected in response to such objections, we cannot avoid asking what it was that corrected the revelation.

>! God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent:
>! — Numbers 23:19 (KJV)

The Bible says that God's word does not get revised the way human words do. If the content came from God, it should have been right from the start; if it had to be corrected, we need to check again where it came from.

## 2. If There Is a Reality, Does That Mean It Happened According to the Bible?

### An Actual Fulfillment Can Be Manufactured

"There was a reality behind it" sounds compelling. But organizations, people, and events can all be created at will. Gather twelve people and call each of them a tribe leader, and outwardly you have something shaped like twelve tribes. The mere existence of that shape is no evidence that it is the very thing the Bible spoke of.

### The Key Is Matching the Blueprint

>! See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
>! — Hebrews 8:5 (KJV)

When Moses built the tabernacle, the standard was not "Is there a tabernacle?" but "Was it built according to the pattern God showed?" A building may be standing, but if it differs from the blueprint, no one calls it the building in that blueprint.

The same goes for the actual fulfillment. Rather than asking whether there is a reality, we have to ask whether that reality came about according to the text of the Bible. If dates and people had to be corrected again and again because they did not match the biblical record, that in itself may be a sign that they did not match the blueprint.

>! When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken,
>! — Deuteronomy 18:22 (KJV)

### Who Stands at the Center?

If the Bible is the blueprint, then the center of that blueprint is Jesus Christ (John 5:39). If, the more the actual fulfillment is explained, the experiences and testimony of one particular person become more important than Jesus Christ, it is worth calmly reconsidering which blueprint that reality was built from.

## Summary

The objection "Dates and people may have changed, but the reality was there" calls for checking two things. First, whether the changed date was the result of fading memory or a revision made to answer an outside objection. If content said to have been received by revelation was corrected after being challenged, the source of that revelation must be questioned again. Second, the existence of a reality only means that something was built; it is not evidence that it came about according to the Bible. The standard of judgment is not whether a reality exists but whether it matches the blueprint, which is the Bible.
selfCheckQuestions: Could anyone forget the day they received revelation from God the way they forget a lunch menu?
Have you ever compared when the date was changed with when the outside objection was raised?
Of the first explanation and the revised one, which was the revelation?
Is the existence of a reality evidence that something was fulfilled according to the Bible?
When the actual fulfillment is explained, who stands at the center: Jesus Christ, or the testimony of one particular person?
